Chapter 00

Accounting Basics Bootcamp

Learning outcome. After this bootcamp you will be able to read any transaction, name the accounts it touches, say what increased or decreased, and write the debit and credit.

What this chapter covers (official syllabus)

  • What is accounting
  • Why accounting is needed
  • Business transactions
  • Assets, Liabilities, Capital
  • Revenue, Expenses, Profit, Loss, Drawings
  • Accounting equation
  • Debit and Credit
  • Basic accounting rules
  • How transactions affect accounts

Meet Rahul. He is 24. He has saved ₹1,00,000 and he is opening a small stationery shop — pens, notebooks, files, copier paper — on a rented lane in Pune. He will call it Rahul Stationery. He has never kept books. This bootcamp starts at zero and walks with him, rupee by rupee, until you can read any transaction the way an accountant reads it.

You do not need any earlier chapter. You do not need commerce at school. If you can add and subtract, you can do this. Every number is shown. Nothing is skipped.

By the last page you will: (1) name the accounts a transaction touches, (2) say whether each account increased or decreased, (3) place the amount on the debit or the credit, (4) write the journal line, and (5) prove that the accounting equation still balances.

Key point

One shop. One owner. Ten transactions. Every idea in this bootcamp is hung on Rahul. When you later open a factory, a hospital, or a listed company, the same ten ideas still hold. Only the names of the accounts get longer.

1. What is accounting?

1. What is it? — Definition

Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and communicating money information about a business so that the owner and outsiders can take decisions.

2. In simple words

Accounting is the memory and the language of a business. It notices every rupee that comes in or goes out, writes it down under a proper name, totals it, and then tells a story: did we make a profit? what do we own? what do we owe?

3. Why do we need it?

Without accounting Rahul will forget, mix his personal spending with the shop, not know whether a notebook is sold at a profit, and have nothing to show a bank or the tax officer. Accounting turns a pile of bills into a picture of the shop.

4. Real-life example

Rahul sells a pack of pens for ₹150 cash. Accounting does not stop at “money came in”. It identifies that this is a sale, measures it at ₹150, records it in the cash book and the sales account, classifies it as income, summarises it with all other sales at month-end, analyses whether pens are a good line, and communicates the profit in a statement Rahul can read.

5. Accounting logic

Business events happen in the real world. Accounting translates them into a common unit — the rupee — and into a common structure — accounts. That translation is why a bank in Mumbai can read the books of a shop in Pune without visiting the counter.

The seven steps, in the order they actually happen:

Accounting is a process, not a single entry
StepNameWhat Rahul doesTiny example
1IdentifyingSpot the events that change the shop’s money or value. Ignore the rest.A customer pays ₹150 — identify. A customer window-shops — ignore.
2MeasuringPut a rupee figure on the event. Accounting records only what can be measured in money.The pens sold are measured at ₹150, not as “a happy customer”.
3RecordingWrite the event in the books on the date it happened, with evidence (bill, voucher, cheque).Cash book: cash in ₹150. Sales book: sale ₹150.
4ClassifyingPut each amount under the right account name so similar things sit together.₹150 is Sales, not Capital, not a loan.
5SummarisingTotal the accounts and present short statements — profit, and a list of what is owned and owed.Month sales ₹80,000, expenses ₹55,000, profit ₹25,000.
6AnalysingAsk what the numbers mean. Compare, find the cause, spot the leak.Rent is 20% of sales — too high for this lane? Stock of diaries is not moving.
7CommunicatingGive the picture to the people who need it: Rahul, the bank, the tax officer, a partner.A one-page profit statement and a one-page list of assets and liabilities.
Formula

Accounting = Identify → Measure → Record → Classify → Summarise → Analyse → Communicate

Skip a step and the picture is either incomplete or useless to the reader.

7. How to process one event (exam procedure)
  1. Read the event. Did money or value of the business change? If no, stop — it is not accounting yet.
  2. Measure it in ₹. Use the bill, the invoice, the cheque, or the agreed price. Do not guess.
  3. Name the accounts. At least two names, because every event has two sides (you will see why under the equation).
  4. Write the record. Date, accounts, amounts, a one-line narration of what happened.
  5. Later, add similar records together (classify and summarise) and read the totals (analyse and communicate).
Solved example 0.1 · Easy

Which of these is accounting, and which is just a thought?

Rahul thinks, “I might buy a photocopy machine next year.” A supplier delivers the machine today for ₹40,000 cash and leaves a tax invoice.

Answer. The thought is not accounting — no money moved, no evidence, nothing to measure. The delivery is accounting: identify (machine bought), measure (₹40,000), record (Cash down, Furniture/Machinery up), classify (asset), and later summarise it on the list of things the shop owns.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “define accounting” or “accounting is the process of…”, write the seven verbs in order: identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing, communicating. Then add “in terms of money, to help users take decisions.”

10. Common mistakes
  • Writing only “recording of transactions”. That is bookkeeping, which is one part of accounting, not the whole.
  • Forgetting measuring. If you cannot put a rupee figure, accounting does not record it (a loyal customer is valuable — but not in the books).
  • Stopping at recording. The exam wants the full process, including analysis and communication.
11. Memory trick

I-M-R-C-S-A-C: I Measure, Record, Classify, Summarise, Analyse, Communicate. Say it as “I mark rupees clearly so anyone can count.”

12. Exam-ready answer

Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording, classifying, summarising, analysing and communicating financial information of a business. Identification picks the events that change the resources of the firm. Measurement expresses those events in money. Recording writes them in the books with evidence. Classification groups them under account heads. Summarising presents totals as statements. Analysis interprets the statements. Communication reports the picture to owners, lenders, the tax authority and other users so that decisions can be taken. Accounting is therefore both a record and a language.

2. Why do businesses keep accounts?

1. What is it? — Definition

Businesses keep accounts so that they have a reliable memory of every rupee, can compute profit or loss, can pay the correct tax, can borrow from a bank, can control theft and waste, and can decide what to do next.

2. In simple words

Rahul cannot keep 400 bills in his head. Accounts are a notebook that never gets tired, never takes sides, and can be shown to other people.

3. Why do we need it?

The shop is not a hobby. Money is coming from Rahul’s savings, later from a bank, and the government wants its tax. Accounts are how Rahul proves what happened — to himself first, then to everyone else.

4. Real-life example

A bank manager asks Rahul, “What did you earn last year, and what do you own today?” If Rahul shrugs, there is no loan. If Rahul opens a set of books that add up, the manager has something to read.

5. Accounting logic

Every reason below is a different reader of the same books. The books do not change for each reader. The statements pulled from the books do.

Six reasons — memory, profit, tax, bank loan, control, decision
NeedQuestion the books answerWhat goes wrong without books
MemoryWhat happened on 12 June? Who still owes us? Whom do we still owe?Rahul forgets that Aman is still to be paid ₹18,000.
ProfitDid the shop earn more than it spent? How much?Busy counter, empty pocket — he sold below cost and never noticed.
TaxWhat is taxable income? What GST was collected and paid?He pays too much, or too little and faces a notice.
Bank loanIs the shop able to repay? What security does it have?The manager has no numbers. The file is closed.
ControlIs cash matching the till? Is stock walking out the door?An employee can pocket cash and there is no trail.
DecisionShould we drop diaries and add art supplies? Is rent too high?Decisions are made on a feeling, which is how shops quietly die.
Solved example 0.2 · Easy

Name the reason

Rahul wants to know whether notebooks or greeting cards give him more leftover money after cost. Which reason is this?

Answer. Decision (and profit). Accounts will show sales and cost of each line so he can keep the better one.

9. How to identify the question

If the question is “why is accounting needed / objectives of accounting”, list these six: memory (record), profit (result), tax (statutory), bank loan (creditworthiness), control (stewardship), decision (management). One line of explanation under each.

10. Common mistakes
  • Writing only “to know profit”. That is one reason, not the full answer.
  • Mixing “control” with “tax”. Control is internal (cash, stock, people). Tax is a duty to the government.
11. Memory trick

MP-TB-CD: Memory, Profit, Tax, Bank-loan, Control, Decision. “My Profit To Bank Comes Daily.”

3. Bookkeeping versus accounting

1. What is it? — Definition

Bookkeeping is the recording of transactions in the books, in a systematic way. Accounting is bookkeeping plus classifying, summarising, analysing and communicating — that is, recording plus interpreting.

2. In simple words

Bookkeeping is writing it down correctly. Accounting is writing it down and then reading what it means. Every accountant book-keeps. Not every bookkeeper accounts.

3. Why do we need it?

Exam papers love this pair. If you treat them as the same word you lose marks. In a small shop Rahul may do both. In a company a clerk book-keeps and a manager accounts.

4. Real-life example

Rahul’s cousin Neha writes every cash receipt and payment in a register. That is bookkeeping. At month-end Rahul takes Neha’s totals, computes profit, compares this month with last month, and decides to cut the greeting-card order. That is accounting.

5. Accounting logic

Recording is the foundation. Interpretation is the roof. You cannot interpret what was never recorded. You also cannot call a pile of recordings “accounts” until someone has totalled and read them.

Bookkeeping
  • Identifying and recording transactions.
  • Journal, cash book, ledger postings.
  • Clerical, rule-based, day to day.
  • Output: a complete record.
  • Does not, by itself, explain profit or position.
Accounting
  • Recording + classifying + summarising + analysing + communicating.
  • Trial balance, profit statement, balance sheet, ratios.
  • Includes bookkeeping, then goes further.
  • Output: statements plus meaning.
  • Answers “so what?” for owner, bank, tax.
Formula

Accounting = Bookkeeping + Interpreting (summarising, analysing, communicating)

Bookkeeping is necessary. It is not sufficient.

Solved example 0.3 · Moderate

Is Neha an accountant?

Neha posts every bill to the correct page and her totals always match. She never prepares a profit figure and never comments on the numbers. Is she doing accounting?

Answer. She is doing bookkeeping. Accounting begins when those records are summarised into profit and position and then analysed. If Rahul takes her ledger and prepares a profit statement, that extra work is accounting.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “distinguish between bookkeeping and accounting”, draw a two-column table: meaning, scope, level of work, output, who does it. End with the line: bookkeeping is a part of accounting.

10. Common mistakes
  • Saying accounting is “only interpretation” — it includes recording.
  • Saying bookkeeping is useless. Without it, accounting has nothing to interpret.
11. Memory trick

Bookkeeping = the book. Accounting = the book + the story of the book.

4. The business is not the owner

1. What is it? — Definition

The business entity concept says that the business is treated as a person separate from its owner. The books of Rahul Stationery record the shop, not Rahul’s private life.

2. In simple words

Imagine the shop is a box. Rahul can put money into the box and take money out of the box, but the box has its own list of belongings and debts. We never mix the box with Rahul’s rent for his flat, his dinner, or his bike.

3. Why do we need it?

If we mix them, profit becomes a lie. Paying for a movie ticket from the till would look like a shop expense and would hide the true profit of selling pens.

4. Real-life example

Rahul takes a notebook from the shelf for his sister’s homework. In his head “it is my shop, my notebook”. In the books it is drawings — the owner took goods — not an expense of selling stationery to customers.

5. Accounting logic

Capital is the amount the owner has put into the box. Drawings are the amount the owner has taken out of the box. Both exist only because the box and the owner are recorded as two parties talking to each other.

Key point

Business ≠ owner. The shop can owe the owner (capital). The owner can owe the shop (if he takes goods without recording drawings — which we will not allow). Every personal withdrawal is drawings. Every personal bill paid from the till is drawings, not rent, not salary, not “miscellaneous”.

Solved example 0.4 · Easy

Whose electricity?

Rahul pays ₹800 for the shop’s electricity and ₹1,200 for his home electricity, both from the shop’s cash box.

Answer. ₹800 is an expense of the business (electricity). ₹1,200 is drawings — the owner took cash for a personal bill. Recording the ₹1,200 as electricity would understate profit by ₹1,200.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “business entity / accounting entity / separate entity”, write: the business is assumed to be distinct from the owner; only business transactions enter the books; owner’s private expenses are drawings, not business expenses.

10. Common mistakes
  • Treating a sole proprietor’s shop as legally a company. Entity is an accounting idea. A sole shop is not a separate legal person, but we still keep separate books.
  • Calling drawings an expense. Drawings reduce capital. They do not go to the profit calculation as rent or purchases would.
11. Memory trick

Two names, two pockets: “Rahul” and “Rahul Stationery”. If it is not for the shop, it is not a shop expense.

12. Exam-ready answer

Under the business entity concept the enterprise is treated as a unit separate from its owner. Transactions are recorded from the point of view of the business, not the owner. Money introduced by the owner is capital of the business (a claim on the business). Money or goods taken by the owner for personal use are drawings, which reduce capital, and are not expenses of the business. This separation is what makes profit of the shop measurable.

5. What is a business transaction?

1. What is it? — Definition

A business transaction is an event that changes the money or the value of the business, can be measured in rupees, and is supported by evidence (bill, invoice, cheque, receipt, voucher, contract).

2. In simple words

If the shop’s pocket got heavier or lighter, or what the shop owns or owes changed, and you can prove it with a paper (or a bank SMS), it is a transaction. If nothing moved except a thought or a handshake, it is not.

3. Why do we need it?

Accounting records transactions, not hopes. If we recorded every idea, the books would be fiction. Evidence is what lets a bank, an auditor, or an examiner trust the figure.

4. Real-life example

A customer says, “I will definitely buy 20 diaries next week.” That is not a transaction. Next week she pays ₹2,000 and takes the diaries — now it is a transaction: cash in, stock out, evidence = bill.

5. Accounting logic

Three tests, all must pass: (1) change in money or value of this business, (2) measurable in ₹, (3) evidence. Fail any one, leave it out of the books.

What is a transaction, and what is not
EventTransaction?Why
Rahul thinks of buying a glass display for ₹8,000.NoOnly a thought. Nothing moved. No evidence.
Rahul shakes hands with a carpenter “to discuss a counter”.NoHandshake without money or a signed order. No value change yet.
Rahul starts the shop with cash ₹1,00,000.YesCash of the shop rose. Capital rose. Bank deposit slip / cash in hand is evidence.
Buys furniture for ₹20,000 cash, takes a bill.YesCash down, furniture up. Bill in hand.
Orders 100 notebooks by a WhatsApp message. Nothing delivered, nothing paid.NoA mere order. Stock has not come. Cash has not gone. (When goods or invoice arrive, then yes.)
A friend praises the shop.NoGoodwill in conversation is not measured in ₹ in these books.
Rahul’s sister studies at the counter.NoNo money, no value change of the shop.
Pays rent ₹5,000 by cheque.YesBank down, expense up. Cheque and rent receipt.
Aman supplies stock of ₹30,000 on credit, invoice received.YesStock up, a creditor (Aman) up. Invoice is evidence. Cash need not move.
Rahul takes ₹4,000 from the till for a personal trip.YesCash of the shop down, drawings up. Even though it is personal, the shop’s cash changed — so the shop must record it.
Watch out

Credit purchases and credit sales are transactions. “On credit” does not mean “not yet a transaction”. Value changed: you have the goods, you owe Aman. Record it the day the invoice/goods arrive, not the day you pay.

Solved example 0.5 · Easy

Tick the transactions

From this list, which two enter the books today? (a) Rahul plans to take a loan next month. (b) A customer pays ₹500 cash for pens. (c) Rahul dreams of a second shop. (d) Furniture of ₹20,000 is delivered and paid for.

Answer. (b) and (d). (a) is a plan. (c) is a dream. Both fail the three tests.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “which of the following is not a transaction”, look for: thoughts, plans, orders not executed, personal events that do not touch the shop, or things that cannot be measured in money.

10. Common mistakes
  • Waiting for cash before recording. Credit purchases and credit sales are transactions on the invoice date.
  • Recording a signed “we will do business sometime” handshake. No goods, no money, no invoice — no transaction.
  • Leaving drawings out because “it is personal”. Personal for Rahul, but the shop’s cash moved — the shop must record it.
11. Memory trick

C-M-E: Change, Money-measure, Evidence. All three, or it stays out.

6. The five elements — a map

Every amount in Rahul’s books belongs to one of five families. Learn the families first. Names of accounts come after.

Five families. Every account is a child of one family.
FamilyIn one lineRahul exampleWhere it lives in the equation
AssetsWhat the shop owns or is owed.Cash, bank, stock, furniture, debtors.Left side — resources.
LiabilitiesWhat the shop owes to outsiders.Aman the creditor, a bank loan, unpaid rent.Right side — outsiders’ claims.
CapitalWhat the shop owes to the owner.Rahul’s ₹1,00,000 put in.Right side — owner’s claim.
Revenue (income)Value earned by the shop from its work.Sales, commission received, interest received.Increases capital (profit).
ExpensesCost of earning that revenue.Rent, salary, electricity, cost of goods sold.Decreases capital (and may create a loss).
Key point

Revenue and expenses are not a sixth and seventh side of the equation. They explain why capital changed. Profit (revenue − expenses) is added to capital. A loss is subtracted. Drawings are also subtracted from capital, but drawings are not an expense.

Formula

Assets = Liabilities + Capital,   and Capital grows with profit and shrinks with loss and drawings

Master this map. Debit and credit are only a way of writing the map.

7. Assets

1. What is it? — Definition

An asset is a resource of the business that has money value and will give a benefit in the future — something the shop owns, or something someone owes the shop.

2. In simple words

If Rahul can point to it and say “this belongs to the shop and it is worth rupees”, it is an asset. Cash in the drawer. Money in the bank. Pens on the shelf. The wooden counter. A customer who has not yet paid.

3. Why do we need it?

We list assets so that we know what the shop has to work with, and so that the bank and Rahul can see the resources that stand behind the liabilities and capital.

4. Real-life example

Rahul’s wooden display is an asset because it will be used for years to hold goods. A chocolate he eats at lunch is not an asset of the shop — it is gone, and it was personal.

5. Accounting logic

An asset is a future benefit stored in rupees. Cash is a benefit now. Stock is a benefit when sold. Furniture is a benefit while it is used. A debtor is a benefit when the customer pays. Prepaid rent is a benefit because next month’s occupancy is already paid.

Assets Rahul will meet — and whether they are current
AssetWhat it isCurrent or non-currentWhy it is an asset
CashNotes and coins in the till / cash box.CurrentCan be spent immediately.
BankMoney in the shop’s bank account.CurrentCan be drawn by cheque or UPI.
Inventory / StockGoods held for sale — pens, notebooks, files.CurrentWill turn into cash when customers buy.
Debtors / ReceivablesCustomers who bought on credit and still owe the shop.CurrentThey are expected to pay in a short time.
FurnitureCounter, shelves, chairs, display.Non-currentUsed for years, not sold to customers.
MachineryPhotocopy machine, billing printer.Non-currentUsed to run the shop, not held for sale.
BuildingThe shop premises if Rahul owns it.Non-currentUsed for years.
Prepaid (e.g. prepaid insurance, prepaid rent)An expense paid in advance, benefit still to come.CurrentThe unused portion is a resource — we have already paid for a future benefit.

Current versus non-current, in simple words

Current assets

Things that are cash, or will become cash, or will be used up, within about a year (one operating cycle).

  • Cash, bank
  • Stock
  • Debtors
  • Prepaid expenses
  • Short-term deposits
Non-current assets

Things the shop will use for more than a year, not sell in the ordinary course of business.

  • Furniture, fixtures
  • Machinery, computers
  • Building, land
  • Goodwill, patents (intangible)

Simple test. Will this turn into cash, or get used up, inside a year? Current. Will we still be using it next year and the year after? Non-current. Stock of pens is current even if a few diaries stay on the shelf for 14 months — we hold them to sell, not to use.

Watch out

Buying a photocopy machine is not “purchases”. Purchases means goods bought to sell. A machine is an asset (machinery). Mixing these two is one of the most common exam mistakes and we will hit it again.

Solved example 0.6 · Easy

Sort these into current and non-current

Cash ₹53,000, furniture ₹20,000, stock of pens ₹20,000, prepaid insurance ₹3,000, building ₹5,00,000, debtors ₹8,000.

Answer. Current: cash, stock, prepaid insurance, debtors. Non-current: furniture, building.

Solved example 0.7 · Moderate

Is a debtor an asset even if the customer is a friend?

Rahul sells ₹2,000 of files to his college friend on credit.

Answer. Yes. The shop is owed ₹2,000. That claim is a debtor, a current asset. Friendship is not recorded. If the friend never pays, the asset will later be written off as a loss — but on the day of sale it is an asset.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “what are assets / classify assets / current vs fixed (non-current)”, define, then split current (cash, bank, stock, debtors, prepaid) and non-current (furniture, machinery, building, goodwill). Give one line on the “within a year” test.

10. Common mistakes
  • Calling the owner’s personal bike a shop asset. Entity concept — only if the shop owns it.
  • Listing capital as an asset. Capital is the owner’s claim, on the other side.
  • Calling stock a non-current asset “because we always keep stock”. Stock is held for sale, so it is current.
11. Memory trick

Asset = a future benefit the shop controls. Current = cash-ish within a year. Non-current = used for years (furniture, machines, building).

8. Liabilities

1. What is it? — Definition

A liability is an amount the business owes to an outsider — a present duty to pay money or to give goods/services, arising from a past event.

2. In simple words

If someone who is not Rahul can knock on the shop door and say “pay me”, that amount is a liability. Aman who supplied stock on credit. The bank that gave a loan. The landlord if this month’s rent is still unpaid.

3. Why do we need it?

Liabilities are claims on the assets. We list them so that we never confuse “what we have” with “what is ours”. A shop can be full of stock and still be in trouble if most of it is owed to suppliers.

4. Real-life example

Aman delivers notebooks worth ₹30,000 and says “pay me in 30 days”. Rahul has the notebooks (asset) and he has a creditor called Aman (liability). Both must be recorded the same day. Recording only the stock would pretend the notebooks are free.

5. Accounting logic

A liability is the other side of an asset that arrived before cash left, or of cash that arrived with a promise to return it (a loan). Dual aspect: something came in, a claim was created.

Liabilities — outsiders’ claims
LiabilityWhat it isCurrent or non-currentRahul example
Creditors / PayablesSuppliers from whom we bought on credit.CurrentAman ₹30,000 for stock.
Bank loan (due after 12 months)Money borrowed from a bank, repayable later.Non-current (the long-term part)A 3-year loan of ₹50,000.
Bank overdraft / loan due within 12 monthsShort borrowing, or the instalment due this year.CurrentOverdraft to pay a supplier this week.
Outstanding expensesExpenses incurred but not yet paid (rent unpaid, salary unpaid).CurrentOutstanding rent ₹5,000 if Rahul has used the shop but not paid.

Current versus non-current liabilities

Current liabilities

Duties we expect to settle within a year.

  • Creditors (Aman)
  • Outstanding rent, outstanding salary
  • Bank overdraft
  • Short-term loan / this year’s instalment
  • GST payable, tax deducted but not deposited
Non-current liabilities

Duties that stretch beyond a year.

  • Term loan from a bank (the part due after 12 months)
  • Long-term deposit from a customer or tenant
  • Debentures (in a company)
Key point

Capital is not a liability to an outsider. It is a claim of the owner. In the equation it sits with liabilities because both are claims on assets, but we never call capital “a liability” in a classification question — we call it capital / equity / owner’s equity.

Solved example 0.8 · Easy

Is a bank loan a liability or capital?

Rahul’s bank credits ₹50,000 as a loan. His aunt also gifts him ₹10,000 which he puts into the shop.

Answer. The ₹50,000 is a liability (bank loan) — it must be repaid. The ₹10,000 is capital — the owner (via his aunt’s gift, now his money) put it in; it is not repayable on demand as a loan is.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “what are liabilities / classify liabilities”, define as amounts owed to outsiders, then split current (creditors, outstanding expenses, overdraft) and non-current (term loan). Stress: capital is not a liability.

10. Common mistakes
  • Calling capital a liability. Capital is the owner’s claim, shown with liabilities in the equation, but classified separately.
  • Forgetting outstanding expenses. If the shop has used electricity this month and not paid, a liability already exists.
  • Treating a loan as income. A loan increases cash/bank and increases a liability. It is not sales. It is not profit.
11. Memory trick

Liability = we owe an outsider. Current = due within a year (Aman, unpaid rent). Non-current = due after a year (term loan). Capital is the owner, not an outsider.

9. Capital

1. What is it? — Definition

Capital is the amount the owner has invested in the business — the owner’s claim on the assets after outsiders have been provided for. In equation form, Capital = Assets − Liabilities.

2. In simple words

Capital is Rahul’s money in the shop. When he puts ₹1,00,000 into the cash box on day one, the shop now owes that claim to Rahul. It is not a gift the shop can forget. It is not a loan with interest. It is the owner’s stake.

3. Why do we need it?

Without capital we cannot say whose leftover the assets are. After Aman and the bank have been provided for, what remains is Rahul’s. That remainder is capital.

4. Real-life example

Rahul puts ₹1,00,000 cash in. Later the shop makes a profit of ₹2,000 and Rahul takes ₹4,000 home. Closing capital is ₹1,00,000 + ₹2,000 − ₹4,000 = ₹98,000. You will watch this happen, transaction by transaction, in the equation section.

5. Accounting logic

Capital is a claim, so it lives on the same side as liabilities. It grows when the owner introduces money or when the shop makes a profit. It shrinks when the shop makes a loss or when the owner takes drawings.

Formula

Closing capital = Opening capital + Additional capital + Profit − Loss − Drawings

Profit itself is Revenue − Expenses. If expenses exceed revenue, there is a loss and capital falls.

6. Format — How capital moves
EventEffect on capital
Owner puts cash/goods inCapital increases
Shop earns revenue (sales, commission, interest received)Capital increases (via profit)
Shop incurs expenses (rent, salary, cost of goods sold)Capital decreases (via profit/loss)
Owner takes cash or goods for personal use (drawings)Capital decreases
Loss for the periodCapital decreases
Solved example 0.9 · Moderate

Compute closing capital

Opening capital ₹1,00,000. Profit ₹2,000. Drawings ₹4,000. No extra capital introduced.

Working. ₹1,00,000 + ₹2,000 − ₹4,000 = ₹98,000.

Answer. Closing capital ₹98,000.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “what is capital / compute closing capital”, write the definition, then the formula Opening + additional capital + profit − loss − drawings. Never subtract drawings from profit as if drawings were an expense — subtract them from capital.

10. Common mistakes
  • Treating capital as cash. Cash is an asset. Capital is a claim. On day one they may be equal; after a few transactions they are not (see T2: cash is ₹80,000, capital is still ₹1,00,000).
  • Adding a bank loan to capital. A loan is a liability.
11. Memory trick

Capital is the owner’s stake, not the cash in the till. Formula: start + profit − drawings (and − loss if any).

10. Revenue / Income

1. What is it? — Definition

Revenue (income) is the value earned by the business from its ordinary activities and from other permitted gains — sales of goods, commission received, interest received, rent received.

2. In simple words

Revenue is the shop earning. Not a loan. Not capital introduced. Earning. When a customer buys a notebook, that selling price is sales (revenue). When a neighbour pays Rahul a small commission for collecting a courier, that is commission received (revenue).

3. Why do we need it?

Revenue is one half of profit. Without naming it we cannot say whether the shop earned more than it spent.

4. Real-life example

Rahul sells a box of files for ₹15,000 cash. The ₹15,000 is sales, a revenue. It is not “cash capital”. It is not a loan. Cash rose because a customer paid for goods.

5. Accounting logic

Revenue increases capital. That is why, under the modern rule, an increase in income is credited — the same side as an increase in capital.

Incomes you must name correctly
IncomeWhat it isNot to be confused with
SalesSelling price of goods sold to customers.Capital introduced; a bank loan; cash withdrawn.
Commission receivedEarning for a service or a referral.Commission paid (that is an expense).
Interest receivedEarning on money the shop has lent or deposited.Interest paid on a loan (expense).
Rent receivedIf Rahul sub-lets a corner of the shop.Rent paid for the shop (expense).
Watch out

“Received” in the name (interest received, commission received, rent received) signals income. “Paid” (interest paid, rent paid) signals expense. The exam uses these two words as a trap. Read them.

Solved example 0.10 · Easy

Is a loan income?

The bank credits ₹50,000 into Rahul’s account as a loan. Is this revenue?

Answer. No. The shop must repay it. Bank (asset) increases and Bank loan (liability) increases. Revenue would increase capital without creating a repayable duty. A loan is not earning.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “what is revenue / give examples of income”, write: value earned by the business. Examples: sales, commission received, interest received, rent received. Explicitly exclude capital introduced and loans.

10. Common mistakes
  • Crediting cash because “money came in”. Money coming in is a debit to Cash/Bank. The credit is to Sales, Commission, Loan, or Capital — depending on why the money came in.
  • Treating sales and capital as the same because both “bring money”. Why the money came in is the whole point.
11. Memory trick

Income = earned. Sales, commission received, interest received, rent received. If we have to give it back (loan) or if the owner put it in (capital), it is not income.

11. Expenses

1. What is it? — Definition

An expense is a cost incurred to earn the revenue of the period — rent, salary, electricity, insurance expired, interest paid, and the cost of goods that were sold.

2. In simple words

Expenses are the shop spending in order to run and to sell. Paying the landlord. Paying a helper. Paying the electricity board. The cost of the notebooks that actually left the shelf.

3. Why do we need it?

Profit is a leftover. You cannot know the leftover until you have named every cost of earning this period’s revenue.

4. Real-life example

Rahul pays ₹5,000 rent by cheque. That ₹5,000 is an expense. It does not buy him a lasting asset. It buys him one month of occupying the lane. The benefit dies with the month — that is the mark of an expense.

5. Accounting logic

Expenses decrease capital. That is why an increase in expense is debited — the same side as a decrease in capital (and the same side as drawings).

Purchases of goods versus buying a machine

Purchases means goods bought for resale — the stock of a stationery shop: pens, notebooks, files, erasers. In the journal we debit Purchases A/c (a nominal account, treated as an expense of buying goods). Those goods sit as stock (an asset) until they are sold. Unsold goods remain an asset. Sold goods become an expense (cost of goods sold).

Buying a machine, furniture, or a building is not purchases. Those are assets the shop will use, not sell. Debit Furniture or Machinery, not Purchases. This single mix-up costs marks in almost every exam.

Purchases of goods are not the same as buying a machine
SpendingAccount to debitFamilyWhy
Pens and notebooks to sell, ₹30,000Purchases (and they become Stock)Expense / Asset (stock)Goods for resale.
Wooden counter, ₹20,000FurnitureAsset (non-current)Will be used, not sold to customers.
Photocopy machine, ₹40,000MachineryAsset (non-current)A tool of the shop, not merchandise.
Shop rent, ₹5,000RentExpenseBenefit of one month, then gone.
Helper’s salary, ₹8,000SalaryExpenseCost of labour this month.
Electricity bill, ₹800ElectricityExpenseUsed up in the month.
Interest on loan, ₹500Interest paidExpenseCost of borrowing, not a repayment of the loan itself.
Goods (purchases / stock)
  • Bought to be sold.
  • Account: Purchases (journal), Stock (equation / balance sheet).
  • Unsold = asset. Sold = expense (cost).
Use-assets (furniture / machinery)
  • Bought to be used for years.
  • Account: Furniture, Machinery, Building.
  • Never “Purchases”. Never an expense on day one.
Solved example 0.11 · Moderate

Three payments, three families

Rahul pays by cheque: (i) ₹12,000 to Aman for stock bought earlier, (ii) ₹5,000 rent, (iii) ₹20,000 for a new display cabinet.

Answer. (i) is not an expense today — it reduces a liability (Aman) and reduces Bank. The expense/stock was recorded when the goods arrived. (ii) is an expense (Rent). (iii) is an asset (Furniture), not purchases and not an expense.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “purchases”, think goods for resale. If it says furniture / machinery / building / vehicle, think asset. If it says rent, salary, electricity, interest paid, think expense.

10. Common mistakes
  • Debiting Purchases when a machine is bought. Debit Machinery.
  • Debiting Rent when last month’s outstanding rent is paid. That payment reduces a liability (Outstanding rent); the expense was recorded last month.
  • Treating repayment of a loan as an expense. Repayment reduces the liability and reduces Bank. Interest on the loan is the expense.
11. Memory trick

Expense = used up to earn this period’s income. Purchases = goods to sell. Furniture/machinery = goods to use. Paying a creditor is not a new expense.

12. Profit and loss

1. What is it? — Definition

Profit is the excess of revenue over expenses for a period. Loss is the excess of expenses over revenue. Profit increases capital. Loss decreases capital.

2. In simple words

Profit is leftover earning. If the shop earned ₹17,000 and spent ₹15,000 to earn it, leftover is ₹2,000 — profit. If it had spent ₹20,000, leftover would be negative — a loss of ₹3,000.

3. Why do we need it?

Profit is the score of the shop. Rahul did not open a stationery shop to move cash from one pocket to another. He opened it to have more capital at the end than at the start, after drawings.

4. Real-life example

In our ten transactions Rahul will: sell stock that cost ₹10,000 for ₹15,000 (sales ₹15,000, cost ₹10,000), pay rent ₹5,000, receive commission ₹2,000. Revenue = ₹15,000 + ₹2,000 = ₹17,000. Expenses = ₹10,000 + ₹5,000 = ₹15,000. Profit = ₹17,000 − ₹15,000 = ₹2,000.

5. Accounting logic

Profit is not cash. Rahul can be in profit and still be short of cash (money stuck in stock or debtors). Profit is a change in capital, not a change in the till. We will prove this with the running equation.

Formula

Profit (or Loss) = Revenue − Expenses

If the result is negative, it is a loss. Add profit to capital. Subtract a loss from capital. Do not touch drawings here — drawings are not an expense.

Rahul’s profit from T1–T10 (full working)
Item₹Family
Sales₹15,000Revenue
Commission received₹2,000Revenue
Total revenue₹17,000
Cost of stock sold₹10,000Expense
Rent₹5,000Expense
Total expenses₹15,000
Profit₹2,000Added to capital
Solved example 0.12 · Exam-level

Profit is not cash

Suppose Rahul had sold the same goods on credit instead of cash. Sales still ₹15,000, cost still ₹10,000, rent still paid ₹5,000, commission still ₹2,000 cash. Is profit still ₹2,000? Is cash the same?

Answer. Profit is still ₹2,000 — revenue and expenses did not change. Cash is lower by ₹15,000, and Debtors are higher by ₹15,000. Profit ≠ cash. This is why later chapters separate the profit statement from the cash flow statement.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “calculate profit” or “does the firm make a profit or a loss”, list all revenues, list all expenses, subtract. Do not include capital introduced, loans, drawings, or purchase of furniture in this arithmetic.

10. Common mistakes
  • Subtracting drawings from revenue as if drawings were an expense. Drawings reduce capital, not profit.
  • Including purchase of furniture in expenses. Furniture is an asset.
  • Including a loan received as revenue. A loan is a liability.
  • Equating profit with the increase in cash. Cash also moves when we buy furniture, pay creditors, take loans, and make drawings.
11. Memory trick

Profit = Revenue − Expenses. Negative = loss. Profit goes to capital. Drawings do not enter this formula.

13. Drawings

1. What is it? — Definition

Drawings are money or goods the owner takes from the business for personal use. Drawings reduce capital. Drawings are not an expense of the business.

2. In simple words

When Rahul takes ₹4,000 from the till to pay for a personal trip, the shop did not incur a trip expense. The owner took his own money out of the box. We reduce cash and we reduce capital, through an account called Drawings.

3. Why do we need it?

If we called drawings an expense, profit of the shop would depend on how much pizza Rahul ate, which is nonsense. The shop’s profit should measure the shop, not the owner’s kitchen.

4. Real-life example

Two cases, same idea: (1) Rahul takes cash ₹4,000 — Drawings Dr., Cash Cr. (2) Rahul takes a box of pens costing ₹500 for his cousins — Drawings Dr., Purchases/Stock Cr. Both reduce capital. Neither is rent, sales, or salary.

5. Accounting logic

The shop and the owner are separate (entity). When the owner takes from the shop, the shop’s claim owed to the owner (capital) shrinks. That is a capital movement, not a cost of earning sales.

Drawings — not an expense
  • Owner taking cash for home.
  • Owner taking goods for family.
  • Owner’s personal electricity paid from the till.
  • Owner’s medical bill paid by the shop.
  • Effect: capital ↓. Profit is not charged.
These ARE expenses
  • Shop rent.
  • Shop salary.
  • Shop electricity.
  • Cost of goods sold to customers.
  • Effect: profit ↓, and therefore capital ↓.
Formula

Closing capital = Opening capital + Profit − Drawings

Drawings sit in this capital formula, not inside Profit = Revenue − Expenses.

Solved example 0.13 · Easy

Where does ₹4,000 go?

Rahul withdraws ₹4,000 cash for personal use. A student writes: Debit Rent ₹4,000, Credit Cash ₹4,000.

Answer. Wrong. Rent is a shop expense. This is drawings. Debit Drawings ₹4,000, Credit Cash ₹4,000. Profit is unaffected. Capital falls by ₹4,000.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “withdrew / took for personal use / household / private”, the account is Drawings. Never Rent, never Miscellaneous expense, never Salary of the owner in a sole-proprietor set of books (the owner is rewarded by profit, not by a salary, unless the question specifically creates a salary).

10. Common mistakes
  • Debiting Salary when the owner takes cash. The owner is not an employee of himself in a sole shop (unless the question says so).
  • Debiting Purchases when the owner takes goods — that would leave purchases too high and profit too low. Credit Purchases or Stock, debit Drawings.
  • Showing drawings on the profit statement as an expense. Show them in the capital working only.
11. Memory trick

Drawings = owner taking. Reduces capital. Not an expense. Mantra: “Personal take = Drawings. Shop spend = Expense.”

12. Exam-ready answer

Drawings are cash or goods withdrawn by the proprietor for personal use. They are not a business expense because they are not incurred to earn revenue of the firm. Drawings are deducted from capital. If cash is withdrawn: Drawings A/c Dr. To Cash A/c. If goods are withdrawn: Drawings A/c Dr. To Purchases (or Stock) A/c. Treating drawings as rent, salary or purchases understates profit and violates the business entity concept.

14. The accounting equation

1. What is it? — Definition

The accounting equation is Assets = Liabilities + Capital. It is always true, after every transaction, because every event has two sides (dual aspect).

2. In simple words

Think of a weighing scale. On the left, everything the shop has (assets). On the right, who provided those things: outsiders (liabilities) and Rahul (capital). The two pans must weigh the same. Always.

3. Why do we need it?

If the scale does not balance, a transaction was recorded on only one side, or an amount was mistyped. The equation is the first error-check in accounting. The trial balance in Chapter 1 is this idea in list form.

4. Real-life example

Rahul puts ₹1,00,000 cash into the shop. The shop now has cash of ₹1,00,000 (asset). Who provided it? Rahul. So capital is ₹1,00,000. Left ₹1,00,000, right ₹1,00,000.

5. Accounting logic

Assets are resources. Claims on those resources are either outsiders’ (liabilities) or the owner’s (capital). There is nothing left to be a third pan. So A = L + C, always. When the shop earns a profit, assets rise (or a liability falls) and capital rises by the same profit. When the owner draws, assets fall and capital falls.

Formula

Assets = Liabilities + Capital

This is the compact form. It never takes a holiday.

Formula

Assets = Liabilities + Opening capital + Profit − Drawings

And Profit = Revenue − Expenses. Substituting: Assets = Liabilities + Opening capital + Revenue − Expenses − Drawings.

Formula

Assets + Expenses + Drawings = Liabilities + Opening capital + Revenue

This rearranged form is why, in Chapter 1, a trial balance still totals. Expenses and drawings sit on the debit side with assets; revenue and capital sit on the credit side with liabilities.

6. Format — How to use the equation on any transaction
  1. Name what changed (at least two things — dual aspect).
  2. Classify each as Asset, Liability, or Capital (revenue/expense/drawings are capital-changes).
  3. Write the + or − rupee amount against each.
  4. Add the new totals. Check Assets = Liabilities + Capital.
  5. If they do not match, you missed a side. Go back.

We now walk ten transactions of Rahul Stationery. After every one you will see: (1) a snapshot of each account, (2) the proof A = L + C, (3) a running table that keeps Cash, Bank, Furniture, Stock, Debtors, Prepaid, Creditors, Loan and Capital. Debtors and Prepaid stay ₹0 — the columns are there so you can see the empty slots. All arithmetic is shown. Indian commas throughout.

Opening position. Before T1 the shop does not exist. Every account is ₹0. Assets ₹0 = Liabilities ₹0 + Capital ₹0.

What happened? Rahul puts his savings of ₹1,00,000 into the shop’s cash box. The shop is born. The shop now has cash. The shop now owes that claim to Rahul (capital).

One asset up, capital up, same amount. 1,00,000 = 0 + 1,00,000. Nothing is “profit”. He moved money from his personal pocket into the shop’s pocket.

5. Accounting logic

In the journal we debit Purchases (the name Chapter 1 will use for goods bought). In the equation we show those goods as Stock, an asset, because they are sitting on the shelf. Stock 0 + 30,000 = 30,000. Creditors 0 + 30,000 = 30,000. Assets 40,000 cash + 40,000 bank + 20,000 furniture + 30,000 stock = 1,30,000. L + C = 30,000 + 1,00,000 = 1,30,000. Both sides rose together.

Watch out

Two names, one pile of pens: Purchases is the journal name (nominal, goods bought). Stock is the equation / balance-sheet name (asset, goods still in hand). Unsold purchases = stock. Do not debit Furniture. Do not debit Aman. Aman is credited because he is the giver of credit — the shop received goods from him.

T5 — Sells stock that cost ₹10,000 for ₹15,000 cash

What happened? A customer buys a chunk of the stock. The stock had cost Rahul ₹10,000. The customer pays ₹15,000 cash. Two things happen at once: (1) an asset swap — cash in, stock out; (2) a profit of ₹5,000 which increases capital. You must show both. Showing only the ₹15,000 would pretend the goods were free.

T5: which accounts moved
AccountNature₹ changeIncrease or decreaseDebit or credit
CashAsset+₹15,000IncreaseDebit

5. Accounting logic

Cash 40,000 + 15,000 = 55,000. Stock 30,000 − 10,000 = 20,000. Net assets rise by 15,000 − 10,000 = 5,000. That 5,000 is profit, so capital 1,00,000 + 5,000 = 1,05,000. Assets 55,000 + 40,000 bank + 20,000 furniture + 20,000 stock = 1,35,000. L + C = 30,000 + 1,05,000 = 1,35,000. In Chapter 1 you will often write only Cash Dr. To Sales, and match cost later through opening/closing stock. For this bootcamp we take stock down now, at cost, so every row of the equation is true on the day.

Key point

Selling price ₹15,000 minus cost ₹10,000 = profit ₹5,000. Never reduce stock by the selling price. Stock leaves at cost. Cash enters at selling price. The gap is profit.

Solved example 0.14 · Exam-level

Prove the expanded equation after T10

Using A = L + Opening capital + Rev − Exp − Drawings, plug in every figure.

Assets = ₹1,66,000.

Liabilities = ₹18,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹68,000.

Opening capital = ₹1,00,000.

Revenue = ₹15,000 + ₹2,000 = ₹17,000.

Expenses = ₹10,000 + ₹5,000 = ₹15,000.

Drawings = ₹4,000.

Right-hand side = 68,000 + 1,00,000 + 17,000 − 15,000 − 4,000.

1,68,000 + 17,000 = 1,85,000; 1,85,000 − 15,000 = 1,70,000; 1,70,000 − 4,000 = 1,66,000.

Left-hand side = right-hand side = ₹1,66,000. Proved.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “explain the accounting equation with an example”, write A = L + C, one sentence on dual aspect, then a 3-to-5 line numerical example (opening capital, one purchase of an asset, one expense) and a mini statement that totals. A 5-mark ready answer is at the end of this bootcamp.

10. Common mistakes
  • Writing Assets = Liabilities − Capital. The sign is plus. Capital is added, because it is a claim.
  • Forgetting that profit lives inside capital. If you add profit as a fourth item without reducing the way you show capital, you will double-count.
  • Changing only one side. If cash goes up, something else moved — capital, loan, sales, or another asset.
11. Memory trick

A = L + C. Left = what we have. Right = who provided it. After every transaction, re-total both sides. If they differ, you missed a side.

15. Debit and credit — left and right, not good and bad

1. What is it? — Definition

Debit means the left side of an account. Credit means the right side of an account. They are directions, like east and west. They are not praise and blame. They are not “good” and “bad”.

2. In simple words

Picture a big T. The name of the account sits on the top bar. The left arm is Debit (Dr). The right arm is Credit (Cr). Every amount goes on one arm or the other. “Debit Cash” means “write the amount on the left of the Cash account”.

3. Why do we need it?

We need a convention so that two people, or a person and a computer, put the same amount in the same place. Left and right is that convention. The modern rules in the next section tell you which side to use for which family.

4. Real-life example

When Rahul’s bank sends an SMS “INR 50,000 credited”, the bank is speaking from the bank’s books. In the bank’s books Rahul is a liability, so an increase is a credit. In Rahul’s books the bank account is an asset, so the same money is a debit to Bank. Same rupees, two books, opposite sides — because the two entities are facing each other. This confuses every beginner. Hold it: we always record from the shop’s point of view.

5. Accounting logic

Because A = L + C, the two sides of the equation must keep equal. Debits record increases in the left family (assets, and also expenses and drawings). Credits record increases in the right family (liabilities, capital, income). That is why total debits always equal total credits. It is the equation wearing a T-shirt.

6. Format — The T-account

Every account is written as a T:

Dr   Name of the account   Cr

Particulars₹Particulars₹
Left side = DEBIT (Dr)…Right side = CREDIT (Cr)…
All debit amounts sit here…All credit amounts sit here…

The difference between the two sides is the balance. If debits are bigger, it is a debit balance. If credits are bigger, it is a credit balance. Assets normally have debit balances. Liabilities and capital normally have credit balances.

Watch Cash take shape across T1, T2, T3. After three transactions the T already looks like a real account:

Dr   Cash   Cr

Particulars₹Particulars₹
To Capital (T1)₹1,00,000By Furniture (T2)₹20,000
By Bank (T3)₹40,000
Balance c/d₹40,000

Debits 1,00,000. Credits 20,000 + 40,000 = 60,000. Balance (debits bigger) = 1,00,000 − 60,000 = ₹40,000 debit, which is cash in hand after T3. The words To (on the debit) and By (on the credit) are traditional labels for the other account involved.

Solved example 0.15 · Easy

Is “credit” a compliment?

A student says: “Credit Cash because cash coming in is a good thing.”

Answer. No. Cash coming in is an increase in an asset, so it is a debit to Cash. “Credit” here is the right-hand column, not a compliment. This single superstition — cash in = credit — produces the most common journal error in first-year scripts.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “what do you mean by debit and credit”, write: debit = left, credit = right; they are not good/bad; every account has both sides; the rules in the next section decide which side an increase goes to.

10. Common mistakes
  • Thinking debit is bad and credit is good (or the reverse).
  • Crediting Cash whenever cash is received. Cash received is Debit Cash.
  • Using the bank SMS language (“amount credited”) as if it were the shop’s books.
11. Memory trick

Dr is the door on the left. Cr is the corridor on the right. Good and bad have left the building.

16. Modern rules of debit and credit (best for MBA)

1. What is it? — Definition

The modern (equation) rules follow the five families. Increase an asset or an expense: debit. Increase a liability, capital or income: credit. Reverse the side for a decrease.

2. In simple words

Look at the equation A = L + C. Left family grows on the left (debit). Right family grows on the right (credit). Expenses and drawings behave like negative capital, so they grow on the debit. Income behaves like positive capital, so it grows on the credit.

3. Why do we need it?

MBA papers and every computerised system (Tally, Zoho, SAP) use this. If you remember five lines you can journal any transaction without first asking “is this personal, real or nominal?”. Learn these first. Keep the golden rules as a second language.

4. Real-life example

T6: rent paid by cheque. Rent is an expense → increase in expense → debit Rent. Bank is an asset → decrease in asset → credit Bank. You did not need to classify Rent as “nominal” to get this right. You only needed “expense up = debit”.

5. Accounting logic

These rules are the equation, itemised. They cannot contradict A = L + C. If a posting made from these rules fails to balance, the classification of the account was wrong, not the rule.

Modern rules — five families plus drawings
FamilyIncreaseDecreaseNormal balance
AssetDebitCreditDebit
LiabilityCreditDebitCredit
CapitalCreditDebitCredit
ExpenseDebitCreditDebit
Income / RevenueCreditDebitCredit
Drawings (contra-capital)Debit (drawings up = capital down)CreditDebit
6. Format — The five lines to memorise
  • Increase in Asset = Debit; Decrease in Asset = Credit.
  • Increase in Liability = Credit; Decrease in Liability = Debit.
  • Increase in Capital = Credit; Decrease in Capital (drawings, loss) = Debit.
  • Increase in Expense = Debit; Decrease in Expense = Credit.
  • Increase in Income = Credit; Decrease in Income = Debit.
11. Memory trick

DEAD CLIC — Debit: Expenses, Assets, Drawings. Credit: Liabilities, Income, Capital. To increase the account, use its DEAD-or-CLIC side. To decrease it, use the other side.

7. How to journal any transaction with modern rules
  1. Read the transaction in plain English (ignore debit/credit for ten seconds).
  2. Name two (or more) accounts.
  3. Put each account in a family: Asset, Liability, Capital, Expense, Income (or Drawings).
  4. Say increase or decrease for each.
  5. Apply the table: asset/expense/drawings up → debit; liability/capital/income up → credit.
  6. Check: at least one debit and one credit, and the rupees match.
Solved example 0.16 · Easy

Apply DEAD CLIC

Paid salary ₹8,000 cash.

Salary = expense, increase → Debit Salary. Cash = asset, decrease → Credit Cash.

Salary paid
DateParticularsL.F.Debit (₹)Credit (₹)
—Salary A/c …… Dr.₹8,000
To Cash A/c₹8,000
(Being salary paid in cash)
Solved example 0.17 · Moderate

A decrease in a liability

Paid Aman ₹12,000 by cheque (our T9).

Aman = liability, decrease → Debit Aman. Bank = asset, decrease → Credit Bank. Two decreases, still one debit and one credit, still in balance, both sides of the equation fall by ₹12,000.

Solved example 0.18 · Exam-level

Four accounts in one story

Rahul sells goods costing ₹4,000 to a customer for ₹6,000 on credit, and the customer pays ₹2,500 immediately in cash, balance later.

Accounts. Cash (asset ↑ ₹2,500) Debit. Debtors (asset ↑ ₹3,500) Debit. Stock (asset ↓ ₹4,000) Credit. Sales/profit (income ↑ ₹2,000) Credit.

Debits 2,500 + 3,500 = 6,000. Credits: stock 4,000 + profit 2,000 = 6,000. Or, in Chapter-1 style: Debit Cash 2,500, Debit Debtors 3,500, Credit Sales 6,000; and take stock down by cost 4,000.

Equation: assets net +2,500 +3,500 −4,000 = +2,000; capital +2,000. Holds.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “rules of debit and credit” in an MBA / management accounting paper, write the five modern lines first, with DEAD CLIC. Add a one-line example for each family. Give golden rules only if marks remain or the question says “traditional”.

10. Common mistakes
  • Debiting a liability when it increases (taking a loan and debiting Bank loan). Loan increase = credit.
  • Crediting an expense when it increases (crediting Rent because “we paid, so credit”). Expense increase = debit.
  • Using DEAD CLIC on the decrease side without flipping. DEAD CLIC is the increase side.

17. Traditional golden rules (personal, real, nominal)

1. What is it? — Definition

The traditional Indian rules first classify every account as personal, real or nominal, and then apply one sentence per class. They give the same debit and credit as the modern rules. They are still asked in many B.Com and MBA theory papers.

2. In simple words

Three families of names. Personal = people and institutions (including the owner, the bank, Aman, outstanding rent). Real = things (cash, stock, furniture, goodwill). Nominal = incomes and expenses (sales, rent, salary). One sentence each, and you can journal.

3. Why do we need it?

Older examiners and many Indian textbooks still open with these. If a 5-mark question says “golden rules of accounting”, this is the answer they have in the scheme. Learn them. Use modern rules to think; use golden rules to write the theory.

4. Real-life example

T9, paying Aman. Aman is a person → personal account. He is receiving money → “debit the receiver” → Debit Aman. Bank is also personal (the bank as an artificial person) and is giving money → “credit the giver” → Credit Bank. Same entry as the modern rule produced.

5. Accounting logic

Personal accounts track who. Real accounts track what thing. Nominal accounts track why capital changed this year (incomes and expenses). The three sentences are just DEAD CLIC in older clothes.

Three golden rules — textbook wording, use this in the exam
Class of accountGolden ruleMatches modern rule
PersonalDebit the receiver, Credit the giverPeople we owe more to → credit (liability ↑). People who owe us more → debit (asset ↑).
RealDebit what comes in, Credit what goes outThing comes in = asset ↑ = debit. Thing goes out = asset ↓ = credit.
NominalDebit all expenses and losses, Credit all incomes and gainsExpense ↑ = debit. Income ↑ = credit.

How to classify an account — with many examples

1. Personal accounts — people, firms, institutions

Personal accounts — three sub-kinds, this is an exam favourite
KindMeaningExamples
Natural personalA living person.Aman (creditor), Ramesh (debtor), Rahul’s Capital, Drawings, any customer’s name, any supplier’s name.
Artificial personalA body that the law treats as a person.Bank A/c, State Bank of India, XYZ Pvt Ltd, a municipal corporation, a club, the Government, GST payable.
Representative personalAn account that stands in for a person (usually unpaid or prepaid).Outstanding rent (stands for the landlord), Prepaid insurance (stands for the insurer), Accrued commission, Unearned rent, Outstanding salary.

2. Real accounts — things owned

Real accounts — debit what comes in, credit what goes out
KindMeaningExamples
Tangible realThings you can touch.Cash, Stock, Furniture, Machinery, Building, Vehicle, Land, Computer, Fixtures.
Intangible realThings you cannot touch but the shop owns.Goodwill, Patents, Trade marks, Copyrights, Computer software (in many papers).

3. Nominal accounts — incomes, expenses, gains, losses

Nominal accounts — the profit-and-loss family
KindExamples (debit these — expenses/losses)Examples (credit these — incomes/gains)
Trading itemsPurchases, Wages, Carriage inwards, Freight, Import duty.Sales, Closing stock (when credited in trading a/c).
Operating expenses / incomesRent, Salary, Electricity, Telephone, Advertising, Insurance expired, Depreciation, Discount allowed, Bad debts, Interest paid, Commission paid.Commission received, Interest received, Rent received, Discount received.
Gains and lossesLoss on sale of furniture, Loss by fire, Loss by theft.Profit on sale of furniture, Bad debts recovered.
Watch out

Bank A/c is personal (artificial person), not real. Cash A/c is real. Students mix these. Cash in hand = real. Cash at bank = personal. Both are assets. Both increase with a debit. The class differs; the modern rule does not.

T4 through golden rules

Purchases of stock from Aman ₹30,000.

  • Purchases = nominal (expense of goods) → debit all expenses → Debit Purchases.
  • Aman = personal → he is the giver of goods → credit the giver → Credit Aman.
T2 through golden rules

Furniture bought for cash ₹20,000.

  • Furniture = real → what comes in → Debit Furniture.
  • Cash = real → what goes out → Credit Cash.
Solved example 0.19 · Moderate

Classify, then journal

Outstanding rent ₹5,000 at year end (rent of the shop not yet paid).

Classify. Rent = nominal (expense) → debit Rent. Outstanding rent = representative personal (stands for the landlord) → the landlord is a giver of the service we have used → credit Outstanding rent.

Outstanding rent
DateParticularsL.F.Debit (₹)Credit (₹)
Year endRent A/c …… Dr.₹5,000
To Outstanding rent A/c₹5,000
(Being rent of the period still unpaid)

Modern view of the same: expense up = debit; liability up = credit. Same entry.

Solved example 0.20 · Exam-level

Prepaid insurance

Rahul pays ₹12,000 insurance for 12 months on 1 October. Year end is 31 March. Six months are unused.

Unused 6/12 × 12,000 = 6,000. Prepaid insurance is a representative personal account (the insurer still owes six months of cover) and also a current asset.

At year end: Debit Prepaid insurance ₹6,000, Credit Insurance ₹6,000 (reducing the expense to the six months that belong to this year). Golden rule: prepaid = personal → debit the receiver (the prepaid account stands for the insurer who has taken money and still must provide cover). Insurance = nominal → credit it because we are reducing an expense.

Modern: asset up = debit Prepaid; expense down = credit Insurance.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “golden rules / traditional rules / personal real nominal”, write the three sentences exactly: Debit the receiver, Credit the giver. Debit what comes in, Credit what goes out. Debit all expenses and losses, Credit all incomes and gains. Then classify 4–6 accounts as a working. Mention the three kinds of personal account if marks are 5 or more.

10. Common mistakes
  • Calling Bank a real account. Bank is personal (artificial).
  • Calling Capital a nominal account. Capital is personal (the owner).
  • Calling Drawings a nominal (expense) account. Drawings is personal (the owner receiving).
  • Calling Outstanding rent a nominal account. It is representative personal — a liability.
  • Calling Goodwill a nominal account. Goodwill is real (intangible asset).
  • Calling Purchases a real account. Purchases is nominal. Stock/Inventory is real.
11. Memory trick

PNG: Personal — people. Real — things. Nominal — names of incomes and expenses (nominal = “in name”, the profit names). Personal: receiver Dr, giver Cr. Real: in Dr, out Cr. Nominal: expenses Dr, incomes Cr.

12. Exam-ready answer

The traditional golden rules of accounting depend on the class of the account. (1) Personal accounts (natural, artificial, representative): Debit the receiver, Credit the giver. (2) Real accounts (tangible and intangible): Debit what comes in, Credit what goes out. (3) Nominal accounts (expenses, losses, incomes, gains): Debit all expenses and losses, Credit all incomes and gains. Illustration: goods purchased on credit from Aman — Purchases is nominal so it is debited (expense); Aman is personal and is the giver so he is credited. These rules produce the same journals as the modern equation rules.

18. T1–T10 recap: journals, T-accounts, equation effect

You have already seen each of T1–T10 as a full teaching block (what happened, accounts, increase or decrease, debit, credit, journal, equation). This section is the exam desk-view: one summary table, then the ledger T-accounts that Chapter 1 will call posting, then a proof that the T-accounts produce the same closing figures as the equation.

Ledger T-accounts after T10

Posting means taking each journal line to the T of that account. Debit journal line → left of the T. Credit journal line → right of the T. Balance c/d is written on the smaller side so the two sides of the T equal: an asset (debit balance) shows Balance c/d on the credit; a liability or capital (credit balance) shows Balance c/d on the debit. We now post every line of T1–T10. Arithmetic of each balance is shown.

Key point

Journal → T-accounts (ledger) → list of balances (trial balance) → the list is the equation. Chapter 1 is this pipeline, taught as a craft. This bootcamp is why the pipeline cannot fail if you post both sides.

19. Classification drill — 20 accounts

Cover the last two columns with your hand. Name the type (personal / real / nominal — and the sub-kind if you can), the nature (asset / liability / capital / income / expense / drawings), and which side increases the account. Then check.

Twenty accounts — type, nature, and the side that increases them
#AccountType (golden)Nature (modern)To increase: Debit or Credit
1CashReal (tangible)Asset (current)Debit
2BankPersonal (artificial)Asset (current)Debit
3CapitalPersonal (natural — the owner)CapitalCredit
4DrawingsPersonal (natural — the owner receiving)Contra-capital (drawings)Debit
5PurchasesNominal (expense of goods)Expense (goods for resale; unsold = stock)Debit

7RentNominal (expense)ExpenseDebit

13LoanPersonal (the lender)Liability (non-current if long-term)Credit

16StockReal (tangible)Asset (current)Debit

Commission with no adjective is treated here as commission received (income), because that is how T7 used it. Commission paid would be nominal / expense / debit to increase.

Patterns you should now see without thinking:

  • Every asset in this list increases with a debit. Every liability and capital increases with a credit.
  • Every expense (Purchases, Rent, Salary, Interest paid) increases with a debit. Every income (Sales, Interest received, Commission) increases with a credit.
  • Drawings increases with a debit — it is the owner receiving, and it reduces capital.
  • Bank is personal; Cash is real; both are assets; both debit to increase. The golden class differs, the modern side does not.
  • Outstanding … is usually a representative personal liability (credit to increase). Prepaid … is usually a representative personal asset (debit to increase).
  • Goodwill looks “nominal” because it is a word, but it is a real intangible asset. Debit to increase.
Solved example 0.21 · Easy

Fill three blanks

Debtors: type? nature? side to increase? Outstanding rent: type? nature? side to increase? Sales: type? nature? side to increase?

Answer. Debtors — personal, asset, Debit. Outstanding rent — representative personal, liability, Credit. Sales — nominal, income, Credit.

9. How to identify the question

If the question is a classification table (very common for 5–8 marks), use exactly these three columns: Personal/Real/Nominal, Asset/Liability/Capital/Income/Expense, Dr or Cr to increase. Do not leave a cell blank. Bank and Outstanding/Prepaid are the traps.

20. Memory tricks and common mistakes

Memory tricks (keep these on a one-page card)

11. Memory trick

DEAD CLIC. Debit Expenses, Assets, Drawings. Credit Liabilities, Income, Capital. This is the increase-side. Flip it to decrease.

11. Memory trick

A = L + C. What we have = who provided it. After every transaction, re-total both sides.

11. Memory trick

PNG golden. Personal: Debit the receiver, Credit the giver. Real: Debit what comes in, Credit what goes out. Nominal: Debit expenses and losses, Credit incomes and gains.

11. Memory trick

C-M-E for a transaction. Change in money/value, Measurable in ₹, Evidence. All three, or it stays out.

11. Memory trick

Two pockets. Rahul ≠ Rahul Stationery. Personal take = Drawings. Shop spend = Expense.

11. Memory trick

Goods to sell vs goods to use. Pens to sell = Purchases / Stock. A counter to use = Furniture. A photocopier to use = Machinery. Never debit Purchases for a machine.

11. Memory trick

Received vs paid. Interest received / commission received / rent received = income (credit). Interest paid / commission paid / rent paid = expense (debit).

11. Memory trick

Cash coming in is a debit to Cash. Say it out loud. The bank SMS that says “credited” is the bank’s books, not yours.

Common mistakes — and the repair

10. Common mistakes
  • Drawings treated as an expense. Repair: Drawings reduce capital, not profit. Debit Drawings, not Rent, not Salary, not Miscellaneous. Profit = Revenue − Expenses. Drawings do not sit in that formula.
  • Cash received credited to Cash. Repair: Cash is an asset. Asset up = debit. Credit the reason the cash came (Sales, Capital, Loan, Commission, Debtors). “Credit” is the right column, not a compliment.
  • Purchases of goods mixed with furniture / machinery. Repair: Purchases = goods for resale. Furniture/Machinery = assets to use. T2 is Furniture Dr, Cash Cr. T4 is Purchases Dr, Aman Cr.
  • A loan treated as income or as capital. Repair: A loan is a liability. Bank Dr, Bank loan Cr. It must be repaid. It is not sales and not capital.
  • Paying a creditor treated as a new expense. Repair: The expense/stock was recorded when the goods arrived (T4). T9 only reduces Aman and reduces Bank.
  • Stock reduced by selling price. Repair: Stock leaves at cost. Cash/Debtors enter at selling price. The gap is profit. T5: stock −10,000, cash +15,000, capital +5,000.
  • Bank classified as a real account. Repair: Bank is personal (artificial person). Cash is real. Both debit to increase.
  • Outstanding rent classified as nominal. Repair: Outstanding rent is representative personal, a current liability, credit to increase. The nominal account is Rent (the expense).
  • Goodwill classified as nominal. Repair: Goodwill is a real intangible asset. Debit to increase.
  • Capital treated as cash. Repair: Cash is an asset. Capital is a claim. After T2 they are no longer equal: cash 80,000, capital 1,00,000.
  • Waiting for cash before recording a credit purchase or credit sale. Repair: The invoice date is the transaction date. T4 is a transaction on the day Aman delivers, not on the day we pay.
  • Owner’s personal bill recorded as a shop expense. Repair: Entity concept. Personal electricity, personal trip, personal medical bill = Drawings.
  • One-sided posting. Repair: Dual aspect. If you debit, you must credit. If the equation’s last two columns differ, you missed a side.
  • Profit treated as cash. Repair: Profit is a change in capital. Cash also moves for loans, drawings, furniture, and paying creditors. After T10 profit is 2,000; cash is 53,000. They are different numbers.
Five broken journals you will now refuse to write
Wrong journalWhy it is wrongRight journal
Rent Dr 4,000 / Cash Cr 4,000 when owner takes cash homePersonal take is not rentDrawings Dr 4,000 / Cash Cr 4,000
Cash Cr 2,000 / Commission Dr 2,000 when commission is receivedCash in is Debit Cash; income is CreditCash Dr 2,000 / Commission received Cr 2,000
Purchases Dr 20,000 / Cash Cr 20,000 for a wooden counterA counter is furniture, not goods for saleFurniture Dr 20,000 / Cash Cr 20,000
Cash Dr 50,000 / Commission Cr 50,000 for a bank loanA loan is not earningBank Dr 50,000 / Bank loan Cr 50,000
Purchases Dr 12,000 / Bank Cr 12,000 when paying AmanPaying a creditor is not a new purchaseAman Dr 12,000 / Bank Cr 12,000
Solved example 0.22 · Exam-level

Find four errors

A student journals: (i) Started business Cash Cr 1,00,000, Capital Dr 1,00,000. (ii) Bought furniture Purchases Dr 20,000, Cash Cr 20,000. (iii) Commission received Commission Dr 2,000, Cash Cr 2,000. (iv) Drawings Salary Dr 4,000, Cash Cr 4,000.

Repair.

  1. Cash is an asset increasing → Debit Cash, Credit Capital.
  2. Furniture is an asset, not purchases → Debit Furniture, Credit Cash.
  3. Cash in = Debit Cash. Commission is income → Credit Commission received.
  4. Owner taking cash is Drawings, not Salary → Debit Drawings, Credit Cash.

21. Exam-ready 5-mark answer

5 marks

Explain the accounting equation with an example.

Meaning. The accounting equation is Assets = Liabilities + Capital. It is the dual-aspect idea written as algebra. Every transaction has two sides, so the two sides of the equation remain equal after every event.

Assets are resources of the business (cash, bank, stock, debtors, furniture, prepaid expenses). Liabilities are amounts owed to outsiders (creditors, bank loan, outstanding expenses). Capital is the owner’s claim on the business. Capital itself moves: Closing capital = Opening capital + Profit − Drawings, and Profit = Revenue − Expenses. The expanded form is therefore Assets = Liabilities + Opening capital + Revenue − Expenses − Drawings.

Why it always holds. Assets are what the firm has. Liabilities and capital are who provided those assets. There is no third claim, so the two totals cannot differ if both sides of every event have been recorded.

Example — Rahul Stationery (extract).

T1: Rahul starts with cash ₹1,00,000. Assets (cash) ₹1,00,000 = Liabilities ₹0 + Capital ₹1,00,000.

T2: Buys furniture ₹20,000 cash. Cash falls by ₹20,000, furniture rises by ₹20,000. Totals still ₹1,00,000 = ₹0 + ₹1,00,000. One asset replaces another.

T4: Buys stock ₹30,000 on credit from Aman. Stock +₹30,000, Creditors +₹30,000. Assets ₹1,30,000 = Liabilities ₹30,000 + Capital ₹1,00,000.

T5: Sells stock that cost ₹10,000 for ₹15,000 cash. Cash +₹15,000, Stock −₹10,000 (assets net +₹5,000); profit ₹5,000 increases capital. Assets ₹1,35,000 = Liabilities ₹30,000 + Capital ₹1,05,000.

After ten such transactions the books of Rahul Stationery show: Cash ₹53,000 + Bank ₹73,000 + Furniture ₹20,000 + Stock ₹20,000 = Assets ₹1,66,000. Creditors ₹18,000 + Bank loan ₹50,000 = Liabilities ₹68,000. Opening capital ₹1,00,000 + profit ₹2,000 − drawings ₹4,000 = Capital ₹98,000. Liabilities + Capital = ₹68,000 + ₹98,000 = ₹1,66,000. The equation balances, and that equality is the proof asked for in the examination.

Conclusion. The accounting equation is both a definition of financial position and a check on recording. A balance sheet is this equation presented as a statement on a given date. If the two sides ever differ, a transaction has been posted on only one side or an amount has been misstated.

12. Exam-ready answer

Write four blocks: (1) statement of A = L + C and dual aspect, (2) one sentence each on assets, liabilities, capital, and the expanded form with profit and drawings, (3) a short numerical example with at least three transactions and a total that matches, (4) a one-line conclusion that a balance sheet is the equation on a date. Do not skip the arithmetic. Examiners award method marks on the numbers.

Exam tip

If the paper gives you a list of transactions and says “show the accounting equation”, draw a running table with a column per account plus Total Assets and L+C, one row per transaction, and tick every row. That is exactly the T1–T10 table in this bootcamp. You will not lose a mark for layout if every row adds up.

22. How this bootcamp connects to Chapter 1

Connect the chapters

Chapter 1 is Journal → Ledger → Trial Balance. This bootcamp is why those three tools exist and what they are for. You already did all three, quietly, on Rahul’s ten transactions. Chapter 1 teaches the craft: dates, narration, folio numbers, balancing accounts, and the trial-balance listing.
