Unit and rupee check — do this on every numerical

Units. 250 + 150 − 200 + 200 − 150 + 50 − 80 = 220. Running: 250 + 150 = 400; 400 − 200 = 200; 200 + 200 = 400; 400 − 150 = 250; 250 + 50 = 300; 300 − 80 = 220. Available units = 250 + 150 + 200 + 50 = 650; issues 200 + 150 + 80 = 430; 650 − 430 = 220.

Rupees. Available cost = ₹10,000 + ₹7,200 + ₹10,400 + ₹3,125 = ₹30,725. ₹30,725 − COGS ₹19,725 = closing ₹11,000. Check: ₹19,725 + ₹11,000 = ₹30,725.

If the same facts had been asked under periodic WAM (short note, not the main answer)

Period average = ₹30,725 ÷ 650 units available. ₹30,725 ÷ 650 = ₹47.269… (not a clean rate — this is why the paper usually wants moving average when dates are given). Do not mix this figure into the perpetual ledger.

Answer (perpetual WAM). Closing stock = ₹11,000. COGS = ₹19,725.

9. How to identify the question

Use WAM when the question says any of: weighted average, average cost, WAM, weighted average cost, moving average, perpetual average, or periodic average. If it says moving / perpetual / ‘stores ledger with rates after each receipt’, use the moving average. If it says ‘weighted average for the period’ or gives no issue dates, use periodic. If it only says ‘weighted average’ but prints a dated list of receipts and issues, use perpetual and write that assumption in one line at the top of the ledger.

10. Common mistakes
  • Recalculating the average on an issue date. The average changes only when goods come in.
  • Taking the latest purchase rate as the issue rate (that is a FIFO/LIFO confusion, not WAM).
  • Periodic average used inside a dated stores ledger, or moving average used when the question said periodic.
  • Adding freight to the average of all stock instead of to the purchase amount of that lot before dividing.
  • Rounding the average too early and never showing the division. Keep two decimal places consistently, and show ₹47.50 as ₹47.50, not ₹48.
  • Forgetting that leftover units after an issue keep the same average — students sometimes switch the leftover onto the next purchase rate before that purchase is posted.
11. Memory trick

WAM: mix the soup, then ladle. You mix (recompute the average) when a new ingredient is poured in (a purchase). You ladle (issue) at whatever the pot currently tastes of. You do not remix just because you ladled.

12. Exam-ready answer

Under the weighted average method, the rate is total cost of units in hand divided by total units in hand. In the perpetual (moving average) system the rate is revised after every purchase; issues are costed at the rate then ruling, and the rate is not revised on issue. In the periodic system a single average is computed from opening stock plus all purchases of the period; closing stock and COGS both use that one rate. The two systems generally give different rupee answers when purchases and issues alternate. AS-2 / Ind AS-2 permit the weighted average cost formula.

6. FIFO versus WAM — what happens when prices move

Take the easy data already used: opening 100 @ ₹20, purchase 200 @ ₹26, issue 150. Prices are rising (₹20 then ₹26). Cost available = 100 × ₹20 + 200 × ₹26 = ₹2,000 + ₹5,200 = ₹7,200. Closing quantity = 150.

Same goods, two splits of the same ₹7,200
FIFOWAM (here perpetual = periodic, one purchase)
How the 150 issued units are costedOldest first: 100 × ₹20 + 50 × ₹26 = ₹2,000 + ₹1,300 = ₹3,300Average ₹24: 150 × ₹24 = ₹3,600
How the 150 leftover units are costedLatest lot: 150 × ₹26 = ₹3,900Average ₹24: 150 × ₹24 = ₹3,600
Check₹3,300 + ₹3,900 = ₹7,200₹3,600 + ₹3,600 = ₹7,200
Memorise the rising-price row — it is the standard 4-to-6 mark comparison
When purchase prices are…FIFO closing stockWAM closing stockFIFO COGSWAM COGSFIFO profit versus WAM
Rising (inflation)Higher (latest dear lots remain)Lower (average is pulled down by old cheap lots)Lower (old cheap lots issued)HigherFIFO profit is higher
FallingLower (latest cheap lots remain)Higher (average still holds some old dear lots)HigherLowerFIFO profit is lower
ConstantSameSameSameSameNo difference
Key point

In a period of rising prices: FIFO closing stock > WAM closing stock, FIFO COGS < WAM COGS, FIFO gross profit > WAM gross profit, FIFO current assets > WAM current assets. Both methods still split the same cost of goods available. They do not create or destroy rupees; they allocate them.

FIFO, in one breath

Layers stay separate. Oldest leaves first. Closing stock looks ‘up to date’. Balance Sheet asset is closer to replacement cost. In inflation, profit is relatively higher (cheap costs in COGS).

WAM, in one breath

Layers are mixed. Every unit in the pot has the same rate. Profit is smoother because a price jump is spread over sold and unsold units. Useful when goods are identical and physically mixed.

7. How to identify the question

9. How to identify the question

Read the method word before you draw a single column. If you see FIFO / first in first out / latest lots in stock / earliest issues → FIFO layers. If you see weighted average / average cost / WAM / moving average / periodic average → WAM, and then decide perpetual vs periodic from the wording and from whether dates of issues are given. If the question is silent on the method, do not guess quietly: write one line, ‘Assumption: inventory is valued at FIFO (or WAM) cost’, pick one, and proceed. An unnamed method with a dated stores ledger is most often FIFO or moving average — state which one you are using so the examiner can mark the working.

Question decoder — 30 seconds that save the numerical
Phrase in the questionWhat you do
‘FIFO’ / ‘first-in, first-out’ / ‘oldest stock issued first’Perpetual FIFO layers. Latest lots = closing stock.
‘Latest purchases remain in stock’FIFO (that sentence is the definition of FIFO closing stock).
‘Weighted average’ + dates of receipts and issuesPerpetual / moving WAM stores ledger. State it.
‘Moving average’ / ‘perpetual average’Recompute after every purchase only.
‘Periodic weighted average’ / no issue datesOne average from opening + all purchases.
Freight inward / carriage inward against a named purchaseAdd it to that lot’s cost; new lot rate = (invoice + freight) ÷ qty of that lot.
‘Cost or NRV whichever lower’ / damaged / obsolete / prices have fallenFirst find cost by FIFO or WAM, then cap at NRV, item by item.
‘LIFO’One sentence: LIFO is not permitted under AS-2 / Ind AS-2 in India. Do not use it as your method.
Silent on methodState the assumption in the first line of the answer.

8. Common mistakes (whole chapter)

10. Common mistakes
  • Recalculating the weighted average at the time of issue. Average changes only on a receipt.
  • Mixing FIFO layers after an issue — leftover lots with different rates must not be blended.
  • Forgetting opening stock, which breaks both the unit identity and the rupee identity.
  • Using selling price, MRP or list price to value stock. Cost first; NRV only as a ceiling.
  • Units that do not reconcile: opening + purchases − issues must equal closing units. If this fails, stop and find the missing posting before you compute rupees.
  • Loading freight inward onto all stock, or onto issues. It belongs to the purchase lot that travelled.
  • Treating cash discount as a reduction of inventory cost. Trade discount is deducted; cash discount is not (it is a financial item).
  • Computing FIFO by issuing from the newest lot. That is LIFO, and LIFO is not allowed.
  • Leaving the method unnamed when the question was silent. Always write the assumption.
  • Skipping the rupee check (available − COGS = closing). A one-minute check catches 90% of arithmetic slips.

9. Memory tricks

11. Memory trick

FIFO: old goods leave first; new goods remain. Closing stock is a photograph of the latest invoices. WAM: mix the soup, then ladle. Stir on purchase, never on issue. Seesaw: closing stock and profit sit on the same side of the seesaw; COGS sits on the other side. Conservatism: cost or NRV, whichever is lower — and compare item by item. India: FIFO and WAM yes; LIFO no.

10. Exam-ready theory answers

4 marks

What is inventory? Where is it shown in the financial statements? (4 marks)

Inventory is the goods held for sale in the ordinary course of business, together with materials and work-in-progress used in production. A trader holds stock-in-trade. A manufacturer holds raw material, WIP and finished goods. Closing inventory is a current asset in the Balance Sheet. It is also used in the Trading Account / Statement of Profit and Loss to arrive at cost of goods sold and gross profit. Opening inventory is last period’s closing inventory brought forward.

4–6 marks

Why is the valuation of inventory important? (4–6 marks)

Closing stock is the rare figure that appears in both the income statement and the Balance Sheet. Cost of goods sold = opening stock + purchases − closing stock, and gross profit = sales − COGS. If closing stock is overstated, COGS is understated, profit is overstated and current assets are overstated. The opposite follows from understatement. The error reverses next year because this year’s closing stock is next year’s opening stock, but each year’s accounts and the year-end financial position are still wrong. Hence a consistent, conservative method (cost or NRV, whichever is lower, under AS-2 / Ind AS-2) is required.

4 marks

State the AS-2 rule for valuation of inventories. Why is LIFO not used in India? (4 marks)

Inventories are valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Cost is determined using FIFO or the weighted average cost formula. NRV is estimated selling price less costs of completion and costs to sell. The comparison is made item by item (or by group of similar items); a surplus on one item cannot offset a deficit on another. LIFO is not a permitted cost formula under AS-2 or Ind AS-2, so Indian companies do not value inventory on a LIFO basis.

6 marks

Distinguish between FIFO and the weighted average method. (6 marks)

FIFO assumes the earliest lots are issued first, so closing stock is the latest lots at the latest rates. Lots are kept as separate layers. In a period of rising prices FIFO reports higher closing stock, lower COGS and higher profit than WAM.

WAM applies an average rate = total cost of units in hand ÷ units in hand. Under the moving-average (perpetual) system the average is revised after every purchase and issues go out at the current average. Under the periodic system one average is computed for the period. WAM is natural when units are identical and mixed. Both methods are permitted by AS-2; LIFO is not.

2 marks

Write the formulae for cost of goods sold and gross profit. (2 marks)

COGS = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock. Gross profit = Sales − COGS. Equivalently, Opening stock + Purchases = COGS + Closing stock (the rupee identity used to check numericals).

11. Practice questions — try them, then open the solution

Sit with rough paper. Do the unit check and the rupee check before you look. Easy is FIFO, moderate is moving WAM, exam-level is FIFO with freight loaded on the correct lot.

Exam tip

In the hall: (1) write the method in the heading, (2) convert freight into a lot rate before posting, (3) after every date rewrite the layers or the average, (4) box closing stock and COGS, (5) spend one minute on the unit identity and the rupee identity. Those five habits convert a 12-mark numerical into a full-score numerical.

Chapter 03

Depreciation

Learning outcome. You will be able to explain what depreciation is (and what it is not), state why it is provided, compute it under the Straight Line Method and the Written Down Value Method — including part-year charges, a second asset, and sale — pass the journals, and present the asset in the Profit & Loss Account and the Balance Sheet, as expected in an Indian MBA exam.

What this chapter covers (official syllabus)

  • Meaning of depreciation
  • Reasons for providing depreciation
  • Straight Line Method (SLM)
  • Written Down Value Method (WDV)
  • Numerical problems (part-year, installation, sale, comparison)

Before you open a numerical — the words

Every depreciation question is built from six words. If you can name them on a blank page, the arithmetic becomes a recipe, not a puzzle.

Six words that unlock every depreciation question
Word you will seeWhat it actually meansExam alias
Cost / original costWhat the business spent to bring the asset to working condition (purchase + installation + freight + non-refundable taxes, minus trade discount).Gross block, invoice price + extras
Residual / scrap / salvageEstimated amount we expect to recover at the end of useful life, after selling or scrapping the asset.Scrap value, residual value
Useful lifeThe period (usually in years) over which the business will use the asset.Life, estimated life, n years
Depreciable amountCost minus residual. This is the bundle of cost that must be expensed over the life.Amount to be written off
WDV / NBV / book valueCost minus accumulated depreciation so far. The unexpired cost still sitting on the Balance Sheet.Written down value, net book value, carrying amount
Accumulated depreciationThe running total of depreciation charged from the date of purchase up to today. A contra-asset, not cash.Provision for depreciation
Key point

Depreciation is an allocation of cost already spent. It is not a valuation of the asset at today’s market price, and it is not cash leaving the business this year.

1. Meaning of depreciation

1. What is it? — Definition

Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount of a tangible fixed asset over its useful life. Depreciable amount = Cost − Residual (scrap) value. We charge this allocation as an expense of each year that enjoyed the asset’s services.

2. In simple words

You buy a delivery van for ₹5,00,000 and you will use it for 5 years. You did not “lose” ₹5,00,000 in year 1. You prepaid for five years of deliveries. Each year you expense a portion of that prepaid bundle. That portion is depreciation. No cash goes to the garage, the bank, or the owner when you pass the depreciation entry — the cash already left on the day you bought the van.

3. Why do we need it?

Without depreciation, year 1 would swallow the whole cost (profit would look terrible) and years 2–5 would ride free (profit would look fake). Depreciation spreads the cost so that each year is charged with the services it used. That is the matching concept.

4. Real-life example

A café buys an espresso machine for ₹1,20,000. It will steam milk for about 6 years and then be sold as scrap for ₹12,000. The café is not poorer by ₹1,20,000 on day one. It is poorer, each year, by the slice of machine-life that year consumed. Depreciation is the name of that slice.

5. Accounting logic

The accounting equation is Assets = Liabilities + Capital. When you buy the van with cash, one asset (van) replaces another (bank) — capital is unchanged. As the van is used, part of that asset is consumed. We reduce the asset (or raise a contra-asset) and reduce profit (which reduces capital). The business is honestly smaller by the cost consumed, not by a cash payment that never happened this year.

12. Exam-ready answer

Depreciation is a non-cash expense representing the expired cost of a tangible fixed asset. It is charged to the Profit and Loss Account so that profit is not overstated, and deducted from the asset (directly or through accumulated depreciation) so that the Balance Sheet does not show the asset at a cost that has already been used up. It is not the same thing as a fall in market price: a building may rise in the property market and we still depreciate it, because we are allocating historical cost, not marking the asset to market.

Watch out

Three sentences students write that examiners cross out: (1) “Depreciation is cash paid for wear and tear.” — No cash is paid. (2) “Depreciation is the fall in market price of the asset.” — Not the definition; market may even rise. (3) “Accumulated depreciation is money kept aside to replace the asset.” — It is only a contra-asset on paper, unless the business separately invests cash in a replacement fund.

Connect the chapters

In the Cash Flow Statement (later chapter) you will add depreciation back to net profit while computing cash from operations. That is because profit was reduced by a non-cash expense. If you treat depreciation as an outflow there, you double-count a payment that already happened when the asset was purchased. Remember the slogan: depreciation is in the P&L; it is not in this year’s cash.

2. Why do we provide depreciation?

3. Why do we need it?

We provide depreciation for five interlocking reasons. Learn them as a 5-mark theory answer, not as a list you half-remember. The examiner wants the matching idea, the Balance Sheet idea, and the honesty that a “fund” is not automatic.

Five reasons for providing depreciation (theory favourite)
ReasonWhat to write in the exam
To show true profit (matching)The year that used the machine must bear a share of its cost. If we skip depreciation, profit is overstated. Owners may then withdraw or distribute cash that is not really “earned”. Matching concept: expenses of a period against revenue of that period.
To show a true asset value (not overstated)A three-year-old van is not worth its original cost on the Balance Sheet. We show cost less accumulated depreciation = net book value. This is still not market value — it is unexpired cost — but it is not a lie that the whole cost is still “there”.
Replacement-funds idea — with the common confusion namedBy charging depreciation we retain that amount of profit inside the business (we do not declare it as fully available). Over the life, retained earnings plus the reduced book value keep the accounting equation in balance. But accounting does not physically set cash aside. The cash from sales sits in the bank and can be spent on anything — inventory, salaries, dividends — unless management separately creates a depreciation fund and invests it. Most businesses do not. So: depreciation helps in principle to retain resources for replacement; it does not create a locked cash box.
Legal / true and fair viewUnder the Companies Act, 2013, financial statements must give a true and fair view. Schedule II indicates useful lives for companies. Skipping depreciation would overstate profit and assets — not true and fair. For MBA theory, write: “Depreciation is necessary to present a true and fair view of profit and of the financial position.”
The cost is a prepaid bundle of servicesA machine is not one day’s expense. It is a packet of future services bought in advance. Depreciation is how we open that packet, year by year. This is the same logic as prepaid insurance: you do not expense 3 years of premium in January of year 1.
12. Exam-ready answer

Depreciation is provided: (i) to ascertain true profit by matching the expired cost of the asset against the revenue of the period; (ii) to state assets at a true (unexpired) amount in the Balance Sheet rather than at original cost; (iii) to retain a portion of profit in the business which, in principle, is available towards replacement — though a separate invested fund is created only if management so decides; (iv) to comply with the true-and-fair requirement of company law; and (v) because the cost of a fixed asset is a prepaid bundle of services that must be allocated over the years that receive those services.

11. Memory trick

Five fingers: Profit, Picture, Piggy-bank (optional), Police (law), Prepaid services. Profit = matching. Picture = Balance Sheet. Piggy-bank = replacement idea, cash not auto-locked. Police = Companies Act / true and fair. Prepaid = the asset is a bundle of future uses.

3. Why depreciation occurs — the physical and economic causes

2. In simple words

Section 2 answered “why we record it”. This section answers “why the asset loses service potential”. Examiners ask both. Do not mix them up.

Causes of depreciation (do not confuse with ‘reasons for providing’)
CauseWhat is happeningTypical assetsOne-line example
Wear and tearPhysical use: friction, running hours, kilometres, copies printed.Vehicles, plant, furnitureA delivery van’s engine after 80,000 km is not the engine you bought.
Passage of time (effluxion of time)Even an unused asset can expire: patents of time, leases, rust, weather.Leasehold, buildings, seasonal plant left idleA 9-year lease has 8 years left on 1 April next year whether you used the shop or not.
ObsolescenceA better, cheaper, or legally required substitute arrives. The old asset is outdated, not necessarily broken.Computers, phones, specialised machineryA 5-year-old billing server still switches on; the business has moved to the cloud.
DepletionExtraction of a wasting resource. The “asset” is physically removed.Mines, oil wells, quarries, timber tractsEvery tonne of ore taken out of the mine is a tonne that is gone.
Accident / abnormal damageFire, flood, crash, beyond ordinary wear. Often written down immediately, not dribbled over remaining life.Any tangible assetA forklift dropped from a trailer is not “this year’s 10% WDV” — it may be a loss on write-off.

Depletion is the word used for mines and wells; amortisation is the cousin-word used for intangible assets (patents, goodwill). Depreciation, in the strict exam sense, is for tangible fixed assets other than wasting assets.

Key point

Land is generally not depreciated — it has an unlimited useful life (the site does not get “used up”). The building on the land is depreciated. A mine is not “land” in this sense; a mine is depleted. If an MCQ says “which of the following is not depreciated?”, the answer is almost always freehold land.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “state the causes of depreciation” → wear and tear, time, obsolescence, depletion, accident (the table above). If it says “state the reasons for providing depreciation” → true profit, true asset value, replacement idea, legal/true and fair, prepaid bundle (Section 2). Two different questions. Two different lists.

4. What is “cost”? (before any method)

1. What is it? — Definition

For depreciation, cost is the amount spent to acquire the asset and bring it to the location and condition necessary for it to be used. Residual value is an estimate of what will come back at the end. Neither figure is “the invoice alone” unless the question is that simple.

6. Format — Cost of a tangible fixed asset
  • Purchase price (after trade discount; cash discount is usually a finance item, not a cut in cost)
  • + Freight / carriage inward / transit insurance
  • + Installation, erection, commissioning, trial-run costs (until ready for use)
  • + Non-refundable taxes and duties
  • − Refundable GST / CENVAT (if the business can claim it input)
  • = Cost to capitalise — this is the figure you depreciate from

Depreciation starts from the date the asset is put to use , not merely the date of placing the order. If bought on 1 September and installed on 1 October, count from 1 October.

Exam tip

“Installation ₹20,000” is not an expense of the year. Add it to cost. “Scrap 10% of cost” means 10% of this total cost, unless the question says 10% of purchase price. When in doubt, cost = all amounts spent to make the asset ready.

Solved example 0 · Easy

Build the cost figure before you touch a rate

Invoice price of a machine ₹5,00,000 . Freight ₹8,000 . Installation ₹12,000 . Refundable GST ₹90,000 (claimable). Scrap estimated at 10% of cost. Life 10 years. SLM.

  1. Cost = 5,00,000 + 8,000 + 12,000 = ₹5,20,000. GST is refundable, so it is not added.
  2. Scrap = 10% of ₹5,20,000 = ₹52,000.
  3. Depreciable amount = 5,20,000 − 52,000 = ₹4,68,000.
  4. Annual SLM depreciation = 4,68,000 ÷ 10 = ₹46,800.
Key point

If you depreciate ₹5,00,000 and ignore installation, every later number is wrong. Cost is step zero of every numerical in this chapter.

5. Accounting treatment — journal, P&L, Balance Sheet

1. What is it? — Definition

Recording depreciation means: (i) recognise an expense for the year, which reduces profit; and (ii) reduce the asset’s net book value, either by crediting the asset directly or by crediting a contra-asset called Accumulated Depreciation (also called Provision for Depreciation).

2. In simple words

Two things move, and cash is not one of them. Expense goes up → profit goes down. Net book value of the asset goes down. Bank is untouched.

5. Accounting logic

Debit the expense (Depreciation Account) because expenses are debited. Credit Accumulated Depreciation (or the Asset) because that credit shrinks the net asset. Then close Depreciation Account to Profit and Loss — so the year’s profit bears the charge. MBA exams usually prefer the accumulated-depreciation (provision) method, because the Balance Sheet can then show cost and accumulated depreciation separately. Both methods are taught below.

6. Format — The two journal entries every year (provision method)
Year-end recording and closing (provision / accumulated depreciation method)
DateParticularsL.F.Debit (₹)Credit (₹)
31 MarDepreciation A/c …… Dr.xx
To Accumulated Depreciation A/cxx
(Being depreciation charged for the year)
31 MarProfit and Loss A/c …… Dr.xx
To Depreciation A/cxx
(Being depreciation transferred to Profit and Loss Account)

Some solutions skip the Depreciation Account and write a single entry: Profit and Loss A/c Dr.   To Accumulated Depreciation A/c. Either form is accepted if the amounts and the two effects (expense + contra-asset) are clear.

6. Format — Where it appears in the statements

Statement of Profit and Loss (extract)

P&L — depreciation is an operating expense, not a cash payment

If the book charges depreciation directly to the asset, the Balance Sheet shows only the WDV figure (₹82,000) and the original cost is not visible. Examiners prefer the “at cost less accumulated depreciation” presentation.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Compute the year’s depreciation under the method named in the question (SLM or WDV), for the months the asset was used.
  2. Pass: Depreciation A/c Dr.   To Accumulated Depreciation A/c (or To Asset A/c).
  3. Close Depreciation A/c to Profit and Loss A/c.
  4. In the Balance Sheet, show Gross Block (cost) minus Accumulated Depreciation = Net Block (NBV).
  5. If the asset is sold during the year: first charge depreciation up to the date of sale, then remove cost and accumulated depreciation, then recognise profit or loss on sale.

Dr   Depreciation A/c   Cr

Particulars₹Particulars₹
To Accumulated Depreciation A/c18,000By Profit and Loss A/c18,000

Dr   Accumulated Depreciation A/c   Cr

Particulars₹Particulars₹
To Balance c/d18,000By Depreciation A/c18,000

The Depreciation Account is a nominal account — it opens at zero, collects the year’s charge, and is emptied into P&L. The Accumulated Depreciation Account is a contra-asset — it lives on from year to year, growing until the asset is sold or fully written off. It is not a pile of cash.

6. Straight Line Method (SLM)

1. What is it? — Definition

Under the Straight Line Method (also called the Original Cost Method or the Fixed Instalment Method), a constant amount of depreciation is charged every full year. The line of remaining book value, plotted against time, is a straight line falling from cost to scrap.

2. In simple words

Take the amount that will die (cost minus scrap), cut it into equal yearly slices, and serve one slice each year. Year 1’s slice = year 5’s slice. If you owned the asset for only part of a year, serve a matching fraction of the slice.

3. Why do we need it?

SLM is simple, and it is fair when the asset gives roughly equal service every year — buildings, furniture, patents of time, a lease. It is a poor fit for assets that collapse in usefulness in the first years (phones, laptops), which is why WDV exists.

4. Real-life example

A shop’s display counters cost ₹1,00,000, will be used 5 years, and will fetch ₹10,000 as scrap. Every year the shop “uses up” ₹18,000 of counter. Customers see the same counters in year 1 and year 4 — equal service, equal charge.

5. Accounting logic

Depreciable amount is a finite pie. SLM assumes each year eats an equal piece of the pie. When the years are done, the pie is gone and only scrap remains. That is why, if residual and life are honoured, WDV at the end of life equals scrap — exactly.

Formula

Annual depreciation = (Cost − Residual) ÷ Useful life in years

Rate on original cost = (Annual depreciation ÷ Cost) × 100. Part-year depreciation = Annual depreciation × (months used ÷ 12). The rate is always applied to original cost, never to the falling WDV.

6. Format — Depreciation schedule (keep four columns every time)
The four-column schedule that stops most SLM mistakes
Year / FYDepreciation for the year (₹)Accumulated depreciation (₹)WDV / NBV at year-end (₹)
Opening (date put to use)—0Cost
Year 1same each full yearrunning totalCost − accum.
…………
Last year of lifelast slice (maybe a stub period)Cost − ResidualResidual
7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Build cost (add installation, freight; exclude refundable tax).
  2. Read residual. If “10% of cost”, compute 10% of the cost you just built.
  3. Depreciable amount = Cost − Residual.
  4. Annual depreciation = Depreciable amount ÷ life in years. Show the division.
  5. Rate % (if asked) = (Annual depreciation ÷ Cost) × 100. This rate is on original cost.
  6. Count months from date put to use to the accounting year-end. Indian FY: 1 April to 31 March. 1 October → 6 months; 1 July → 9 months; 1 January → 3 months; 1 April → 12 months.
  7. First year (and last year, and year of sale) = Annual × months/12. Intervening years = full annual amount.
  8. Useful life is a clock starting on the date put to use, not “n financial years”. A 4-year life from 1 July 2023 ends on 30 June 2027 — there will be a 3-month stub in FY 2027–28.
  9. Fill the schedule. Check: last WDV = residual (if you have charged the full life).
Solved example 1 · Easy

SLM from cost, scrap and life — the master template

Given. Cost ₹1,00,000 , scrap ₹10,000 , useful life 5 years. Method: SLM. Prepare a 5-year schedule and the rate of depreciation.

Step 1 — depreciable amount and annual charge

Depreciable amount = Cost − Scrap = 1,00,000 − 10,000 = ₹90,000 .

Annual depreciation = 90,000 ÷ 5 = ₹18,000 every full year.

Rate on original cost = (18,000 ÷ 1,00,000) × 100 = 18% . Check: 1,00,000 × 18% = 18,000, but remember this 18% is not applied to the falling WDV — we only used cost to find the rate.

Step 2 — the schedule (show every year’s arithmetic)

SLM schedule — charge is identical every year; WDV falls in a straight line

Closing WDV of year 5 = ₹10,000 = scrap. If this check fails, a year’s arithmetic is wrong.

How the WDV column is built (year 1 as a model): 1,00,000 − 18,000 = 82,000. Year 2: 82,000 − 18,000 = 64,000. And so on.

Accumulated depreciation of year 3 = 18,000 × 3 = ₹54,000 . Closing WDV = 1,00,000 − 54,000 = ₹46,000 .

Solved example 2 · Moderate

SLM with Indian financial year — purchased 1 July, last year is a stub

Given. Plant purchased on 1 July 2023 for ₹2,40,000 . Residual ₹24,000 . Useful life 4 years . Books close on 31 March (Indian financial year). Method: SLM. Compute depreciation for each financial year until the asset is fully depreciated down to scrap.

Step 1 — annual slice

Depreciable amount = 2,40,000 − 24,000 = ₹2,16,000 .

Annual depreciation = 2,16,000 ÷ 4 = ₹54,000 .

Depreciation per month = 54,000 ÷ 12 = ₹4,500 .

Step 2 — the life is a clock, not “four FYs”

Put to use: 1 July 2023. Life of 4 years ends on 30 June 2027 . Total months of service = 4 × 12 = 48 months . 48 × 4,500 = ₹2,16,000 — the whole depreciable amount.

FY 2023–24 (1 July 2023 to 31 March 2024) = July, August, September, October, November, December, January, February, March = 9 months .

Year-1 depreciation = 54,000 × 9/12.

54,000 × 9 = 4,86,000.

4,86,000 ÷ 12 = ₹40,500 .

Or: 4,500 × 9 = ₹40,500 .

Step 3 — every financial year until the clock hits 48 months

Part-year first, full years in the middle, stub year at the end — WDV lands on scrap
Financial yearMonths usedWorkingDepreciation (₹)Accum. dep. (₹)Closing WDV (₹)
2023–24 (from 1 Jul)954,000 × 9/1240,50040,5001,99,500
2024–2512full year54,00094,5001,45,500
2025–2612full year54,0001,48,50091,500
2026–2712full year54,0002,02,50037,500
2027–28 (to 30 Jun)354,000 × 3/1213,5002,16,00024,000

Check the months: 9 + 12 + 12 + 12 + 3 = 48. Check the rupees: 40,500 + 54,000 + 54,000 + 54,000 + 13,500 = 2,16,000. Check the WDV: 2,40,000 − 2,16,000 = 24,000 = residual.

Last-year working, shown fully: 54,000 × 3/12 = (54,000 × 3) ÷ 12 = 1,62,000 ÷ 12 = ₹13,500 .

Closing WDV after FY 2023–24: 2,40,000 − 40,500 = ₹1,99,500 .

After FY 2024–25: 1,99,500 − 54,000 = ₹1,45,500 .

After FY 2025–26: 1,45,500 − 54,000 = ₹91,500 .

After FY 2026–27: 91,500 − 54,000 = ₹37,500 .

After the 3-month stub: 37,500 − 13,500 = ₹24,000 = scrap. The clock has run out.

Watch out

A very common wrong answer is to charge ₹40,500 + three full years of ₹54,000 and stop (total 9 + 36 = 45 months). That leaves ₹13,500 of depreciable amount hanging, and WDV would be ₹37,500 instead of scrap ₹24,000. Life is measured from the date put to use.

Exam tip

On the answer sheet, write the month-count in words once (“July to March = 9 months”) before you multiply. Examiners award method marks for the 9/12 even if a later total slips.

Solved example 3 · Exam

Installation added to cost, part-year SLM, then sale — profit of ₹400

Given. A machine is bought on 1 October 2022 for ₹5,00,000 . Installation costs ₹20,000 . Scrap is 10% of cost . Useful life 10 years. Year-end 31 March. SLM.

The machine is sold on 30 September 2025 for ₹3,80,000 . Prepare the depreciation schedule up to the date of sale, compute profit or loss on sale, and pass the journals on the date of sale. Use the accumulated-depreciation method.

Step 1 — cost, scrap, annual depreciation

Cost = 5,00,000 + 20,000 = ₹5,20,000 (installation is capitalised).

Scrap = 10% of 5,20,000 = (10/100) × 5,20,000 = ₹52,000 .

Depreciable amount = 5,20,000 − 52,000 = ₹4,68,000 .

Annual depreciation = 4,68,000 ÷ 10 = ₹46,800 .

Rate on original cost = (46,800 ÷ 5,20,000) × 100 = 9%. Check: 5,20,000 × 9% = 46,800.

Step 2 — months in the first year

1 October 2022 to 31 March 2023 = October, November, December, January, February, March = 6 months .

FY 2022–23 depreciation = 46,800 × 6/12 = (46,800 × 6) ÷ 12 = 2,80,800 ÷ 12 = ₹23,400 .

Or: 46,800 × 1/2 = ₹23,400 .

Step 3 — schedule until 30 September 2025

Charge depreciation in the year of sale up to the date of sale — then stop and sell

2022–23 (1 Oct–31 Mar)646,800 × 6/1223,40023,4004,96,600
2023–2412full year46,80070,2004,49,800
2024–2512full year46,8001,17,0004,03,000
2025–26 (1 Apr–30 Sep)646,800 × 6/1223,4001,40,4003,79,600

NBV walk: 5,20,000 − 23,400 = 4,96,600; − 46,800 = 4,49,800; − 46,800 = 4,03,000; − 23,400 = 3,79,600.

Accumulated depreciation on the date of sale = 23,400 + 46,800 + 46,800 + 23,400.

23,400 + 23,400 = 46,800.

46,800 + 46,800 = 93,600.

93,600 + 46,800 = ₹1,40,400 .

NBV on 30 September 2025 = Cost − Accum. dep. = 5,20,000 − 1,40,400 = ₹3,79,600 .

Step 4 — profit or loss on sale

Formula

Profit / (Loss) on sale = Sale proceeds − NBV on the date of sale

If proceeds > NBV → profit (credited to P&L). If proceeds < NBV → loss (debited to P&L).

Sale proceeds ₹3,80,000 − NBV ₹3,79,600 = ₹400 profit .

A profit of four hundred rupees is still a profit. Write it. Do not round it away.

Step 5 — journals on 30 September 2025

Entry 1 — depreciation for the 6 months of FY 2025–26 up to the date of sale.

Always depreciate up to the date of sale before you touch the asset account

Exam tip

Date discipline wins this question. FY 2022–23 is 6 months, FY 2023–24 and 2024–25 are full, FY 2025–26 up to 30 September is 6 months. Students who charge three full years and then sell from a wrong NBV lose the 4-mark tail of the question.

9. How to identify the question

Use SLM when the question says any of: straight line, original cost method, equal instalment, fixed instalment, equal amount each year, rate % per annum on cost / on original cost. If it gives life and residual and is silent on the method, many Indian MBA papers still expect SLM — but if a WDV rate is printed, that wins. Never apply an SLM rate to the falling book value.

10. Common mistakes
  • Applying the SLM rate to WDV in year 2 onwards. The rate is on original cost. Every full year the rupee charge is identical.
  • Forgetting to add installation / freight to cost, then taking scrap as 10% of the invoice only.
  • Charging a full year when the asset was put to use on 1 October (that is 6/12, not 12/12).
  • Treating “life 4 years” as four financial years when the asset arrived on 1 July — you will miss the 3-month stub and will not land on scrap.
  • Stopping depreciation in the year of sale. You must charge up to the date of sale, then compute profit or loss on the NBV of that date.
  • Writing residual off every year. Residual is subtracted once, when you compute the annual slice.
11. Memory trick

SLM = Same Load every year, like equal slices of a cake. The cake is (Cost − Scrap). The number of slices is the life. A part-year is a part-slice. At the end of the last slice you are staring at scrap.

7. Written Down Value Method (WDV)

1. What is it? — Definition

Under the Written Down Value Method (also called the Diminishing Balance Method or the Reducing Balance Method), depreciation for a year is a fixed percentage of the book value at the start of that year (or of the cost, in year 1, because year-1 book value is cost). The rupee charge falls every full year. Residual is not subtracted each year — the rate is designed (or given) so that book value declines towards scrap.

2. In simple words

Each year you tax a smaller number with the same percentage. Year 1: 10% of ₹1,00,000 = ₹10,000. Year 2: 10% of the leftover ₹90,000 = ₹9,000. The asset never quite hits zero if you keep going, which is why a residual usually remains.

3. Why do we need it?

A new laptop loses a lot of usefulness in year 1 (new model, falling resale) and less in year 4. WDV front-loads the expense to match that pattern. It is also the method many tax rules historically favoured, so Indian papers are full of “20% p.a. on WDV”.

4. Real-life example

You buy a phone for ₹80,000. On a resale app it is worth far less after 12 months than after the next 12. Charging the same SLM slice every year would under-charge year 1 and over-charge year 4. WDV follows the gadget.

5. Accounting logic

Book value at the start of the year is the unexpired cost. WDV says: expire a constant fraction of whatever is still unexpired. Because the base shrinks, the rupee amount shrinks. You do not deduct scrap from the base each year — if you did, you would mix SLM arithmetic into a WDV question.

Formula

Depreciation for the year = Opening WDV × Rate × (months used ÷ 12)

Year 1 opening WDV = Cost. Residual is NOT deducted in the annual working. If the exam gives life and residual but no rate, there is a formula R = 1 − (Scrap ÷ Cost)1/n — shown below for completeness. MBA numericals almost always give the rate. Use the rate you are given.

6. Format — WDV rate when life and scrap are given (completeness, rarely needed)

R = 1 − (Scrap / Cost)(1/n), where n is useful life in years.

Illustration: Cost ₹5,00,000 , scrap ₹50,000 , n = 5. Scrap/Cost = 0.10. (0.10)1/5 ≈ 0.63096. R ≈ 1 − 0.63096 = 0.3690 = 36.90% . You would then apply 36.90% each year on WDV, and after 5 years WDV would be very close to scrap.

In the exam, if you are given “20% p.a. on WDV”, do not invent this formula. The given rate already is the answer. With an arbitrary given rate, WDV at the end of life will usually not equal the residual — and that is acceptable.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Build cost (same as SLM). Residual is noted but not subtracted from the yearly base.
  2. Read the rate. Confirm it is “on WDV / on book value / diminishing / reducing”.
  3. Year 1: Depreciation = Cost × Rate × months/12. Closing WDV = Cost − that depreciation.
  4. Year 2: Depreciation = Closing WDV of year 1 × Rate × 1 (if a full year). Never go back to original cost.
  5. Repeat. Each closing WDV becomes the next opening WDV.
  6. Part-year: multiply that year’s full-year WDV charge by months/12. Do this in two multiplications: first Rate on opening WDV, then the month fraction.
  7. On sale: charge WDV depreciation up to the date of sale (opening WDV × Rate × months/12), then compare sale proceeds with the NBV of that date.
Solved example 4 · Easy

WDV at 10% for three years — falling charge, fixed rate

Given. Cost ₹1,00,000 , rate 10% p.a. on WDV . Prepare a 3-year schedule.

Year 1

Opening WDV = cost = ₹1,00,000 .

Depreciation = 1,00,000 × 10/100 = ₹10,000 .

Closing WDV = 1,00,000 − 10,000 = ₹90,000 .

Year 2

Opening WDV = ₹90,000 (not 1,00,000).

Depreciation = 90,000 × 10/100 = ₹9,000 .

Closing WDV = 90,000 − 9,000 = ₹81,000 .

Year 3

Depreciation = 81,000 × 10/100 = ₹8,100 .

Closing WDV = 81,000 − 8,100 = ₹72,900 .

Solved example 5 · Moderate

WDV 25% with purchase on 1 October — 6/12 then falling full years

Given. Cost ₹4,00,000 , rate 25% p.a. on WDV , purchased 1 October , year-end 31 March. Compute depreciation and WDV for the first three financial years.

Year 1 — six months

1 October to 31 March = 6 months.

Full-year depreciation on cost = 4,00,000 × 25/100 = ₹1,00,000 .

Part-year depreciation = 1,00,000 × 6/12 = (1,00,000 × 6) ÷ 12 = 6,00,000 ÷ 12 = ₹50,000 .

Combined in one line: 4,00,000 × 25/100 × 6/12 = 4,00,000 × 1/4 × 1/2 = 1,00,000 × 1/2 = ₹50,000 .

Closing WDV = 4,00,000 − 50,000 = ₹3,50,000 .

Year 2 — full year, new base

Opening WDV = ₹3,50,000 .

Depreciation = 3,50,000 × 25/100 = 3,50,000 × 1/4.

3,50,000 ÷ 4 = ₹87,500 .

Closing WDV = 3,50,000 − 87,500 = ₹2,62,500 .

Year 3 — full year

Depreciation = 2,62,500 × 25/100 = 2,62,500 × 1/4.

2,62,500 ÷ 4 = ₹65,625 .

Closing WDV = 2,62,500 − 65,625 = ₹1,96,875 .

WDV part-year — fraction in year 1 only; later years use the already-reduced base for a full year

Year 1 (6 months)4,00,0004,00,000 × 25% × 6/1250,0003,50,000
Year 2 (12 months)3,50,0003,50,000 × 25%87,5002,62,500
Year 3 (12 months)2,62,5002,62,500 × 25%65,6251,96,875
Watch out

Wrong path: “Year 2 = 4,00,000 × 25% = ₹1,00,000.” That is SLM-on-cost thinking. Once year 1 has been charged, original cost is retired as a base forever.

Key point

A useful identity: 25% for 6 months is not 25%. It is 12.5% of the opening WDV of that year. Write it as Rate × months/12 so the examiner sees the method, even if you then multiply in one step.

Solved example 6 · Exam

WDV with a second asset and a sale — keep columns apart

Given. Year-end 31 March. Depreciation 20% p.a. on WDV.

  • 1 April 2022: purchased Machinery A for ₹8,00,000.
  • 1 October 2023: purchased Machinery B for ₹3,00,000.
  • 1 January 2025: sold Machinery A for ₹4,20,000.

Compute depreciation for FY 2022–23, 2023–24 and 2024–25, and the profit or loss on sale of A. Keep a separate column for each machine.

Machinery A (bought 1 April 2022 — a full year from day one)

FY 2022–23. Opening WDV = ₹8,00,000 .

Depreciation = 8,00,000 × 20/100 = ₹1,60,000 .

Closing WDV = 8,00,000 − 1,60,000 = ₹6,40,000 .

FY 2023–24. Opening WDV = ₹6,40,000 .

Depreciation = 6,40,000 × 20/100 = ₹1,28,000 .

Closing WDV = 6,40,000 − 1,28,000 = ₹5,12,000 .

FY 2024–25, used until 1 January 2025. 1 April 2024 to 1 January 2025 = April to December = 9 months .

Full-year depreciation on 5,12,000 = 5,12,000 × 20/100 = ₹1,02,400 .

Part-year = 1,02,400 × 9/12 = (1,02,400 × 9) ÷ 12.

1,02,400 × 9 = 9,21,600.

9,21,600 ÷ 12 = ₹76,800 .

Or: 1,02,400 × 3/4 = ₹76,800 .

NBV on the date of sale = 5,12,000 − 76,800 = ₹4,35,200 .

Sale proceeds ₹4,20,000 − NBV ₹4,35,200 = −₹15,200 — a loss of ₹15,200 .

Accumulated depreciation on A at sale = 1,60,000 + 1,28,000 + 76,800 = ₹3,64,800 .

Check: cost 8,00,000 − accum. 3,64,800 = NBV 4,35,200. Loss = 4,35,200 − 4,20,000 = ₹15,200 .

Machinery B (bought 1 October 2023)

FY 2023–24. 1 October 2023 to 31 March 2024 = 6 months.

Depreciation = 3,00,000 × 20/100 × 6/12 = 60,000 × 6/12 = ₹30,000 .

Closing WDV = 3,00,000 − 30,000 = ₹2,70,000 .

FY 2024–25. Full year on 2,70,000.

Depreciation = 2,70,000 × 20/100 = ₹54,000 .

Closing WDV = 2,70,000 − 54,000 = ₹2,16,000 .

Combined depreciation (what actually goes to P&L)

Two assets, one rate, separate columns — then add
Financial yearDep. on A (₹)Dep. on B (₹)Total to P&L (₹)
2022–231,60,000— (not yet bought)1,60,000
2023–241,28,00030,0001,58,000
2024–2576,800 (9 months, then sold)54,0001,30,800

1,28,000 + 30,000 = 1,58,000. 76,800 + 54,000 = 1,30,800.

Journals on 1 January 2025 for the sale of A

Sale under WDV — same journal shape as SLM; the amounts came from a different computation
DateParticularsL.F.Debit (₹)Credit (₹)
1 Jan 2025Depreciation A/c …… Dr.76,800
To Accumulated Depreciation A/c76,800
(Being 20% WDV depreciation on Machinery A for 9 months up to the date of sale)
1 Jan 2025Bank A/c …… Dr.4,20,000
Accumulated Depreciation A/c …… Dr.3,64,800
Loss on Sale of Machinery A/c …… Dr.15,200
To Machinery A/c8,00,000
(Being Machinery A sold at a loss of ₹15,200)

Debit cross-add: 4,20,000 + 3,64,800 + 15,200 = ₹8,00,000 = cost credited. The loss is whatever is needed to make this identity true. If your three debits do not add to cost, you have the wrong loss or the wrong accumulated depreciation.

Exam tip

When a second asset arrives, draw two mini-ledgers on the rough page. Never apply 20% to (A’s WDV + B’s cost) as one soup. B has its own 6-month first year; A does not.

9. How to identify the question

Use WDV when the question says any of: written down value, WDV, diminishing balance, reducing balance, on book value, on the reducing balance. “Rate % per annum on WDV” is the giveaway. “Rate % per annum on cost / on original cost” is SLM, even if the word “rate” made you think WDV.

10. Common mistakes
  • Deducting scrap every year before applying the WDV rate. Scrap is not part of the yearly working.
  • Applying the rate to original cost in year 2 and year 3. Year 2’s base is year 1’s closing WDV.
  • Using the SLM formula (Cost − Scrap) / n when the question has clearly given a WDV rate.
  • Forgetting the 6/12 (or 9/12, 3/12) in the year of purchase or the year of sale. WDV part-year is still months/12.
  • Adding a second asset into the first asset’s WDV and applying one rate to a mixed lump — always keep a column per asset, then add the depreciation.
11. Memory trick

WDV = What Decreases Yearly in rupees, even though the percentage is fixed. New gadgets lose more in year 1 — that is the picture to hold. Base next year = leftover, never the original price tag.

8. SLM versus WDV — comparison the examiner actually wants

2. In simple words

Same asset, two stories about how its cost dies. SLM kills it in equal rupees. WDV kills a larger rupee chunk up front and a smaller one later. The journals look the same. The numbers, the profit pattern, and the end-of-life book value do not.

SLM vs WDV — eight rows that cover a 5-to-8 mark distinguish question
PointStraight Line (SLM)Written Down Value (WDV)
Base of the rateOriginal cost, every yearOpening book value of that year
Amount patternSame rupees every full yearFalling rupees every full year
Residual in the yearly workingSubtracted once, in the formula (Cost − Scrap) / nNot subtracted yearly; rate is supposed to steer towards it
End of lifeWDV hits residual exactly (if life and scrap are honoured)Approaches residual; hits it only if the rate was derived from R = 1 − (S/C)1/n
Effect on profitEqual charge → comparable profits across years (other things equal)Heavier charge in early years → lower early profits, higher later profits
Best suited forBuildings, furniture, leases — equal service each yearPlant, vehicles, electronics — heavier usefulness (and repair later) in a skewed pattern
Repairs pattern (theory extra)Repairs usually rise as the asset ages, so total “dep + repairs” rises over timeFalling dep + rising repairs can keep the combined charge smoother
Calculation comfortOne division, then copy the answer each yearMust recompute every year on a new base; part-year needs two multiplications
Question-paper flags“straight line / original cost / equal / fixed instalment / on cost”“WDV / diminishing / reducing / on book value”
12. Exam-ready answer

Under SLM a fixed amount equal to (Cost − Residual) / Life is written off each full year, so book value falls in a straight line and meets residual exactly. Under WDV a fixed rate is applied to the book value brought forward, so the charge is higher in early years and lower later, and residual is not deducted annually. SLM suits assets with even service (buildings); WDV suits assets that lose efficiency or resale value quickly (plant, electronics). Total depreciation over the whole life equals the depreciable amount under SLM; under WDV it equals Cost minus the leftover book value, which equals residual only if the rate was derived from the residual formula.

Solved example 7 · Exam

Compute both methods for 3 years and comment — the comparison numerical

Given. Cost ₹5,00,000 , residual ₹50,000 , life 5 years. Compute depreciation for 3 years under (i) SLM and (ii) WDV at 20% p.a. Comment.

(i) SLM

Annual depreciation = (5,00,000 − 50,000) ÷ 5 = 4,50,000 ÷ 5 = ₹90,000 .

Rate on original cost = (90,000 ÷ 5,00,000) × 100 = 18%.

SLM — equal charge, lands on residual
YearDepreciation (₹)Accum. dep. (₹)WDV (₹)
190,00090,0004,10,000
290,0001,80,0003,20,000
390,0002,70,0002,30,000
4 (shown for the comment)90,0003,60,0001,40,000
5 (shown for the comment)90,0004,50,00050,000 = scrap

(ii) WDV at 20% (rate is given — do not derive it)

Year 1: 5,00,000 × 20/100 = ₹1,00,000 . WDV = 5,00,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹4,00,000 .

Year 2: 4,00,000 × 20/100 = ₹80,000 . WDV = 4,00,000 − 80,000 = ₹3,20,000 .

Year 3: 3,20,000 × 20/100 = ₹64,000 . WDV = 3,20,000 − 64,000 = ₹2,56,000 .

Year 4: 2,56,000 × 20/100 = ₹51,200 . WDV = 2,56,000 − 51,200 = ₹2,04,800 .

Year 5: 2,04,800 × 20/100 = ₹40,960 . WDV = 2,04,800 − 40,960 = ₹1,63,840 .

Three-year comparison the question asked for
YearSLM dep. (₹)WDV dep. (₹)Which method charges more this year?
190,0001,00,000WDV (front-loaded)
290,00080,000SLM
390,00064,000SLM
Total of 3 years2,70,0002,44,000SLM has charged ₹26,000 more by the end of year 3

1,00,000 + 80,000 + 64,000 = 2,44,000. 90,000 × 3 = 2,70,000. Difference = 26,000.

Comment (write this, not a vague “they are different”)

  1. WDV charges more in year 1 (₹1,00,000 vs ₹90,000) and less thereafter. Early profits are lower under WDV; later profits are higher.
  2. After 5 years SLM has written the asset down to residual ₹50,000 exactly. WDV at the given 20% still shows ₹1,63,840 — because 20% was not the residual-derived rate (that would have been about 36.90%).
  3. Total depreciation over the whole life is therefore not the same: SLM takes the full depreciable amount ₹4,50,000; WDV at 20% has taken only 5,00,000 − 1,63,840 = ₹3,36,160 after 5 years.
  4. If the question had asked which method is “conservative” in the early years, the answer is WDV — it recognises more expense sooner.

9. Two presentations: charge the asset, or keep a provision

1. What is it? — Definition

There are two bookkeeping styles for the same depreciation number. Direct method: credit the asset; the ledger then shows WDV as the asset’s balance. Indirect / provision / accumulated-depreciation method: credit a separate contra-asset; the asset ledger continues to show original cost. MBA papers usually want the provision method.

2. In simple words

Think of a price tag and a stack of “already-used” stickers. Direct method rewrites the price tag every year. Provision method leaves the price tag (cost) alone and piles stickers next to it. Anyone reading the Balance Sheet under the provision method can still see what you originally paid.

3. Why do we need it?

Companies Act / Schedule III style statements show Gross Block, Accumulated Depreciation and Net Block. That layout is impossible if you have already credited the asset and thrown cost away. So the provision method is the one you should default to in an exam unless told otherwise.

6. Format — Same ₹18,000, two journals, two Balance Sheets (from Example 1, year 1)

Direct method

Credit the asset
DateParticularsL.F.Debit (₹)Credit (₹)
31 MarDepreciation A/c …… Dr.18,000
To Machinery A/c18,000
(Being depreciation charged directly to the asset)
Cost has disappeared from the face of the statement
Balance Sheet extract₹
Machinery (at WDV)82,000

Provision method (preferred)

Credit the contra-asset
DateParticularsL.F.Debit (₹)Credit (₹)
31 MarDepreciation A/c …… Dr.18,000
To Accumulated Depreciation A/c18,000
(Being depreciation transferred to the provision / accumulated account)
Cost remains visible — this is the MBA default
Balance Sheet extract₹₹
Machinery (at cost)1,00,000
Less: Accumulated depreciation18,00082,000
Key point

Profit is identical under both presentations — ₹18,000 expense either way. Only the display of the asset changes. Do not compute depreciation twice because you saw two methods.

On sale, the direct method is shorter because the asset already sits at NBV. After charging dep up to the date of sale (Example 3’s machine, NBV ₹3,79,600; sold for ₹3,80,000):

Sale under the direct method — no accumulated-depreciation line, because that account does not exist
DateParticularsL.F.Debit (₹)Credit (₹)
30 Sep 2025Bank A/c …… Dr.3,80,000
To Machinery A/c3,79,600
To Profit on Sale of Machinery A/c400
(Direct method — asset already at NBV, so we credit NBV and recognise the ₹400 profit)

Under the provision method (already shown in Example 3) you must debit Accumulated Depreciation to kill the contra-asset, and credit Machinery with original cost. Same profit of ₹400. If the question has been using a Provision for Depreciation account all along, stay with that account on the sale date.

10. How to identify, what to avoid, how to remember

9. How to identify the question

Straight line / original cost / equal / fixed instalment / “rate % p.a. on cost” → SLM. Annual amount = (Cost − Residual) / Life, or Cost × the given on-cost rate. WDV / diminishing / reducing balance / written down / “on WDV” / “on book value” → WDV. Amount = Opening WDV × Rate. Part-year: always count months from the date put to use to the year-end (or to the date of sale). Indian year-end 31 March and “put to use on 1 October” → 6/12. A second asset → a second column. A sale → depreciate first, then remove the asset, then profit or loss.

10. Common mistakes
  • Applying an SLM rate to WDV (or a WDV rate to original cost after year 1).
  • Deducting scrap every year under WDV.
  • Forgetting installation, freight or non-refundable duty in cost.
  • Charging a full year when the asset was purchased on 1 January (3/12) or 1 October (6/12).
  • Treating depreciation as a cash outflow in a cash-flow question (that belongs to the cash-flow chapter — add it back).
  • Skipping depreciation in the year of sale.
  • Taking “10% of cost” as 10% of the invoice when installation has been added — scrap follows total cost.
  • Mixing two machines into one WDV base.
  • Calling accumulated depreciation a cash reserve or a replacement fund.
11. Memory trick

SLM = Same Load every year, like equal slices (equal “principal” in an EMI picture). WDV = new gadgets lose more in year 1. Part-year = months/12, always. Sale = depreciate → strip the accounts → proceeds versus NBV. Cash left the business on the purchase date, not on the depreciation date.

Exam tip

Before you multiply, write one heading on the rough page: “SLM on cost” or “WDV on book”. Circle the date put to use and the year-end. Circle installation. Circle “sold on”. Those four circles are the entire exam technique for this chapter.

11. Practice questions (try, then open the solution)

Three questions, rising in difficulty, using numbers you have not already seen in the worked examples. Write the full working — including the multiplications — before you scroll.

Practice 1 · Easy

SLM furniture — annual charge, 3-year schedule, residual check

Furniture is purchased for ₹80,000 . Residual value ₹8,000 . Useful life 8 years. SLM.

Required:

  1. Annual depreciation and the rate on original cost.
  2. A 3-year schedule showing cost, depreciation, accumulated depreciation and WDV.
  3. WDV at the end of year 8 (without listing every year).
  4. The year-1 journal under the provision method, and the Balance Sheet extract after 3 years.

Answer / solution

Step 1. Depreciable amount = 80,000 − 8,000 = ₹72,000 .

Annual depreciation = 72,000 ÷ 8 = ₹9,000 .

Rate on original cost = (9,000 ÷ 80,000) × 100 = 11.25% .

Check: 80,000 × 11.25/100 = 80,000 × 0.1125. 80,000 × 0.10 = 8,000; 80,000 × 0.0125 = 1,000; total 9,000.

Step 2. Schedule of 3 years.

Practice 1 — SLM schedule

Year-1 WDV: 80,000 − 9,000 = 71,000. Year-2: 71,000 − 9,000 = 62,000. Year-3: 62,000 − 9,000 = 53,000. Accum. year 3 = 9,000 × 3 = 27,000.

Step 3. After 8 years accumulated depreciation = 9,000 × 8 = ₹72,000 .

WDV at the end of year 8 = 80,000 − 72,000 = ₹8,000 = scrap. That is the SLM landing-check.

Step 4. Journals and presentation.

Practice 2 · Moderate

WDV 20% — purchased 1 January, year-end 31 March

A plant costs ₹6,00,000 . It is put to use on 1 January 2024 . Depreciation is charged at 20% p.a. on WDV . The accounting year ends on 31 March.

Required: depreciation and closing WDV for FY 2023–24, 2024–25 and 2025–26. Show every multiplication. Then pass the FY 2023–24 journal.

Answer / solution

FY 2023–24. Put to use 1 January 2024 to 31 March 2024 = January, February, March = 3 months .

Full-year depreciation on cost = 6,00,000 × 20/100 = ₹1,20,000 .

Part-year = 1,20,000 × 3/12 = (1,20,000 × 3) ÷ 12 = 3,60,000 ÷ 12 = ₹30,000 .

Combined: 6,00,000 × 20/100 × 3/12 = 6,00,000 × 1/5 × 1/4 = 1,20,000 × 1/4 = ₹30,000 .

Closing WDV = 6,00,000 − 30,000 = ₹5,70,000 .

FY 2024–25. Full year on ₹5,70,000 .

Depreciation = 5,70,000 × 20/100 = 5,70,000 × 1/5 = ₹1,14,000 .

Closing WDV = 5,70,000 − 1,14,000 = ₹4,56,000 .

FY 2025–26. Full year on ₹4,56,000 .

Depreciation = 4,56,000 × 20/100 = 4,56,000 × 1/5 = ₹91,200 .

Closing WDV = 4,56,000 − 91,200 = ₹3,64,800 .

Trap you should have avoided: charging ₹1,20,000 in FY 2023–24 (a full year) even though the plant worked only 3 months. 1 January to 31 March is the shortest common part-year in Indian papers — and the most often missed.

Practice 3 · Exam

Installation, 10% scrap, SLM, sold on 1 October — loss and journals

On 1 April 2021 a company bought a machine for ₹4,00,000 . Installation ₹40,000 . Residual is 10% of cost. Useful life 8 years. SLM. Year-end 31 March.

On 1 October 2024 the machine was sold for ₹2,50,000 .

Required:

  1. Cost, scrap, annual depreciation and the SLM rate.
  2. Depreciation for each financial year up to the date of sale, and NBV on 1 October 2024.
  3. Profit or loss on sale.
  4. Journal entries on the date of sale (provision method), with a cross-add check.

Answer / solution

(a) Cost, scrap, annual dep, rate.

Cost = 4,00,000 + 40,000 = ₹4,40,000 .

Scrap = 10% of 4,40,000 = (10/100) × 4,40,000 = ₹44,000 .

Depreciable amount = 4,40,000 − 44,000 = ₹3,96,000 .

Annual depreciation = 3,96,000 ÷ 8 = ₹49,500 .

Rate on original cost = (49,500 ÷ 4,40,000) × 100 = 11.25%.

Check: 4,40,000 × 11.25/100 = 4,40,000 × 0.1125. 4,40,000 × 0.10 = 44,000; 4,40,000 × 0.0125 = 5,500; total 49,500.

(b) Year-by-year up to sale.

Bought 1 April 2021, so FY 2021–22, 2022–23 and 2023–24 are full years.

Sold 1 October 2024 → FY 2024–25 from 1 April to 1 October = April to September = 6 months .

6-month depreciation = 49,500 × 6/12 = 49,500 × 1/2 = ₹24,750 .

Practice 3 — SLM until the morning of the sale

2021–221249,50049,5003,90,500
2022–231249,50099,0003,41,000
2023–241249,5001,48,5002,91,500
2024–25 to 1 Oct624,7501,73,2502,66,750

NBV walk: 4,40,000 − 49,500 = 3,90,500; − 49,500 = 3,41,000; − 49,500 = 2,91,500; − 24,750 = 2,66,750. Accum. = 49,500 × 3 + 24,750 = 1,48,500 + 24,750 = 1,73,250. Cost − accum. = 4,40,000 − 1,73,250 = 2,66,750.

(c) Profit or loss.

Sale proceeds ₹2,50,000 − NBV ₹2,66,750 = loss of ₹16,750 .

Working: 2,66,750 − 2,50,000 = 16,750.

(d) Journals on 1 October 2024.

To Accumulated Depreciation A/c24,750
(Being SLM depreciation for 6 months up to the date of sale)
