How to identify the question, traps, and a 5-mark theory answer

9. How to identify the question

The question is this chapter when it says any of: 'prepare the Statement of Profit and Loss and Balance Sheet as per Schedule III'; 'as per Companies Act, 2013'; 'in the prescribed form'; the entity is 'Ltd' / 'Limited' / 'Pvt Ltd' and you are given a trial balance plus adjustments. If it asks only for a cash flow, that is the next chapter. If it asks ratios, that is the ratios chapter — but those ratios are computed from the Schedule III statements you have just learned to build.

10. Common mistakes
  • Putting drawings in a company problem. Companies do not have drawings; they have dividends.
  • Mixing Trade payables with borrowings (bank overdraft) and with Other current liabilities (outstanding expenses, current maturities, accrued interest).
  • Forgetting the current vs non-current split — dumping a 5-year loan and next year's instalment in one line.
  • Showing proposed dividend as an expense in the Statement of Profit and Loss. It is not an expense. Modern treatment: note only, no liability until declared.
  • Not netting provision for doubtful debts against Trade receivables, and instead parking it under liabilities.
  • Forgetting outstanding interest on both sides: it is Finance costs AND Other current liabilities.
  • Charging depreciation inside Other expenses instead of the prescribed Depreciation line.
  • Putting interest received inside Revenue from operations, or interest paid inside Other expenses.
  • Adding authorised capital into the Balance Sheet total.
  • Leaving current-year profit out of Reserves and surplus — then the Balance Sheet will not tie.
  • Using a 1956 horizontal T-shape instead of the vertical Schedule III order.
  • Ignoring 'increase in provision': if the TB already has a provision, only the extra amount is this year's expense.
11. Memory trick

Liabilities tell you who funded the assets. Notes are the footnotes of the story. P&L is the movie of the year; Balance Sheet is the photograph on 31 March. Current = within a year (or the cycle). Interest paid is finance cost; interest earned is other income. No drawings. Dividend is not an expense. Proposed dividend, today, is a note.

5 marks

What is Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013? State the major heads of the Balance Sheet.

Schedule III is the schedule to the Companies Act, 2013 that prescribes the format of the Balance Sheet and the Statement of Profit and Loss of a company. It requires vertical presentation, classification of items into current and non-current, corresponding figures of the previous year, and Notes to Accounts, so that the statements give a true and fair view and can be compared across companies.

Major heads of the Balance Sheet:

Equity and Liabilities — (1) Shareholders' funds: share capital; reserves and surplus; money received against share warrants. (2) Share application money pending allotment. (3) Non-current liabilities: long-term borrowings; deferred tax liabilities (net); other long-term liabilities; long-term provisions. (4) Current liabilities: short-term borrowings; trade payables; other current liabilities; short-term provisions.

Assets — (1) Non-current assets: property, plant and equipment / fixed assets (tangible and intangible); non-current investments; deferred tax assets (net); long-term loans and advances; other non-current assets. (2) Current assets: current investments; inventories; trade receivables; cash and cash equivalents; short-term loans and advances; other current assets.

12. Exam-ready answer

Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes the vertical form of the Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit and Loss. The Balance Sheet major heads are: Shareholders' funds; Share application money pending allotment; Non-current liabilities; Current liabilities; Non-current assets; Current assets — each with the sub-heads listed in the 5-mark answer above. Items are classified current or non-current using the operating cycle / 12-month rule, and the face is supported by Notes to Accounts.

7. 16-mark procedure you can write in the margin
  1. Underline 'Schedule III' / 'Companies Act 2013' / 'Ltd'. Draw the empty P&L and BS skeletons with heads.
  2. Tick every TB item into a skeleton line (or into a working that feeds a line). Do not leave an item un-ticked.
  3. Process adjustments in order: stock, outstanding, prepaid, accrued, unearned, depreciation, interest, provision, PFDD, samples, commission, tax, dividend.
  4. Compute P&L down to Profit for the period. Transfer that profit to surplus.
  5. Build notes. Cross-foot each note to the face.
  6. Total Equity and Liabilities. Total Assets. If they differ, hunt outstanding interest, closing stock, and the profit transfer first.

Practice — then check the solution

Practice 4.1 · Easy

Where does each item sit?

State the Schedule III line (P&L or Balance Sheet) for: (i) Bank overdraft (ii) Outstanding audit fee (iii) Securities premium (iv) Interest on debentures (v) Dividend received (vi) Provision for tax (vii) Prepaid rent (viii) Calls in arrears.

Answer / solution

  • (i) Balance Sheet — Current liabilities — Short-term borrowings.
  • (ii) Balance Sheet — Other current liabilities; and P&L — Other expenses (if not already in TB).
  • (iii) Balance Sheet — Shareholders' funds — Reserves and surplus.
  • (iv) P&L — Finance costs. Unpaid slice: Other current liabilities.
  • (v) P&L — Other income.
  • (vi) P&L — Tax expense; Balance Sheet — Short-term provisions.
  • (vii) Balance Sheet — Other current assets; and it reduces Other expenses.
  • (viii) Deducted from called-up capital in the Share capital note; face shows paid-up.
Practice 4.2 · Moderate

Commission after charging, plus outstanding interest

Profit before commission, interest outstanding and tax is ₹2,30,000. This figure has not yet been charged with: (a) outstanding interest on 10% loan of ₹1,00,000 for the full year (nothing paid yet); (b) manager's commission 10% on profit after charging such commission but before tax; (c) provision for tax ₹30,000. Compute finance cost, commission, profit before tax, and profit for the period.

Answer / solution

Step 1 — finance cost.

Interest outstanding = 10/100 × ₹1,00,000 = ₹10,000. This is Finance costs. It is also Other current liabilities ₹10,000.

Step 2 — profit before commission and tax.

₹2,30,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹2,20,000.

Step 3 — commission after charging such commission.

Commission = ₹2,20,000 × 10 / 110.

₹2,20,000 × 10 = ₹22,00,000. ₹22,00,000 / 110 = ₹20,000.

Check: profit after commission = ₹2,20,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹2,00,000. 10% of ₹2,00,000 = ₹20,000. Holds.

Step 4 — profit before tax.

₹2,20,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹2,00,000.

Step 5 — profit for the period.

Tax ₹30,000. Profit for the period = ₹2,00,000 − ₹30,000 = ₹1,70,000.

Employee benefits include outstanding commission ₹20,000. Finance costs ₹10,000. Tax expense ₹30,000. Short-term provisions (tax) ₹30,000. Other current liabilities: interest ₹10,000 + commission ₹20,000 = ₹30,000.

Practice 4.3 · Exam-level

Rebuild three Horizon figures from memory

Without looking back: (i) write the identity that makes 'Purchases + Changes in inventories' equal COGS for Horizon; (ii) compute the increase in PFDD; (iii) name the two items inside Other current liabilities and their total. Then state why proposed dividend, had the board proposed ₹1 per share, would not appear in those liabilities under current Schedule III.

Answer / solution

  • (i) Opening ₹80,000 + Purchases ₹6,20,000 − Closing ₹1,10,000 = COGS ₹5,90,000. Purchases ₹6,20,000 + Change (₹30,000) = ₹5,90,000.
  • (ii) 5/100 × ₹1,40,000 = ₹7,000 required; existing ₹6,000; increase ₹1,000.
  • (iii) Outstanding salaries ₹10,000 + Outstanding debenture interest ₹12,000 = ₹22,000.
  • Proposed dividend of 50,000 × ₹1 = ₹50,000 would be disclosed in notes. It is not a liability until declared, so it does not sit in Other current liabilities or Short-term provisions on 31 March 2026.
Connect the chapters

You can now wrap any adjusted trial balance of a company in Schedule III clothing. The next chapter typically takes this Profit before tax / Profit for the period and the Balance Sheet and asks you to explain cash (cash flow statement) or to compute ratios. Garbage in, garbage out: if outstanding interest never reached Finance costs, every profitability and coverage ratio later will be wrong.

Chapter 5

Cash Flow Statements

Learning outcome. You will be able to explain why profit is not cash, classify every item into operating / investing / financing activities (AS-3), and prepare a complete Cash Flow Statement by the indirect method — including working notes for plant, depreciation, tax, dividend and interest — so that net cash (A+B+C) equals the change in cash on the Balance Sheet.

What this chapter covers (official syllabus)

  • Need and importance of Cash Flow Statement
  • Preparation of Cash Flow Statement
  • Indirect Method

Profit is not cash — start here, or the whole chapter will feel like magic

This is the heart of the chapter. If you only remember one sentence, remember this: a business can make a handsome profit and still run out of cash — and it can make a loss and still have cash coming in. The Profit and Loss Account does not tell you what happened to the bank balance. The Cash Flow Statement does.

Meet Meera. She runs a small garment shop in Pune. At the year-end her accountant smiles and says, “Madam, you made a profit of ₹1,00,000 this year.” Meera opens her bank app. She expected the balance to have grown by about the same amount. It has not. She is confused, and a little angry. This chapter exists because of Meera.

Here is everything that happened in Meera’s year. We will walk through each item and ask two questions: Did this change profit? Did this change cash? Those two answers are often different. That difference is the whole subject.

Meera’s year, item by item

Meera’s four items — profit and cash disagree on every one of them
What happenedIn the Profit & Loss Account?In the bank account?
Credit sales still receivable ₹40,000 (customers have the clothes; Meera does not have the money yet)Yes — sales (and therefore profit) include this ₹40,000No cash received. Debtors went up. The bank did not.
Bought a stitching machine for ₹70,000 cashNo — this is an asset, not an expense. Profit is untouched (except later, a little, through depreciation).Yes — ₹70,000 left the bank today.
Depreciation on shop fittings ₹15,000Yes — it is an expense. It reduced profit by ₹15,000.No cash moved. Depreciation is a book entry, not a cheque.
Took a bank loan of ₹50,000No — a loan is not income. Profit does not include it.Yes — ₹50,000 came into the bank.

Now let us put full numbers on the same story, so you can see the gap. Assume the rest of her trading is ordinary cash business, and she started the year with cash of ₹25,000.

Step 1 — How the accountant got profit of ₹1,00,000

Meera’s sales for the year were ₹5,00,000. Out of this, ₹40,000 is still to be collected from customers, so cash actually collected from customers is ₹5,00,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹4,60,000.

Cash operating expenses (purchases of cloth, wages, rent, electricity, all paid in cash) were ₹3,85,000. Depreciation was ₹15,000. There were no other expenses.

Meera’s Profit and Loss Account (condensed)
Particulars₹
Sales₹5,00,000
Less: Cash operating expenses(₹3,85,000)
Profit before depreciation (₹5,00,000 − ₹3,85,000)₹1,15,000
Less: Depreciation (expense, but not cash)(₹15,000)
Net profit (₹1,15,000 − ₹15,000)₹1,00,000

The accountant is not wrong. Profit really is ₹1,00,000. The P&L Account is doing its job. It is just answering a different question from the one Meera asked her bank app.

Step 2 — What actually happened to the bank balance

Write every cash movement. Do not skip a line. This is how cash works.

Meera’s actual cash movement for the year
MovementWork₹
Opening cash / bankgiven₹25,000
Add: Cash collected from customers₹5,00,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹4,60,000₹4,60,000
Less: Cash operating expensesgiven(₹3,85,000)
Sub-total after running the shop₹25,000 + ₹4,60,000 − ₹3,85,000 = ₹1,00,000₹1,00,000
Less: Machine purchased (cash)given(₹70,000)
Sub-total after buying the machine₹1,00,000 − ₹70,000 = ₹30,000₹30,000
Add: Loan takengiven₹50,000
Closing cash / bank₹30,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹80,000₹80,000
Key point

Profit = ₹1,00,000. Increase in cash = ₹80,000 − ₹25,000 = ₹55,000. They are not equal. ₹1,00,000 ≠ ₹55,000. Anyone who treats “profit” as “cash generated” is reading the wrong statement.

Step 3 — The same story, rewritten as a Cash Flow Statement

The indirect method (the method this chapter teaches, and the method your exam will ask) starts from profit and then undoes every item that is not cash, and every item that is not operating. Watch how Meera’s four items become four adjustments.

Meera — first Cash Flow Statement (indirect method)
Particulars₹
Cash flows from operating activities
Net profit₹1,00,000
Add: Depreciation (expense deducted in P&L, but no cash left)₹15,000
Less: Increase in debtors (profit counted a sale that brought no cash)(₹40,000)
Net cash from operating activities (A) (₹1,00,000 + ₹15,000 − ₹40,000)₹75,000
Cash flows from investing activities
Purchase of machinery (cash)(₹70,000)
Net cash from investing activities (B)(₹70,000)
Cash flows from financing activities
Loan taken₹50,000
Net cash from financing activities (C)₹50,000
Net increase in cash (A + B + C) (₹75,000 − ₹70,000 + ₹50,000)₹55,000
Add: Opening cash and cash equivalents₹25,000
Closing cash and cash equivalents (₹55,000 + ₹25,000)₹80,000

Proof: A + B + C = 75,000 − 70,000 + 50,000 = 55,000, which equals closing cash 80,000 − opening cash 25,000. The statement is internally true.

5. Accounting logic

Profit measures performance using accrual accounting: you count a sale when you earn it, and an expense when you consume it — even if cash moves on a different day, or never moves (depreciation). Cash flow measures liquidity: what actually went into and out of the bank. Both are true. They answer different questions. The Cash Flow Statement is the bridge: it starts from the profit figure you already trust, and walks you, line by line, to the cash figure you can see in the bank.

11. Memory trick

Three moves, always, in this order: (1) Add back non-cash expenses (depreciation, written-off items). (2) Undo non-operating items that sat inside profit (profit/loss on sale, interest, dividend income) so they can be placed in investing or financing. (3) Squeeze working capital — stock, debtors, prepaid, creditors, outstanding — because extra current assets lock cash and extra current liabilities keep cash in the business. Then tax paid. That is operating cash. Then buy/sell the tools (investing). Then talk to owners and lenders (financing).

Connect the chapters

Chapter on the Profit and Loss Account told you whether the business earned. Chapter on the Balance Sheet told you what it owns and owes on a date. This chapter tells you where the cash came from and where it went during the period. The three statements are a set. A Cash Flow Statement that does not reconcile to the change in cash on the two Balance Sheets is simply wrong — the examiner will see it in ten seconds.

What is a Cash Flow Statement?

1. What is it? — Definition

A Cash Flow Statement (CFS) is a statement that shows the inflows (receipts) and outflows (payments) of cash and cash equivalents during an accounting period, classified into operating, investing and financing activities. It explains the movement from the opening cash balance to the closing cash balance. In India it is prepared as per AS-3 (Cash Flow Statements) or, for companies following Ind AS, Ind AS-7 (Statement of Cash Flows).

2. In simple words

Imagine a video of your bank account for the whole year, sorted into three folders: (A) money from running the shop, (B) money spent on or received from long-term assets, (C) money from owners and lenders. That video, printed as a statement, is the Cash Flow Statement. It does not replace the P&L. It sits beside it.

3. Why do we need it?

Profit can hide a cash crisis. A fast-growing firm that sells on credit, fills its godown, and buys a new machine can show a profit and still bounce a cheque. Lenders, owners and managers cannot wait until the cash actually runs out. They need a statement whose last line is the same number as the cash on the Balance Sheet — with every rupee of movement labelled.

4. Real-life example

A Mumbai trader earns ₹8,00,000 profit in a year of boom. Almost all of it is sitting in debtors (retail chains pay in 90 days) and in extra Diwali stock. He has also paid ₹5,00,000 for a delivery van. His bank account is tight. The P&L says “well done”. The CFS says “operating cash is weak; investing ate the rest; you need a working-capital loan or slower growth.” Both statements are useful. Only one of them would have stopped him bouncing the VAT payment.

5. Accounting logic

Accrual accounting records when the right to cash arises, not when cash arrives. To convert accrual profit into cash, we reverse every accrual and every non-cash charge, and we park non-operating cash in the activity that actually produced it. That conversion is the indirect method.

The three statements are a set — each answers one question
StatementQuestion it answersWhat it will not tell you
Profit & Loss AccountDid we earn a profit this year?Whether that profit is sitting in the bank, in debtors, or was never cash (depreciation).
Balance SheetWhat do we own and owe on one date?How we moved from last year’s cash to this year’s cash.
Cash Flow StatementWhere did cash come from, and where did it go, during the year?Whether the business is “profitable”. A firm can have positive cash and a loss, or the reverse.

Need and importance of a Cash Flow Statement

1. What is it? — Definition

The need for a Cash Flow Statement arises because profit is an accrual figure. Users who care about liquidity, solvency and the quality of earnings cannot read those things from the P&L alone. The CFS is the statement that reports the generation and use of cash, classified by activity, so that users can judge whether the firm can pay its bills, repay loans, pay dividends and fund growth from its own operations.

2. In simple words

You need a CFS for the same reason you look at your bank SMS thread and not only at your salary slip. The salary slip is the P&L. The SMS thread is the cash flow. Both matter. They are not the same document.

3. Why do we need it?

Without a CFS: (i) a lender cannot see whether instalments will be paid from operations or from fresh borrowing; (ii) management cannot see that stock and debtors are swallowing cash; (iii) investors cannot see whether dividends are being paid from genuine operating cash or from selling the family silver (fixed assets) or from new loans; (iv) the P&L and Balance Sheet remain two unconnected photographs instead of a film of the year.

Who uses it, and for what

Users of the Cash Flow Statement
UserWhat they look forWhy it matters
ManagementOperating cash vs profit; working-capital squeeze; free cash after investingDeciding credit policy, stock levels, capex, and whether a loan is needed.
Lenders and bankersCash from operations compared with interest and principal dueA firm that borrows to pay interest is not the same as a firm that generates cash and then borrows to grow.
Investors and analystsQuality of earnings: is profit turning into cash?Profit built on rising debtors is weaker than the same profit collected in cash.
Suppliers and employeesAbility to pay on timeOutstanding wages and creditors are paid in cash, not in profit.
Regulators / tax authoritiesA complete set of financial statementsListed and prescribed companies must present a CFS with the annual accounts.

Legal and accounting status in India (exam points)

  • AS-3 Cash Flow Statements is the Accounting Standard for companies that are not on Ind AS. It requires a CFS classifying cash flows into operating, investing and financing, and permits both direct and indirect methods for operating cash (Indian MBA exams almost always want the indirect method).
  • Ind AS-7 Statement of Cash Flows is the Ind-AS version (aligned with IAS-7). The three-activity structure is the same. The main exam-relevant difference is that Ind AS-7 allows options for classifying interest and dividend; AS-3 is stricter. For MBA we teach the AS-3 classic classification unless the question names Ind AS-7 and asks for the option.
  • Companies Act, 2013: a Cash Flow Statement is part of the financial statements. It is mandatory for companies other than One Person Companies, small companies and dormant companies (they are exempt unless they choose to prepare it). Listed companies must prepare it (SEBI LODR + accounting standards). “Prescribed companies” in older exam language means companies that the Act / rules require to include a CFS.
  • The CFS complements the P&L and the Balance Sheet. It does not replace either. Schedule III presentation still starts with the Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit and Loss; the CFS is the third primary statement.
12. Exam-ready answer

A Cash Flow Statement is needed because the Profit and Loss Account is prepared on the accrual basis and therefore profit is not equal to cash. The CFS reports inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents, classified into operating, investing and financing activities, as required by AS-3 (or Ind AS-7). It is useful to management for liquidity planning, to lenders for assessing debt-servicing capacity, and to investors for judging the quality of earnings. Under the Companies Act, 2013 it is mandatory for companies other than OPC, small companies and dormant companies; listed companies must prepare it. It complements the P&L and the Balance Sheet by reconciling the opening and closing cash balances.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “Explain the need / importance / advantages of a Cash Flow Statement” or “Why is a CFS prepared?” — write the theory answer above: profit ≠ cash, three activities, users (management, lenders, investors), AS-3 / Ind AS-7, mandatory for listed and prescribed companies, complements P&L and BS. This is a 5–8 mark theory question. If it says “Prepare a Cash Flow Statement” / “indirect method” / “AS-3”, it is a practical question — go to the format and the workings, not the theory.

Meaning of cash and cash equivalents

1. What is it? — Definition

Cash comprises cash on hand and demand deposits with banks (cash at bank). Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and that are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value. AS-3 says an investment normally qualifies only when it has a short maturity of, say, three months or less from the date of acquisition.

2. In simple words

Cash equivalents are not “investments” in the ordinary sense. They are parking places for spare money that you can turn back into cash almost at once, without worrying that the price moved. A 60-day Treasury bill bought two months ago is a cash equivalent. Shares of Infosys, even if you plan to sell them tomorrow, are not — equity shares have price risk, so they are investing items, not cash.

3. Why do we need it?

The CFS tracks the movement of the firm’s most liquid resources. If we counted only the notes in the till, a firm could “improve” its cash by shifting money into a 30-day deposit and the statement would show a fake outflow. Treating cash and cash equivalents as one pool stops that game. The last line of the CFS must equal cash + cash equivalents on the Balance Sheet.

4. Real-life example

On 31 March a company holds: currency ₹20,000, current-account balance ₹1,80,000, a 91-day T-bill bought on 1 March (maturity 30 May) ₹50,000, and 1,000 equity shares bought as a temporary parking ₹3,00,000. Cash and cash equivalents = ₹20,000 + ₹1,80,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹2,50,000. The equity shares are investments, not cash equivalents, even though the treasurer thinks of them as spare money.

5. Accounting logic

“Known amount of cash” + “insignificant risk of value change” + “short maturity (≤ 3 months from acquisition)” is a three-part test. Fail any one part and the item is an investment (investing activity), not cash. Equity shares fail the risk test. A two-year bond bought yesterday fails the maturity test. A six-month FD bought four months ago also fails (remaining life is short, but AS-3 looks at maturity from the date of acquisition, not remaining life).

What is (and is not) cash and cash equivalents
ItemCash / cash equivalent?Why
Cash in handYes — cashNotes and coins.
Bank current account (favourable balance)Yes — cashDemand deposit.
Bank savings accountYes — cashWithdraw on demand.
Short-term deposits / T-bills / commercial paper maturing ≤ 3 months from acquisitionYes — cash equivalentHighly liquid, known amount, insignificant value risk.
Equity shares (even listed, even held for 2 days)No — investing itemPrice risk is not “insignificant”. AS-3 specifically excludes equity investments.
Investments with original maturity of 6 months or 1 yearNo — investing itemMaturity from acquisition exceeds about three months.
Advance to a supplier / deposit with a landlordNoNot cash; not a short-term liquid investment. Working capital / other asset.
Bank overdraft repayable on demandExam: follow the questionAS-3: may be included as a cash equivalent (negative cash) if it is an integral part of cash management. Many MBA papers treat overdraft as a financing inflow/outflow. See the box below.
Watch out

Bank overdraft — the exam trap. AS-3 permits a bank overdraft repayable on demand to be treated as a component of cash and cash equivalents (so you net it against cash; the change in overdraft is not shown as financing). In practice, a large number of MBA and professional papers treat an increase in overdraft as a financing inflow and a decrease as a financing outflow, and they keep “cash” as the favourable bank balance only. Rule for the exam: follow the question. If the question shows overdraft separately from cash and does not say “cash and cash equivalents include overdraft”, treat the movement in overdraft as financing. If it says “cash and cash equivalents” and the overdraft is listed under that head, net it. Never invent a treatment that contradicts the question’s own figures.

12. Exam-ready answer

Cash comprises cash on hand and demand deposits with banks. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible into known amounts of cash and that are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value. An investment normally qualifies as a cash equivalent only when it has a short maturity of three months or less from the date of acquisition. Equity shares are not cash equivalents. Bank overdraft repayable on demand may be treated as a cash equivalent under AS-3 if it is an integral part of cash management; however, many examination problems treat overdraft as a financing activity, and that treatment should be followed when the question presents it that way.

The three activities — the skeleton of every Cash Flow Statement

1. What is it? — Definition

AS-3 requires every cash flow to be classified into one of three activities. Operating activities are the principal revenue-producing activities of the enterprise and other activities that are not investing or financing. Investing activities are the acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and other investments not included in cash equivalents. Financing activities are activities that result in changes in the size and composition of the owners’ capital and borrowings of the enterprise.

2. In simple words

Operations = running the shop. Investing = buying and selling the shop’s tools (and spare long-term money). Financing = talking to owners and lenders. Every line you write on a CFS must sit in one of these three rooms. If you cannot decide which room, you have not yet understood the item.

3. Why do we need it?

Classification is the whole point. A firm that generates ₹1,00,00,000 from operations and spends it on a new plant is a different animal from a firm that generates ₹1,00,00,000 by issuing shares and using the money to cover an operating cash drain. The total change in cash can be identical. The story is not. Examiners award marks for putting the rupee in the correct activity, not merely for the final cash figure.

11. Memory trick

Shop / Tools / Owners-and-lenders. If cash moved because a customer, a supplier, an employee or the tax department was involved in day-to-day business → operating. If cash moved because a long-term asset or an investment was bought or sold, or because interest/dividend was received → investing (AS-3). If cash moved because shares, debentures or loans were issued or repaid, or because interest/dividend was paid → financing (AS-3).

Operating activities

1. What is it? — Definition

Operating cash flows are the cash effects of transactions that determine net profit or loss, other than those that are classified as investing or financing. In the indirect method, we do not list cash from customers and cash to suppliers. We start from profit and adjust it until only operating cash remains.

2. In simple words

If you closed the shutters, stopped buying machines, and neither borrowed nor repaid anyone — the cash that would still move is operating cash. Customers pay you. You pay suppliers, staff, rent, power, and income tax. That is the shop running.

4. Real-life example

A restaurant’s operating inflows: cash from diners, collections from credit-card companies. Operating outflows: vegetables, salaries, rent, gas, GST/income tax paid. Buying a new oven is not operating (investing). Taking a loan to buy the oven is not operating (financing). Paying the baker is operating.

Operating activities — what belongs, and how the indirect method handles it
Typical operating itemInflow or outflowIndirect-method treatment
Cash collected from customersInflowHidden inside profit; increase in debtors is deducted, decrease is added.
Cash paid to suppliers of goods / servicesOutflowHidden inside profit; increase in stock/prepaid deducted; increase in creditors/outstanding added.
Wages, salaries, rent, power paidOutflowAlready in profit; outstanding wages movement is a working-capital adjustment.
Income tax paidOutflowShown separately after “cash generated from operations”, not left inside profit.
Depreciation, amortisation, written-off expensesNo cashAdded back to profit (non-cash).
Interest paid / dividend paidNot operating under AS-3Added back if they reduced profit, then shown as financing outflows.
Interest received / dividend receivedNot operating under AS-3Deducted if they increased profit, then shown as investing inflows.

Investing activities

1. What is it? — Definition

Investing activities are the acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and of other investments not included in cash equivalents. They show how much cash was used to obtain resources that will generate future income and cash flows — and how much cash came back when those resources were sold.

2. In simple words

Buying or selling the things the business keeps (plant, buildings, patents, shares of other companies, long-term deposits) is investing. The cash that changes hands is the actual sale proceeds or the actual purchase price, not the book value, not the profit or loss on sale. Profit or loss on sale is only a P&L figure; we remove it from operating and put the real cash in investing.

4. Real-life example

A factory sells an old lathe. Cost ₹80,000, accumulated depreciation ₹50,000, book value ₹30,000, sold for ₹35,000 cash. Investing inflow is ₹35,000 — the proceeds — not ₹30,000 and not the profit of ₹5,000. The ₹5,000 profit is deducted from operating profit so it is not counted twice.

Investing activities — AS-3 list you must memorise
Typical investing item (AS-3)Inflow or outflowNotes
Purchase of property, plant, equipment, intangiblesOutflowCash portion only. If bought by issuing shares, that portion is non-cash — exclude.
Sale proceeds of PPE / intangiblesInflowGross proceeds, not book value.
Purchase of investments (other than cash equivalents)OutflowShares, bonds, mutual funds, long-term deposits.
Sale proceeds of such investmentsInflowGross proceeds.
Loans and advances given to third partiesOutflowAS-3: investing. Repayment received = investing inflow.
Interest receivedInflowAS-3 classic: investing. Deduct from operating if it was inside profit.
Dividend receivedInflowAS-3 classic: investing. Deduct from operating if it was inside profit.
Capital work-in-progress paidOutflowSame family as purchase of PPE.

Financing activities

1. What is it? — Definition

Financing activities are those that result in changes in the size and composition of the owners’ capital (equity, including preference share capital) and borrowings of the enterprise. They answer: how did the firm raise cash from owners and lenders, and how did it return cash to them?

2. In simple words

If the other party to the cash movement is an owner (shareholder) or a lender (bank, debenture-holder), it is financing — with the AS-3 twist that interest paid and dividend paid are also financing, even though interest was an expense in the P&L.

4. Real-life example

A company issues 10,000 equity shares of ₹10 at a premium of ₹5. Cash received = 10,000 × ₹15 = ₹1,50,000. The whole ₹1,50,000 is a financing inflow (share capital ₹1,00,000 + securities premium ₹50,000). The split between capital and premium matters for the Balance Sheet; for the CFS it is one cash inflow: proceeds from issue of shares.

Financing activities — AS-3 list you must memorise
Typical financing item (AS-3)Inflow or outflowNotes
Proceeds from issue of equity / preference shares (for cash)InflowInclude securities premium received in cash.
Proceeds from issue of debentures / bondsInflowCash actually received (after discount, if issued at discount for cash).
Long-term or short-term loans takenInflowBank term loan, deposits accepted, etc.
Repayment of loans / redemption of debentures / preference sharesOutflowCash actually paid. Premium on redemption is part of the outflow.
Buy-back of sharesOutflowFinancing.
Interest paidOutflowAS-3: financing. Add back in operating if it reduced profit.
Dividend paid (equity or preference)OutflowAS-3: financing. Dividend is appropriation, not operating.
Bonus issue / conversion of debentures into shares / asset bought by issuing sharesNeither — non-cashDisclose in a note. Do not put a figure in A, B or C.

AS-3 classic classification of interest and dividend (memorise this)

Formula

AS-3: Interest received = Investing inflow  |  Dividend received = Investing inflow  |  Interest paid = Financing outflow  |  Dividend paid = Financing outflow

This is the default for MBA exams unless the question names Ind AS-7 and asks you to use an option.

Ind AS-7 options (know that they exist; do not use them unless asked): interest paid and interest/dividend received may be classified as operating or as financing/investing respectively; dividend paid may be classified as operating or financing. Once chosen, the policy must be consistent. For this chapter and for almost every MBA problem, use the AS-3 classic four-line rule above.

Exam tip

The examiner’s favourite trick is to leave interest paid inside profit and then also forget it in financing — or the reverse, to show it in financing without adding it back in operating. Both errors understate or overstate total cash by the interest figure. The pair is compulsory: add back interest expense in operating, then show interest paid as a financing outflow. Same pairing for interest/dividend income: deduct in operating, show as investing inflow.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “classify the following into operating, investing and financing”, write three headings and drop each item in the correct bucket using the AS-3 lists above. If it says “interest received” without naming Ind AS-7, it is investing. If it says “dividend paid”, it is financing. If it says “purchase of machinery by issue of shares”, write non-cash investing and financing transaction — disclosed in a note, not in the CFS body.

Indirect method — the format you must memorise

1. What is it? — Definition

Under the indirect method, net cash from operating activities is obtained by adjusting net profit before tax for non-cash items, unpaid/unearned items, non-operating items that belong in investing or financing, and changes in working capital, and then deducting income tax paid. Investing and financing sections then list the actual cash receipts and payments of those activities. Direct method (cash from customers, cash to suppliers) exists in AS-3 but is not the method this syllabus asks you to prepare.

2. In simple words

Indirect means: do not start from the cash book. Start from the profit you already computed. Then repair that profit until it becomes operating cash. It is called “indirect” because cash from customers is never shown as a line; it is buried inside “profit ± adjustments”.

3. Why do we need it?

Indian companies almost always publish the indirect method. MBA exams give you a P&L (or two Balance Sheets from which you reconstruct profit) plus additional information. That data set is designed for the indirect format. Learn one format, in this order, and never shuffle the blocks.

6. Format — Cash Flow Statement (Indirect Method) as per AS-3
Memorise this skeleton. Every practical question is this skeleton with numbers.

  Add: Loss on sale of fixed asset / investments×××

  Add: Interest expense (to move it to financing)×××
  Less: Interest income (to move it to investing)(×××)
  Less: Dividend income (to move it to investing)(×××)
  Add: Other non-cash expenses (goodwill written off, preliminary expenses written off, etc.)×××
Operating profit before working capital changes×××
Adjustments for working capital:
  Add: Decrease in current assets (except cash and cash equivalents)×××
  Less: Increase in current assets (except cash and cash equivalents)(×××)
  Add: Increase in current liabilities (except bank overdraft if treated as financing)×××
  Less: Decrease in current liabilities(×××)

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Read the question and mark three things: the two cash figures (opening and closing), the profit figure (or the two P&L surplus balances from which you will reconstruct profit), and the additional information (depreciation, sales of assets, tax, dividend, interest).
  2. Reconstruct Net profit before tax if it is not given: Closing P&L surplus − Opening P&L surplus + dividend paid (and/or current proposed dividend if appropriated) + transfer to reserves + bonus issue from P&L = Profit after tax. Then PAT + current tax charge = PBT. (Full working is later in this chapter.)
  3. Start the operating section with that PBT. Add back every non-cash expense (depreciation, amortisation, written-off items, loss on sale). Deduct every non-cash / non-operating income (profit on sale, interest income, dividend income). Add back interest expense.
  4. You now have operating profit before working capital changes. For every current asset except cash: increase → deduct, decrease → add. For every current liability except items you are treating as financing (often bank overdraft) and except provision for tax / proposed dividend (those have their own workings): increase → add, decrease → deduct.
  5. This gives cash generated from operations. Deduct income tax paid (not the P&L tax charge). Result is (A).
  6. Build investing (B): actual cash paid for PPE and investments, actual sale proceeds, interest received, dividend received. Derive missing purchase / sale figures from Plant A/c and Accumulated Depreciation A/c.
  7. Build financing (C): cash proceeds of issues and loans, cash repayments, interest paid, dividend paid. Ignore bonus issues and conversions.
  8. Compute A + B + C. Add opening cash and cash equivalents. The total must equal closing cash and cash equivalents on the Balance Sheet. If it does not, a working is wrong — find it before you move on. This equality is the only full-statement check the examiner has, and it is the only full-statement check you have.
Key point

The last three lines are not decoration. A + B + C + Opening cash = Closing cash. If you cannot make this identity true, you have not finished the question. Do not “plug” the difference into some random line. Go back to plant, tax, dividend and working capital — that is where almost every missing rupee hides.

Every common item — added, deducted, included or excluded

Treat this table as a drill sheet. For each item, four questions: Do I touch operating profit? Do I put a cash line in investing or financing? Is it a working-capital movement? Or is it non-cash and therefore excluded from the body of the CFS? Learn the why column; the rest follows.

Master treatment table — pin this beside every practical question
ItemAdded / Deducted / Included / ExcludedWhich activityWhy
DepreciationAdded back to profitOperating (adjustment only — no cash line)It reduced profit but no cash left the bank. Adding it back undoes the deduction.
Amortisation of intangibles / patents / computer softwareAdded back to profitOperating (adjustment)Same logic as depreciation: non-cash expense.
Profit on sale of fixed assetDeducted from profit; sale proceeds included in investingOperating (deduct) + Investing (inflow = proceeds)The profit is inside PBT but the cash is the full sale proceeds, which is an investing inflow. If you do not deduct the profit, you count it twice (once in operating, once inside proceeds).
Loss on sale of fixed assetAdded back to profit; sale proceeds included in investingOperating (add) + Investing (inflow = proceeds)The loss reduced profit without being a cash outflow. Adding it back, then showing actual proceeds in investing, puts the true cash in the right place.
Goodwill written offAdded back to profitOperating (adjustment)Non-cash expense (or appropriation treated as non-cash). No cash moved.
Preliminary expenses written offAdded back to profitOperating (adjustment)Non-cash write-off of a deferred expense. Cash was spent in an earlier year.
Discount on issue of debentures written offAdded back to profitOperating (adjustment)Non-cash. The related cash (issue proceeds, redemption) sits in financing.
Interest paid (interest expense)Added back to profit; then shown as a cash outflowOperating (add back) + Financing (outflow) under AS-3It reduced PBT but it is not an operating cash flow under AS-3. Pair the two entries or you drop the cash once.
Interest received (interest income)Deducted from profit; then shown as a cash inflowOperating (deduct) + Investing (inflow) under AS-3It increased PBT but AS-3 classifies the cash as investing. Pair the two entries.
Dividend paidNot an expense (appropriation). Do not add/deduct in operating. Show the cash paid.Financing outflow under AS-3Dividend never sits inside PBT. Find the cash paid from proposed-dividend workings or from additional information.
Dividend receivedDeducted from profit if included in PBT; then shown as a cash inflowOperating (deduct) + Investing (inflow) under AS-3Same pairing as interest received.
Issue of shares for cash (including premium received in cash)Included as a cash inflow (the actual proceeds)Financing inflowOwners put cash in. Bonus issue is a different item — see below.
Bonus issueExcluded — non-cashNone in the CFS body. Disclose in a note if asked.Reserves (or P&L) are converted into share capital. No cash moves. If bonus was charged to P&L surplus, add it back when reconstructing PAT, then ignore it in A, B and C.
Conversion of debentures into sharesExcluded — non-cashNone in the CFS body. Disclose in a note.Liability becomes equity. No cash. When reconciling debentures and share capital, strip this amount out of “cash proceeds” and “cash redemption”.
Purchase of asset by issuing shares (or debentures)Excluded — non-cash (cash portion, if any, is investing)Note. Cash paid, if mixed consideration, is investing outflow.AS-3: non-cash investing and financing transactions are disclosed in a note, not in the statement.
Increase in debtors (trade receivables)Deducted in working capitalOperatingSales were counted in profit but the cash has not arrived. Cash is locked in debtors.
Decrease in debtorsAdded in working capitalOperatingOld credit sales have been collected. Extra cash came in, over and above this year’s sales.
Increase in stock (inventory)Deducted in working capitalOperatingCash (or credit that will become cash) was used to buy goods that are still unsold. Cash is locked in the godown.
Decrease in stockAdded in working capitalOperatingStock sold (its cost is in P&L as COGS) was bought in an earlier period. You get the cash effect of running down the godown.
Decrease in creditors (trade payables)Deducted in working capitalOperatingYou paid old dues. Extra cash left, over and above this year’s purchases.
Increase in creditorsAdded in working capitalOperatingPurchases were counted in profit/COGS but not fully paid. Cash was retained.
Prepaid expenses (increase)Deducted (increase in current asset)OperatingYou paid this year for an expense that belongs to next year. Extra cash left.
Prepaid expenses (decrease)Added (decrease in current asset)OperatingThis year’s P&L expense includes a prepayment made last year. Cash did not leave this year for that portion.
Outstanding expenses (increase)Added (increase in current liability)OperatingExpense is in the P&L but unpaid. Cash still in the bank.
Outstanding expenses (decrease)Deducted (decrease in current liability)OperatingYou paid last year’s outstanding plus this year’s. Extra cash left.
Provision for tax (the P&L charge)Do not treat as a working-capital item. Start from PBT so the charge is not inside the starting profit. Then deduct tax paid.Operating — the cash line is “Income tax paid”Tax paid = Opening provision + Current tax charge − Closing provision. Using the closing provision as if it were tax paid is a classic error.
Proposed dividendNot a working-capital item in the operating section. The cash line is dividend paid, in financing.Financing outflow = dividend paidDividend paid = Opening proposed + Interim dividend + Current proposed − Closing proposed (when proposed is shown as a liability on both Balance Sheets). If the question simply gives “dividend paid”, use that figure.
Provision for doubtful debtsUse net debtors as per the Balance Sheet. Do not add the provision back as a separate non-cash item, and do not treat the provision as a separate liability.Operating, via the movement in net debtorsIf net debtors fall because the provision rose, that decrease is added in WC and it automatically corrects the non-cash charge that reduced profit. One consistent method: always take current assets as they appear on the BS (net).
Purchase of fixed assetsIncluded as an investing outflow (cash paid)InvestingDerive: Opening FA at cost + Purchases − Cost of assets sold = Closing FA at cost. Purchases = Closing cost − Opening cost + Cost sold. Only the cash portion is an outflow.
Sale of fixed assetsIncluded as an investing inflow (sale proceeds)InvestingProceeds = Book value + Profit − Loss. Book value = Cost of asset sold − Accumulated depreciation on it. Never use book value as the cash figure.

Working-capital rule in one line: increase in current assets (except cash) → deduct; decrease in current assets → add; increase in current liabilities (except tax provision, proposed dividend, and overdraft-if-financing) → add; decrease in current liabilities → deduct.

Formula

Working capital squeeze: CA ↑ = cash locked (deduct). CA ↓ = cash released (add). CL ↑ = cash retained (add). CL ↓ = cash paid out (deduct).

Current assets here exclude cash and cash equivalents. Current liabilities here exclude items given their own cash line (tax paid, dividend paid) and exclude overdraft when you are treating overdraft as financing.

Working notes the examiner expects — how to find the missing figures

A typical exam question does not give you profit before tax, tax paid, purchases of plant, sale proceeds and depreciation in a neat list. It gives two Balance Sheets and four or five lines of additional information. You have to build T-accounts (or equations) to find the missing numbers. These workings carry marks of their own. Show them. Do not hide them inside the CFS.

Working 1 — Reconstruct profit before tax from P&L surplus

6. Format — Profit before tax from two Balance Sheets

Closing balance of Profit & Loss surplus (from BS)

Less: Opening balance of Profit & Loss surplus

= Increase in surplus during the year

Add: Dividend paid / proposed (if it was appropriated out of this year’s profit)

Add: Transfer to general reserve / other reserves

Add: Bonus issue capitalised from P&L

= Profit after tax (PAT)

Add: Current year’s tax charge (provision made this year)

= Profit before tax (PBT) — this is the first line of the CFS

If the question already gives “Net profit before tax”, skip this working and start the CFS with that figure. If it gives “Net profit” after tax, add the current tax charge to reach PBT. Always be sure whether the starting figure is before or after tax, and before or after interest. The standard format starts from profit before tax, after interest — which is why we then add interest back.

Working 2 — Plant (fixed asset) at cost, and purchases

Formula

Opening plant at cost + Purchases − Cost of plant sold = Closing plant at cost

Therefore Purchases = Closing cost − Opening cost + Cost of plant sold. If no sale is mentioned, Purchases = Closing − Opening (when the BS shows cost, not WDV).

Some Balance Sheets show plant at written-down value (after depreciation) with no separate accumulated-depreciation line. Then the equation is:

Formula

Opening WDV + Purchases − WDV of asset sold − Depreciation for the year = Closing WDV

WDV of asset sold = Cost sold − Accumulated depreciation on sold, which equals Sale proceeds − Profit + Loss.

Working 3 — Accumulated depreciation, and depreciation for the year

Formula

Opening accumulated depreciation + Depreciation charged this year − Accumulated depreciation on asset sold = Closing accumulated depreciation

Therefore Depreciation for the year = Closing accum. dep. − Opening accum. dep. + Accum. dep. on asset sold.

Working 4 — Sale proceeds of a fixed asset

Formula

Book value (WDV) of asset sold = Cost of asset sold − Accumulated depreciation on it
Sale proceeds = Book value + Profit on sale − Loss on sale

If the question gives proceeds, you can run the same equation backwards to find profit or loss, and then use that profit/loss in the operating adjustments.

5. Accounting logic

Why we never put book value in the CFS: book value is not cash. The buyer pays the agreed price. That price is the investing inflow. The difference between price and book value is a non-cash gain or loss which we park as an operating adjustment so that it does not contaminate operating cash and is not double-counted.

Working 5 — Tax paid

Formula

Opening provision for tax + Current year’s tax charge − Closing provision for tax = Tax paid

“Current year’s tax charge” is the amount debited to P&L (the provision made this year). It is not the same as tax paid, and it is not the same as the closing provision.

If the question states “tax paid ₹…”, use that figure directly as the operating outflow and use the T-account only to find the current-year charge (which you need to reconstruct PBT). If there is advance tax or TDS, it is part of tax paid — do not show it twice.

Working 6 — Dividend paid

Formula

When proposed dividend is a Balance-Sheet liability in both years:
Dividend paid = Opening proposed dividend + Interim dividend (if any) + Current proposed − Closing proposed

Often there is no interim and current proposed is unpaid, so Dividend paid = Opening proposed dividend. If the question simply says “dividend paid ₹…”, use that. Do not deduct proposed dividend inside operating profit.

Watch out

Modern Company Law / revised AS-4 / Ind AS: proposed dividend is not a liability until it is declared. Many current Balance Sheets therefore do not show proposed dividend. In that case the question will give “dividend paid” in additional information, and P&L surplus is before that appropriation or the appropriation is already reflected — follow the numbers you are given. Older MBA textbooks still show proposed dividend as a current liability. Both presentations appear in papers. Read the BS.

Working 7 — Interest paid / received

Interest on 10% debentures of ₹2,00,000 for a full year = ₹2,00,000 × 10/100 = ₹20,000. Always write the multiplication. If debentures were issued or redeemed during the year, the question will usually tell you the interest figure, or tell you the date so you can compute time-proportion. If it is silent, a reasonable exam assumption is: issued/redeemed at year-end, so interest is on the opening balance (for redemption) or on the opening balance only (for issue at year-end, new money carries no interest this year). State your assumption in a working note.

Exam tip

Outstanding interest is a current liability. If interest expense is ₹20,000 and outstanding interest rose by ₹2,000, then interest paid = ₹20,000 − ₹2,000 = ₹18,000. Put ₹20,000 as the add-back (the P&L figure) and ₹18,000 as the financing outflow (the cash). Do not also count the outstanding-interest movement inside the general “outstanding expenses” line or you will double-count. Cleanest method: keep interest outstanding out of WC, and compute interest paid from the interest T-account.

Provision for doubtful debts — one consistent method

Two methods exist in textbooks. Mixing them is how students lose marks. We use one method only in this chapter:

Key point

Take debtors net of provision, exactly as a typical Balance Sheet presents “Trade receivables”. Do not add back the provision charge as a separate non-cash item. Do not treat the provision as a separate current liability. The movement in net debtors already does the right job: a pure increase in the provision (gross debtors unchanged) reduces net debtors, which you add in working capital, which cancels the non-cash charge that reduced profit.

Solved examples — Easy, then Moderate, then Exam-level

Three fully worked statements follow. Every arithmetic step is shown. After each, A + B + C is compared with the change in cash. That comparison is the proof that the statement is internally true. You should do the same on every exam script.

Solved example 5.1 · Easy

Sneha Stores — first full CFS from a short list of facts

Sneha Stores provides the following information for the year ended 31 March 2026. Prepare a Cash Flow Statement by the indirect method.

  • Net profit before tax: ₹1,00,000
  • Depreciation: ₹20,000
  • Tax paid during the year: ₹25,000
  • Increase in stock: ₹10,000
  • Increase in creditors: ₹8,000
  • Purchase of furniture (cash): ₹40,000
  • Loan taken: ₹30,000
  • Opening cash and cash equivalents: ₹15,000

Closing cash is not given. You must find it. That is normal.

Step 1 — Operating activities (A)

Start with profit before tax. Add back depreciation (non-cash). Then working capital: stock went up — cash locked — deduct. Creditors went up — cash retained — add. Then deduct tax paid.

Operating profit before working capital changes = ₹1,00,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹1,20,000.

After working capital = ₹1,20,000 − ₹10,000 + ₹8,000 = ₹1,18,000 (this is cash generated from operations).

Net cash from operating activities (A) = ₹1,18,000 − ₹25,000 = ₹93,000.

Step 2 — Investing activities (B)

Only one item: furniture purchased for cash ₹40,000. Net cash from investing activities (B) = (₹40,000).

Step 3 — Financing activities (C)

Only one item: loan taken ₹30,000. Net cash from financing activities (C) = ₹30,000.

Step 4 — Net change and closing cash

A + B + C = ₹93,000 − ₹40,000 + ₹30,000.

₹93,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹53,000.

₹53,000 + ₹30,000 = ₹83,000 net increase in cash.

Closing cash = ₹15,000 + ₹83,000 = ₹98,000.

Sneha Stores — Cash Flow Statement for the year ended 31 March 2026 (indirect method)
Particulars₹
Cash flows from operating activities
Net profit before tax₹1,00,000
Adjustments for:
  Depreciation₹20,000
Operating profit before working capital changes₹1,20,000
  Increase in stock(₹10,000)
  Increase in creditors₹8,000
Cash generated from operations₹1,18,000
Income tax paid(₹25,000)
Net cash from operating activities (A)₹93,000
Cash flows from investing activities
Purchase of furniture(₹40,000)
Net cash from investing activities (B)(₹40,000)
Cash flows from financing activities
Loan taken₹30,000
Net cash from financing activities (C)₹30,000
Net increase in cash and cash equivalents (A + B + C)₹83,000
Opening cash and cash equivalents₹15,000
Closing cash and cash equivalents₹98,000

Proof: 93,000 − 40,000 + 30,000 = 83,000 = 98,000 − 15,000.

Solved example 5.2 · Moderate

Ravi Traders Ltd. — two-year Balance Sheets, sale of plant, tax, dividend, interest

Ravi Traders Ltd. gives its summarised Balance Sheets and additional information. Prepare a Cash Flow Statement (indirect method) for the year ended 31 March 2026, with working notes.

Ravi Traders Ltd. — summarised Balance Sheets

Equity and liabilities

10% Debentures₹80,000₹1,00,000
Profit & Loss A/c (surplus)₹60,000₹95,000
Trade creditors₹35,000₹28,000
Outstanding expenses₹4,000₹6,000

Investments₹50,000₹70,000

Trade debtors₹45,000₹38,000

Cash and cash equivalents₹30,000₹42,000
Total₹3,93,000₹4,80,000

Additional information

  1. Plant costing ₹20,000 (accumulated depreciation on it ₹8,000) was sold for ₹15,000.
  2. The rest of the movement in plant at cost is a cash purchase of plant.
  3. Debentures of ₹20,000 were issued at par for cash at the end of the year.
  4. Interest on debentures paid during the year ₹8,000 (computed as ₹80,000 × 10/100 = ₹8,000; new debentures carry no interest this year).
  5. Tax paid during the year ₹23,000.
  6. Dividend paid during the year ₹15,000.
  7. Equity shares were issued at par for cash. No bonus issue.

Working note 1 — Plant at cost (purchases)

Opening plant at cost ₹2,50,000 + Purchases − Cost of plant sold ₹20,000 = Closing plant at cost ₹3,20,000.

Purchases = ₹3,20,000 − ₹2,50,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹70,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹90,000.

Working note 2 — Accumulated depreciation (depreciation for the year)

Opening accum. dep. ₹50,000 + Depreciation for the year − Accum. dep. on asset sold ₹8,000 = Closing accum. dep. ₹70,000.

Depreciation for the year = ₹70,000 − ₹50,000 + ₹8,000 = ₹20,000 + ₹8,000 = ₹28,000.

Particulars₹Particulars₹

Balance c/d₹70,000By Profit & Loss (dep.)₹28,000

Working note 3 — Profit / loss on sale of plant, and sale proceeds

Book value of plant sold = Cost ₹20,000 − Accum. dep. ₹8,000 = ₹12,000.

Sold for ₹15,000. Profit on sale = ₹15,000 − ₹12,000 = ₹3,000.

Investing inflow = sale proceeds ₹15,000 (not the book value, not the profit).

Working note 4 — Provision for tax (current tax charge)

Opening provision ₹14,000 + Current tax charge − Tax paid ₹23,000 = Closing provision ₹11,000.

Check: ₹14,000 + ₹20,000 − ₹23,000 = ₹11,000. Yes.

Particulars₹Particulars₹
To Bank (tax paid)₹23,000By Balance b/d₹14,000

Working note 5 — Profit before tax

Increase in P&L surplus = ₹95,000 − ₹60,000 = ₹35,000.

This increase is after dividend of ₹15,000 was paid (appropriated). So PAT = ₹35,000 + ₹15,000 = ₹50,000.

PBT = PAT + current tax charge = ₹50,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹70,000.

This ₹70,000 is after charging depreciation ₹28,000, after including profit on sale ₹3,000, and after charging interest ₹8,000. Those three will be adjusted in operating.

Working note 6 — Other movements (read off the two Balance Sheets)

  • Equity share capital issued for cash = ₹2,40,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹40,000.
  • Debentures issued for cash = ₹1,00,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹20,000 (matches additional info).
  • Investments purchased = ₹70,000 − ₹50,000 = ₹20,000 (cash; investing outflow).
  • Inventory increased = ₹75,000 − ₹60,000 = ₹15,000 (deduct).
  • Debtors decreased = ₹45,000 − ₹38,000 = ₹7,000 (add).
  • Prepaid expenses decreased = ₹8,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹3,000 (add).
  • Creditors decreased = ₹35,000 − ₹28,000 = ₹7,000 (deduct).
  • Outstanding expenses increased = ₹6,000 − ₹4,000 = ₹2,000 (add).

Cash Flow Statement

Operating profit before WC = PBT ₹70,000 + Dep ₹28,000 − Profit on sale ₹3,000 + Interest expense ₹8,000.

₹70,000 + ₹28,000 = ₹98,000.

₹98,000 − ₹3,000 = ₹95,000.

₹95,000 + ₹8,000 = ₹1,03,000.

Working capital adjustments:

₹1,03,000 − inventory ₹15,000 = ₹88,000.

₹88,000 + debtors ₹7,000 = ₹95,000.

₹95,000 + prepaid ₹3,000 = ₹98,000.

₹98,000 − creditors ₹7,000 = ₹91,000.

₹91,000 + outstanding ₹2,000 = ₹93,000 cash generated from operations.

Tax paid ₹23,000. Net operating (A) = ₹93,000 − ₹23,000 = ₹70,000.

Investing (B) = − plant purchased ₹90,000 + sale proceeds ₹15,000 − investments ₹20,000 = −₹90,000 + ₹15,000 = −₹75,000; −₹75,000 − ₹20,000 = −₹95,000.

Financing (C) = share issue ₹40,000 + debenture issue ₹20,000 − interest paid ₹8,000 − dividend paid ₹15,000.

₹40,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹60,000.

₹60,000 − ₹8,000 = ₹52,000.

₹52,000 − ₹15,000 = ₹37,000.

A + B + C = ₹70,000 − ₹95,000 + ₹37,000.

₹70,000 − ₹95,000 = −₹25,000; −₹25,000 + ₹37,000 = ₹12,000.

Opening cash ₹30,000 + ₹12,000 = ₹42,000 closing cash, which matches the Balance Sheet.

Kaveri Appliances Ltd. — full two-year BS, sale of plant at a loss, redemption, interest received and paid

Kaveri Appliances Ltd. You are given summarised Balance Sheets and additional information. Prepare a complete Cash Flow Statement by the indirect method as per AS-3, with working notes for plant, accumulated depreciation, tax, dividend and interest.

Additional information

Working note 5 — Dividend and profit before tax

Increase in P&L surplus = ₹2,10,000 − ₹1,40,000 = ₹70,000.

This PBT already includes: depreciation ₹60,000 (charged), loss on sale ₹8,000 (charged), interest expense ₹20,000 (charged), interest income ₹6,400 (credited). All four will be adjusted.

Working note 6 — Interest

Interest paid (financing outflow) = ₹2,00,000 × 10/100 = ₹20,000. Add the same {rupee(20000)} back in operating.

Interest received (investing inflow) = ₹80,000 × 8/100 = ₹6,400. Deduct ₹6,400 in operating.

  • Shares issued for cash = ₹5,00,000 − ₹4,00,000 = ₹1,00,000.
  • Debentures redeemed for cash = ₹2,00,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹50,000.
  • Investments purchased for cash = ₹1,20,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹40,000.
  • Inventory decreased = ₹1,50,000 − ₹1,35,000 = ₹15,000 (add).
  • Debtors increased = ₹1,25,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹25,000 (deduct).
  • Prepaid decreased = ₹15,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹5,000 (add).
  • Creditors increased = ₹1,10,000 − ₹90,000 = ₹20,000 (add).
  • Outstanding expenses decreased = ₹12,000 − ₹8,000 = ₹4,000 (deduct).

Build operating profit before working capital changes

PBT ₹1,65,000

+ Depreciation ₹60,000 → ₹1,65,000 + ₹60,000 = ₹2,25,000

+ Loss on sale ₹8,000 → ₹2,25,000 + ₹8,000 = ₹2,33,000

+ Interest expense ₹20,000 → ₹2,33,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹2,53,000

− Interest income ₹6,400 → ₹2,53,000 − ₹6,400 = ₹2,46,600

Working capital, cash generated, tax, (A)

₹2,46,600 + decrease in inventory ₹15,000 = ₹2,61,600

₹2,61,600 − increase in debtors ₹25,000 = ₹2,36,600

₹2,36,600 + decrease in prepaid ₹5,000 = ₹2,41,600

₹2,41,600 + increase in creditors ₹20,000 = ₹2,61,600

₹2,61,600 − decrease in outstanding ₹4,000 = ₹2,57,600 cash generated from operations

− Tax paid ₹45,000 → Net cash from operating activities (A) = ₹2,57,600 − ₹45,000 = ₹2,12,600

Investing (B)

Purchase of plant ₹2,00,000 (outflow)

Sale proceeds of plant ₹42,000 (inflow)

Purchase of investments ₹40,000 (outflow)

Interest received ₹6,400 (inflow)

B = −₹2,00,000 + ₹42,000 − ₹40,000 + ₹6,400

−₹2,00,000 + ₹42,000 = −₹1,58,000

−₹1,58,000 − ₹40,000 = −₹1,98,000

−₹1,98,000 + ₹6,400 = −₹1,91,600

Financing (C)

Issue of shares ₹1,00,000 (inflow)

Redemption of debentures ₹50,000 (outflow)

Interest paid ₹20,000 (outflow)

Dividend paid ₹40,000 (outflow)

C = ₹1,00,000 − ₹50,000 − ₹20,000 − ₹40,000

₹1,00,000 − ₹50,000 = ₹50,000

₹50,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹30,000

₹30,000 − ₹40,000 = −₹10,000

Net change

A + B + C = ₹2,12,600 + (₹1,91,600) + (₹10,000)

₹2,12,600 − ₹1,91,600 = ₹21,000

₹21,000 − ₹10,000 = ₹11,000 net increase in cash

Opening cash ₹57,000 + ₹11,000 = ₹68,000 closing cash — matches the Balance Sheet. The statement is complete and internally true.

How to identify the question, the mistakes that cost marks, and what to remember

9. How to identify the question

You are in this chapter when the question says any of: “Prepare a Cash Flow Statement”, “Cash Flow Statement as per AS-3”, “indirect method”, “from the following Balance Sheets prepare a CFS”, “classify the following into operating, investing and financing”, “need / importance of Cash Flow Statement”. Two-year Balance Sheets plus additional information about depreciation, sale of an asset, tax and dividend is the standard 15-mark practical. A short list of adjustments is the 8–10 mark practical. Theory on need, cash equivalents, or classification is 4–8 marks.

10. Common mistakes
  • Treating depreciation as a cash outflow. Depreciation never leaves the bank. It is added back. Writing it as an investing or operating payment is a full-mark loss on that line.
  • Not deducting profit on sale (or not adding loss on sale) in operating. Then showing the full sale proceeds in investing double-counts the gain (or understates cash by the loss). Always pair: adjust the P&L result of the sale in operating, put proceeds in investing.
  • Putting purchase of a fixed asset in operating because “we paid cash to run the business”. Buying the shop’s tools is investing, not operating.
  • Treating a bonus issue as a financing inflow. Bonus is non-cash. Same error: conversion of debentures into shares, or an asset bought by issuing shares. Exclude from A, B and C; disclose in a note.
  • Using the closing provision for tax as “tax paid”. Tax paid = opening provision + current charge − closing provision. The closing provision is what is still unpaid.
  • Forgetting the interest pair. Add back interest expense in operating, then show interest paid in financing. Doing only one of the two drops (or double-counts) cash by that amount. Same pairing for interest/dividend income with investing.
  • Calling “cash” only the notes in the till and forgetting cash at bank / cash equivalents. The last line must equal the BS figure for cash and cash equivalents.
  • Squeezing provision for tax or proposed dividend through working capital as if they were creditors. They have their own cash lines (tax paid, dividend paid). Putting them in both places is a double count.
  • Using book value as the sale proceeds. Proceeds = WDV + profit − loss. Investing inflow is proceeds.
  • Taking the movement in plant at cost as the purchase, ignoring a sale. Purchases = closing cost − opening cost + cost of assets sold. Ignoring the sale understates purchases and therefore understates the investing outflow.
  • Mixing gross debtors with a separate provision, and also adding the provision charge back. Pick net debtors as per BS and stop. Do not also add back the provision.
  • Plugging the difference so that closing cash magically appears. If A+B+C does not equal the change in cash, a working is wrong. Find it.
11. Memory trick

Operations = running the shop; Investing = buying and selling the shop’s tools; Financing = talking to owners and lenders. Then the three repairs of the indirect method: add back non-cash, undo non-operating, squeeze working capital. CA up → cash down. CL up → cash up. Last line is a lock: A + B + C + opening cash = closing cash. AS-3 interest/dividend rhyme: received → investing; paid → financing.

Practice — two full questions, with solutions

Attempt each question on paper first. Prepare working notes. Do not look at the solution until A + B + C equals the change in cash — or until you are stuck. The solutions show every multiplication.

Practice 5.1 · Easy–Moderate

Hari Tools — full CFS from a list, including the interest pair

Hari Tools extracted the following from its accounts for the year ended 31 March 2026. Prepare a Cash Flow Statement by the indirect method as per AS-3. Find the closing cash.

  • Net profit before tax ₹2,00,000 (this figure is after interest expense, after interest income, after depreciation, and after profit on sale of furniture).
  • Depreciation ₹35,000.
  • Profit on sale of furniture ₹5,000.
  • Interest expense (included in P&L) ₹12,000.
  • Interest income (included in P&L) ₹4,000.
  • Increase in debtors ₹18,000.
  • Decrease in stock ₹10,000.
  • Increase in creditors ₹7,000.
  • Decrease in outstanding expenses ₹3,000.
  • Tax paid ₹40,000.
  • Purchase of machinery ₹90,000.
  • Sale of furniture (proceeds) ₹25,000.
  • Purchase of investments ₹20,000.
  • Dividend paid ₹30,000.
  • Loan raised ₹50,000.
  • Opening cash and cash equivalents ₹22,000.

Answer / solution

Operating profit before WC = ₹2,00,000 + dep ₹35,000 − profit on sale ₹5,000 + interest expense ₹12,000 − interest income ₹4,000.

₹2,00,000 + ₹35,000 = ₹2,35,000

₹2,35,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹2,30,000

₹2,30,000 + ₹12,000 = ₹2,42,000

₹2,42,000 − ₹4,000 = ₹2,38,000

Working capital: − increase in debtors ₹18,000 + decrease in stock ₹10,000 + increase in creditors ₹7,000 − decrease in outstanding ₹3,000.

WC net = −₹18,000 + ₹10,000 = −₹8,000; −₹8,000 + ₹7,000 = −₹1,000; −₹1,000 − ₹3,000 = −₹4,000.

Cash generated = ₹2,38,000 − ₹4,000 = ₹2,34,000.

Net operating (A) = ₹2,34,000 − tax ₹40,000 = ₹1,94,000.

Investing (B) = − machinery ₹90,000 + furniture proceeds ₹25,000 − investments ₹20,000 + interest received ₹4,000.

−₹90,000 + ₹25,000 = −₹65,000; −₹65,000 − ₹20,000 = −₹85,000; −₹85,000 + ₹4,000 = −₹81,000.

Financing (C) = loan ₹50,000 − interest paid ₹12,000 − dividend ₹30,000.

₹50,000 − ₹12,000 = ₹38,000; ₹38,000 − ₹30,000 = ₹8,000.

A + B + C = ₹1,94,000 − ₹81,000 + ₹8,000 = ₹1,13,000 + ₹8,000 = ₹1,21,000.

Closing cash = ₹22,000 + ₹1,21,000 = ₹1,43,000.

Practice 5.2 · Exam-level

Arjun Textiles Ltd. — two-year BS with general reserve, sale of plant at a loss, redemption

Arjun Textiles Ltd. From the following summarised Balance Sheets and additional information, prepare a Cash Flow Statement (indirect method, AS-3) for the year ended 31 March 2026, with working notes.

Arjun Textiles Ltd. — summarised Balance Sheets
Particulars31 March 2025 ₹31 March 2026 ₹
Equity and liabilities
Equity share capital₹3,00,000₹4,00,000
12% Debentures₹1,50,000₹1,00,000
Profit & Loss surplus₹90,000₹1,30,000
General reserve₹40,000₹55,000
Trade creditors₹50,000₹42,000
Outstanding expenses₹8,000₹11,000
Provision for tax₹25,000₹30,000
Total₹6,63,000₹7,68,000
Assets
Land and building (not depreciated; no movement)₹2,00,000₹2,00,000
Plant at cost₹3,50,000₹4,50,000
Less: Accumulated depreciation on plant(₹70,000)(₹95,000)
Plant (net)₹2,80,000₹3,55,000
Inventory₹85,000₹1,00,000
Trade debtors₹60,000₹48,000
Prepaid expenses₹6,000₹9,000
Cash and cash equivalents₹32,000₹56,000
Total₹6,63,000₹7,68,000

Additional information

  1. Plant costing ₹50,000 (accumulated depreciation ₹20,000) was sold for ₹22,000.
  2. The rest of the increase in plant at cost is a cash purchase.
  3. Debentures of ₹50,000 were redeemed at par at the end of the year.
  4. Equity shares of ₹1,00,000 were issued at par for cash. No bonus, no conversion.
  5. Transfer to general reserve ₹15,000.
  6. Tax paid ₹32,000.
  7. Dividend paid ₹25,000.
  8. Interest on 12% debentures paid ₹18,000 (= ₹1,50,000 × 12/100 = ₹18,000).

Answer / solution

Workings

Plant purchases: ₹4,50,000 − ₹3,50,000 + cost sold ₹50,000 = ₹1,00,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹1,50,000.

Depreciation for the year: closing accum. ₹95,000 − opening ₹70,000 + on sold ₹20,000 = ₹25,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹45,000.

Book value of plant sold: ₹50,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹30,000. Sold for ₹22,000. Loss on sale = ₹30,000 − ₹22,000 = ₹8,000.

Current tax charge: closing provision ₹30,000 − opening ₹25,000 + tax paid ₹32,000 = ₹5,000 + ₹32,000 = ₹37,000. Check: ₹25,000 + ₹37,000 − ₹32,000 = ₹30,000.

PAT: increase in P&L ₹1,30,000 − ₹90,000 = ₹40,000, plus transfer to general reserve ₹15,000, plus dividend ₹25,000 → PAT = ₹40,000 + ₹15,000 + ₹25,000 = ₹80,000.

PBT = PAT ₹80,000 + current tax ₹37,000 = ₹1,17,000.

Check on general reserve: ₹40,000 + ₹15,000 = ₹55,000, matches the BS. Transfer to reserve is an appropriation — it is used only to reconstruct PAT. It is not an operating adjustment and not a cash flow.

Interest paid = ₹1,50,000 × 12/100 = ₹18,000 (add back the same amount in operating).

Operating

PBT ₹1,17,000 + dep ₹45,000 + loss on sale ₹8,000 + interest ₹18,000 = operating profit before WC.

₹1,17,000 + ₹45,000 = ₹1,62,000

₹1,62,000 + ₹8,000 = ₹1,70,000

₹1,70,000 + ₹18,000 = ₹1,88,000

WC: inventory increase ₹1,00,000 − ₹85,000 = ₹15,000 (deduct); debtors decrease ₹60,000 − ₹48,000 = ₹12,000 (add); prepaid increase ₹9,000 − ₹6,000 = ₹3,000 (deduct); creditors decrease ₹50,000 − ₹42,000 = ₹8,000 (deduct); outstanding increase ₹11,000 − ₹8,000 = ₹3,000 (add).

WC net = −₹15,000 + ₹12,000 − ₹3,000 − ₹8,000 + ₹3,000 = −₹11,000.

Cash generated = ₹1,88,000 − ₹11,000 = ₹1,77,000.

Net operating (A) = ₹1,77,000 − tax ₹32,000 = ₹1,45,000.

Investing and financing

Investing (B) = − plant purchased ₹1,50,000 + sale proceeds ₹22,000 = −₹1,28,000. (Land and building did not move; no investing item there.)

Financing (C) = share issue ₹1,00,000 − redemption ₹50,000 − interest ₹18,000 − dividend ₹25,000.

₹1,00,000 − ₹50,000 = ₹50,000; ₹50,000 − ₹18,000 = ₹32,000; ₹32,000 − ₹25,000 = ₹7,000.

A + B + C = ₹1,45,000 − ₹1,28,000 + ₹7,000 = ₹17,000 + ₹7,000 = ₹24,000.

Opening cash ₹32,000 + ₹24,000 = ₹56,000 closing cash, matching the Balance Sheet.

Theory questions the examiner actually sets

Practical questions are the bulk of the marks. These theory questions still appear, usually for 4–8 marks. Answer in the shape the examiner rewards: definition, then three or four sharp points, then the standard tag (AS-3 / Companies Act) if it is relevant.

6 marks

Why is profit not equal to cash? Illustrate.

Profit is computed on the accrual basis. Revenue is recognised when earned and expenses when incurred, whether or not cash has moved. Cash is recognised only when it is received or paid. Therefore:

  • Credit sales increase profit but not cash until collected.
  • Depreciation decreases profit but not cash.
  • Purchase of a machine decreases cash but not profit (except later, through depreciation).
  • A loan increases cash but not profit.

Illustration: Meera’s profit ₹1,00,000 against a cash increase of only ₹55,000 in the opening example of this chapter — the gap is exactly these four kinds of item.

8 marks

State the importance of a Cash Flow Statement.

A CFS reports inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents, classified into operating, investing and financing activities (AS-3 / Ind AS-7). It is important because:

  • It reveals liquidity — the ability to pay creditors, lenders, employees and tax — which profit conceals.
  • Management uses it to plan working capital, capex and dividends.
  • Lenders use it to judge whether debt can be serviced from operations.
  • Investors use it to test the quality of earnings (is profit turning into cash?).
  • It complements the P&L and the Balance Sheet by reconciling opening and closing cash.
  • It is mandatory for listed companies and for companies other than OPC, small companies and dormant companies.
5 marks

What are cash and cash equivalents? Is a bank overdraft a cash equivalent?

Cash = cash on hand + demand deposits with banks. Cash equivalents = short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into known amounts of cash and subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value, normally with a maturity of three months or less from the date of acquisition. Equity shares are not cash equivalents.

Bank overdraft repayable on demand may be treated as a component of cash and cash equivalents under AS-3 if it is an integral part of cash management. Many examination problems instead treat the movement in overdraft as a financing inflow or outflow. Follow the question.

8 marks

Distinguish operating, investing and financing activities, with two examples of each. How are interest and dividend classified under AS-3?

Operating — principal revenue-producing activities: cash from customers, cash to suppliers, wages, income tax paid.

Investing — acquisition and disposal of long-term assets and of investments other than cash equivalents: purchase/sale of plant, purchase/sale of investments.

Financing — changes in owners’ capital and borrowings: issue of shares, loans taken, redemption of debentures, repayment of loans.

AS-3 classification of interest and dividend: interest received and dividend received = investing inflows; interest paid and dividend paid = financing outflows. (Ind AS-7 permits options; unless named, use AS-3.)

8 marks

Give the pro-forma of a Cash Flow Statement under the indirect method.

Write the boxed format taught in this chapter, in this order: net profit before tax; adjustments for depreciation, profit/loss on sale, interest, non-cash items; operating profit before working capital changes; changes in current assets and current liabilities; cash generated from operations; tax paid; net operating (A); investing receipts and payments (B); financing receipts and payments (C); A+B+C; opening cash; closing cash. Closing cash must equal the Balance Sheet.

6 marks

How will you treat the following in a Cash Flow Statement (indirect method, AS-3): depreciation; profit on sale of machine; bonus issue; increase in debtors; proposed dividend; purchase of machinery by issue of shares?

  • Depreciation — add back to profit (operating adjustment; non-cash).
  • Profit on sale of machine — deduct from profit; show sale proceeds as investing inflow.
  • Bonus issue — non-cash; exclude from the CFS body; disclose in a note. If capitalised from P&L, add back when reconstructing PAT.
  • Increase in debtors — deduct in working-capital adjustments (operating).
  • Proposed dividend — not an operating item. Dividend paid is a financing outflow (usually equal to opening proposed dividend if that is the unpaid liability brought forward).
  • Purchase of machinery by issue of shares — non-cash investing and financing transaction; disclose in a note; no figure in A, B or C.

Chapter 06

Understanding Annual Reports and Analysis

Learning outcome. After this chapter you will be able to open a real Indian listed-company annual report without panic, name every major section in the order it usually appears, explain why the report exists and who uses it, read the auditor's opinion before trusting the numbers, walk from a management claim down to the supporting note, cash flow and ratio, and write 1-mark, 5-mark and 8–10-mark exam answers on need, importance, composition, Directors' Report and Auditor's Report.

What this chapter covers (official syllabus)

  • Need and importance of Annual Report
  • Composition of Annual Report
  • Contents of Annual Report

6.1 Opening picture — you have never seen an annual report. Here is one.

Imagine a company that makes pickles, spices and ready-to-eat meals. It has thousands of shareholders who do not sit in the factory.
