Narrative bias in the story layerChairman's letter and MD&A are partly investor-relations writing. They rarely lead with bad news.'Spices stable' for +2.9% is a soft word. The note was harder and better.
Inflation and current valuesHistorical-cost accounts do not restate a 2012 factory at 2025 prices. Comparability across high-inflation years suffers.Sagar's land in Andheri is almost certainly worth more than book value. ROE on book equity can mislead.
Off-balance-sheet and contingent itemsSome risks live only in notes (disputes, guarantees, certain commitments).The ₹3 crore excise demand never entered the total of equity and liabilities.
3. Why do we need it?

If annual reports had no limitations, we would not need quarterly results, credit-rating visits, forensic audits, or Chapter 7's habit of interrogating every ratio. Teaching limitations is not cynicism. It is the difference between a reader and a believer.

11. Memory trick

Limitations mnemonic — HAPPY WINDOW is too long; use HAD WIN: Historical, Aggregation, Delay, Window dressing, Inflation / incomplete non-financial, Notes-only (contingent) plus policy/estimate judgement. Three in an importance answer is enough; six in a dedicated 'limitations' question.

6.14 How an MBA should read an annual report in 30 minutes

2. In simple words

You will rarely have a free Sunday for all 168 pages. You need a repeatable sequence that hits identity, reliability, dashboard, faces, notes that matter, story-versus-evidence, and stewardship. This is that sequence. It is also an exam-friendly 'steps' answer: 'Explain how you would analyse an annual report.'

7. Step-by-step method — 30 minutes, exam-friendly
  1. Minutes 0–2 — Identity. Cover, corporate information. Write down: name, CIN, year-end, listed or not, auditor's name, MD, Chairman (same person?). Confirm you are not mixing two companies with similar names.
  2. Minutes 2–5 — Auditor first. Standalone opinion type. Consolidated opinion type. Basis paragraph. Emphasis of matter. Key Audit Matters. If qualified / adverse / disclaimer, the rest of the 25 minutes is about that problem. If clean, write the KAM topics on your pad — they are the note list.
  3. Minutes 5–8 — Dashboard. Highlights / 5-year figures. Compute two growth rates yourself (revenue, PAT). Look at debt and EPS direction. Do not accept a graph without reading the axis.
  4. Minutes 8–13 — Faces. P&L: revenue, gross profit if given, other income, PAT. Balance Sheet: equity, borrowings, inventory, receivables, cash. Cash flow: CFO vs PAT, big investing outflows, financing (debt drawn or repaid, dividend). Glance at consolidated vs standalone revenue to see how big the group is.
  5. Minutes 13–20 — Notes that matter. (1) Significant accounting policies — any change? (2) Revenue breakdown. (3) Receivables ageing and related-party receivables. (4) Borrowings — current portion, defaults. (5) Contingent liabilities. (6) Related parties. (7) Subsequent events. (8) Whatever the KAM named. This block is the highest-value seven minutes in the half-hour.
  6. Minutes 20–25 — Story versus evidence. Read MD&A headings and the Chairman's letter now, not earlier. Tick claims that you have already verified. Circle claims that the notes contradict or that cash flow weakens. You are doing Section 6.12 at speed.
  7. Minutes 25–28 — Stewardship. Directors' Report: dividend, DRS (any departure from standards?), material changes, frauds, CSR. Secretarial audit: qualified or not?
  8. Minutes 28–30 — Governance red flags. Independent directors, audit committee, related-party approvals, auditor rotation / remuneration, any special business in the AGM notice that reveals a transaction the notes already flagged.
6. Format — What you write on a one-page working paper in those 30 minutes
  • Company / year / auditor / opinion type / KAM topics.
  • Revenue this year vs last, PAT this year vs last, CFO vs PAT (three pairs of numbers).
  • One good news, one worry from the notes (Sagar: RTE growth; distributor ₹12 crore).
  • Dividend and any qualification in Board's Report or secretarial audit.
  • One question you still cannot answer (then you know where to spend hour two, if you get it).

If the exam asks for 'steps in analysis of annual report', turn the eight minute-blocks into eight numbered steps without the clock. The clock is for real life; the order is for marks.

Exam tip

A 5-mark 'procedure to read / analyse annual report' answer is this sequence, compressed: (1) identity (2) auditor (3) highlights (4) faces of FS including cash flow (5) notes and policies (6) MD&A versus numbers (7) Directors' Report (8) governance. Starting with MD&A is a common mistake — that is how you get sold the story.

Key point

Practical habit after this chapter: download one real annual report of an FMCG company you know (a listed pickle, biscuit or tea company) and run the 30-minute sequence once. The fictional Sagar pack is the rehearsal. A live PDF is the stage.

6.15 Solved examples

Solved example 1 · Easy

Which section of the annual report do I open?

For each user need, name the first section you would open, and one backup section.

NeedFirst sectionBackup sectionWhy
Is the profit figure trustworthy?Independent Auditor's ReportNotes on revenue and receivables; KAMOpinion first; then the places judgement hides.
Did sales really grow 20%?Statement of Profit and LossRevenue note; then cash flowFace gives the %, note gives the mix, cash flow gives collection.
Can the company pay the proposed dividend?Standalone P&L and Balance Sheet (distributable profits / cash)Cash flow — financing section; Directors' Report dividend paraDividend is a standalone legal act, paid in cash.
Are promoters dealing with themselves?Related-party noteAOC-2 / Directors' Report; governance report; AGM special businessNumbers in notes, approval in stewardship, vote in the notice.
Any court case that could explode?Contingent liabilities noteDirectors' Report (material changes / legal); EOM in audit reportOften invisible on the face.
How does management explain a bad year?MD&AChairman's letter — then verify against notesStory layer, then evidence.

Teaching point. Matching the need to the section is half of this chapter. If you can fill a table like this in the exam, you have 'composition' plus 'use'.

Solved example 2 · Moderate

Sagar's growth: verify the claim and comment on cash quality

Given (from Sagar's annual report). MD&A: 'Revenue grew 20%.' P&L: revenue ₹420 crore (last year ₹350 crore), PAT ₹38 crore (last year ₹31 crore). Revenue note: spices ₹180 cr (LY ₹175 cr); pickles ₹140 cr (LY ₹110 cr); RTE ₹100 cr (LY ₹65 cr). Balance Sheet: trade receivables ₹74 cr (LY ₹46 cr). Cash flow: cash from operations ₹32 cr. Auditor: unmodified, KAM on a ₹12 cr distributor receivable. Loss allowance on that distributor: ₹1 cr.

Required. (a) Verify the 20% claim with arithmetic. (b) Identify which products grew. (c) Comment on cash quality. (d) What should an MBA write in a 4-mark 'analysis' note?

(a) Headline growth

Increase in revenue = 420 − 350 = ₹70 crore.

Growth rate = 70 ÷ 350 = 0.20 = 20.00%. The MD&A claim matches the face.

PAT increase = 38 − 31 = ₹7 crore. PAT growth = 7 ÷ 31 = 0.225806… ≈ 22.58%.

PAT margin now = 38 ÷ 420 = 0.090476… ≈ 9.05%. Last year 31 ÷ 350 = 0.088571… ≈ 8.86%.

(b) Product mix — do not skip this multiplication

Spices: 180 − 175 = ₹5 crore increase. 5 ÷ 175 = 0.028571… ≈ 2.86% — almost flat.

Pickles: 140 − 110 = ₹30 crore. 30 ÷ 110 = 0.272727… ≈ 27.27%.

RTE: 100 − 65 = ₹35 crore. 35 ÷ 65 = 0.538461… ≈ 53.85%.

Check the three products add up: 180 + 140 + 100 = ₹420 crore. Last year 175 + 110 + 65 = ₹350 crore. The note agrees with the face.

Share of the ₹70 crore increase: spices 5/70 ≈ 7%; pickles 30/70 ≈ 43%; RTE 35/70 = 50%. RTE and pickles did the work.

(c) Cash quality

Increase in trade receivables = 74 − 46 = ₹28 crore.

CFO ₹32 crore versus PAT ₹38 crore. Gap = 6, and the receivables jump of 28 is the smoking gun that collections lagged bookings.

Debtor days ≈ (74 ÷ 420) × 365. 74 ÷ 420 = 0.176190… × 365 ≈ 64.31 days.

Last year (46 ÷ 350) × 365. 46 ÷ 350 = 0.131429… × 365 ≈ 47.97 days. Slowdown ≈ 16 days.

Of ₹74 crore, ₹12 crore is one overdue distributor with only ₹1 crore provided. 12 ÷ 74 ≈ 16.2% of book is concentrated and sick-looking.

(d) Four-mark analysis note you could write

The 20% revenue growth is arithmetically correct but uneven: ready-to-eat (+53.85%) and pickles (+27.27%) explain almost all of the ₹70 crore increase; spices grew only 2.86%. Cash did not fully follow accrual: CFO ₹32 crore against PAT ₹38 crore, with receivables up ₹28 crore and debtor days up from ~48 to ~64. The auditor's unmodified opinion lets us use the figures, but the KAM on a ₹12 crore overdue distributor (allowance only ₹1 crore) is the quality-of-earnings issue. An MBA should not describe the year as 'excellent growth' without those two qualifications: mix and collections.

Solved example 3 · Exam

Write the 5-mark 'contents of annual report' and the 5-mark 'Directors' Report' as the examiner wants them

Question A (5 marks): 'Enumerate the contents of an annual report of a listed company.'

Answer (write this shape). An annual report of a typical Indian listed company usually contains the following, in something like this order:

  1. Cover and corporate information — name, year, CIN, registered office, board, bankers, auditors.
  2. Chairman's / MD's message — narrative of the year and outlook.
  3. Board of Directors — names, categories (executive / independent).
  4. Financial highlights / performance at a glance — multi-year dashboard.
  5. Management Discussion and Analysis — industry, segments, risks, internal control, financial review (SEBI LODR).
  6. Directors' Report (Board's Report) and annexures — Section 134: state of affairs, dividend, reserves, DRS, CSR, secretarial audit, related party, etc.
  7. Corporate Governance Report — board, committees, attendance, shareholder information.
  8. Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report — ESG disclosures for specified listed companies.
  9. Standalone financial statements — Balance Sheet, Statement of Profit and Loss, Cash Flow, Changes in Equity, notes.
  10. Consolidated financial statements — parent plus subsidiaries after elimination of intra-group items.
  11. Independent Auditor's Report(s) — opinion on the statements, KAMs, perhaps IFC and CARO.
  12. Significant accounting policies and notes to accounts — measurement rules and detailed disclosures.
  13. Notice of the AGM — date, time, ordinary and special business.

Even 10 of these 13, each with a 4–8 word explanation, fills 5 marks. A bare list of five words ('balance sheet, P&L, cash flow…') does not.

Question B (5 marks): 'What are the contents of the Directors' Report under the Companies Act, 2013?'

Answer (write this shape). The Board's Report under Section 134 (read with the Accounts Rules) includes:

  1. State of the company's affairs.
  2. Amount of dividend, if any, recommended.
  3. Amount, if any, proposed to be carried to reserves.
  4. Material changes and commitments affecting financial position occurring after the end of the year.
  5. Directors' Responsibility Statement (Section 134(5) — standards, policies and estimates, records/assets/fraud, going concern, internal financial controls for listed companies, compliance systems).
  6. Details of frauds reported by the auditor (other than those reportable to the Central Government), if any.
  7. Conservation of energy, technology absorption, foreign exchange earnings and outgo.
  8. CSR particulars (where Section 135 applies), secretarial audit report, related-party contracts (AOC-2), number of meetings, director changes, risk and IFC, web-link of annual return, and other prescribed matters.

If marks remain, unpack DRS as the six clauses. That single unpacking often separates a 3/5 from a 5/5.

Solved example 4 · Exam

Auditor's report types — choose the opinion

For each situation, name the opinion (or paragraph) and say why. This is a typical 4–6 mark application.

SituationOpinion / paragraphWhy
Inventory at 19 depots counted; one small depot of ₹0.4 crore not visited; total inventory ₹62 crore; nothing else wrong.Unmodified (the amount is almost certainly immaterial)Qualification requires materiality. ₹0.4 crore on a ₹420 crore company is not decision-changing.
Same, but the unvisited depot holds ₹18 crore and is material; rest of the statements are all right.Qualified ('except for')Material lack of evidence, not pervasive — confined to inventory / related COGS at that depot.
Management refuses to write down a clearly dead technology plant that is half the total assets; profit is thereby hugely overstated.AdverseMaterial and pervasive — the statements as a whole do not give a true and fair view.
A flood destroyed all stock records and the accounting server; opening stock, closing stock and a large slice of sales cannot be tested.DisclaimerInsufficient evidence; possible effects material and pervasive; auditor does not opine.
A factory fire on 10 April is properly disclosed in a subsequent-event note; 31 March numbers are fairly stated; going concern intact.Unmodified + Emphasis of Matter pointing to that noteSpotlight, not a fail. The matter is disclosed; the opinion remains clean.
Revenue schemes are complex; auditor spent the most hours there; evidence supports the number.Unmodified + Key Audit Matter on revenue schemesKAM ≠ qualification. It is a map of audit effort.

6.16 How to identify the question

9. How to identify the question

This chapter is theory-heavy, so the first 15 seconds in the exam hall are about labelling the question. If the question says 'define annual report' / 'what is an annual report' → 1–2 mark definition: yearly statutory-cum-communication document for shareholders, containing audited financial statements plus Board's Report, auditor's report and other disclosures. If it says 'contents' / 'composition' / 'enumerate the parts' → the ordered list in 6.6 (story, stewardship, evidence, notice). If it says 'need' / 'importance' / 'why annual reports are prepared' → the 8–10 points in 6.5 plus users. If it says 'users' / 'parties interested' → the user table in 6.4. If it says 'Directors' Report' / 'Board's Report' / 'Section 134' → contents list + DRS six clauses. If it says 'Directors' Responsibility Statement' alone → only the six clauses, in legal flavour. If it says 'auditor's report' / 'types of opinion' / 'true and fair' → 6.9, U-QAD + EOM + KAM. If it says 'MD&A' / 'Management Discussion' → what it is, SEBI listed-company context, typical headings, and how it differs from the Directors' Report. If it says 'notes to accounts' → face vs notes, examples, 'notes are part of the statements'. If it says 'limitations' → HAD WIN table. If it says 'how to analyse' / 'procedure to read' → the 30-minute / eight-step sequence. If it says 'standalone vs consolidated' → parent legal entity vs group after elimination. A mixed 8–10 mark question ('importance of annual report to various parties' or 'financial and non-financial parts') is 6.5 + 6.4 + a paragraph on how story, stewardship and evidence must be read together (6.12).

Question identifier — look at the verb before you look at your memory sheet
Question stem (as printed)Marks usuallyYour opening moveDo not
What is an annual report?1–2One tight definition + statutory and communication naturesDump the 13-item contents list
Contents / composition of annual report5Numbered list, one line each, listed-company orderWrite only BS and P&L

Directors' Report5Section 134 list; mention DRSConfuse with MD&A
DRS / Section 134(5)4–5All six clausesWrite only 'directors are responsible'
Auditor's report / types of opinion5U-QAD table + why MBA reads it firstCall a KAM a qualification
MD&A4–5SEBI narrative; typical heads; not statutory Board's ReportSay it is audited like the P&L

6.17 Exam-ready answers (1 mark, 5 mark, 8–10 mark)

1–2 marks

Define annual report.

An annual report is the yearly statutory-cum-communication document published by a company for its shareholders and other users, setting out its activities, performance, financial position, cash flows, governance and outlook for the financial year. It contains the audited financial statements (with notes), the Board's Report, the independent auditor's report, and, in a listed company, MD&A, a corporate governance report and other prescribed disclosures, together with the notice of the AGM.

5 marks

Enumerate the contents / composition of the annual report of a listed company.

A typical Indian listed-company annual report contains, usually in this order:

  1. Cover and corporate information (CIN, board, bankers, auditors, registered office).
  2. Chairman's / Managing Director's message.
  3. Board of Directors.
  4. Highlights / performance at a glance.
  5. Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A).
  6. Directors' Report (Board's Report) with statutory annexures (CSR, secretarial audit, related party, energy / FX).
  7. Corporate Governance Report.
  8. Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR), for specified listed companies.
  9. Standalone financial statements: Balance Sheet, Statement of Profit and Loss, Cash Flow Statement, Statement of Changes in Equity, and notes.
  10. Consolidated financial statements of the group.
  11. Independent Auditor's Report (often placed immediately before the statements it covers; separate reports for standalone and consolidated).
  12. Significant accounting policies and other notes to accounts.
  13. Notice of the Annual General Meeting.

These parts fall in three layers plus an action page: story (Chairman, highlights, MD&A), stewardship (Directors' Report, governance, BRSR), evidence (statements, policies, notes, auditor), and the AGM notice.

8–10 marks

Explain the need and importance of annual reports. Who are the users?

Need. Shareholders do not manage the company day to day. Without a yearly, comparable, audited public pack, stewardship cannot be judged, capital cannot be priced, and the Companies Act / SEBI duties cannot be discharged. The annual report fills that gap.

Importance (write 8 points):

  1. Transparency — performance, position, cash, related parties and risks are made visible.
  2. Stewardship — directors render account of shareholders' money through the Board's Report and audited statements.
  3. Legal compliance — Companies Act (accounts, Board's Report, audit, circulation, filing) and SEBI LODR for listed companies.
  4. Decision-useful information — basis for buy / hold / sell / lend / rate / join.
  5. Comparison — across years (highlights, consistent statements) and, with care, across companies.
  6. Basis for analysis — ratio analysis (Ch 7) and cash-flow analysis (Ch 5) are computed from this pack, especially the notes.
  7. Capital-market reputation — a clean, timely report lowers the cost of capital; a qualification raises it.
  8. Governance and public accountability — independent directors, CSR, BRSR, related-party transparency.

Users and what they look for. Shareholders (dividend, honesty, going concern); prospective investors (growth, margins, risks); lenders (debt, CFO, contingencies); employees (stability); tax authorities (profit, related party, tax notes); analysts and rating agencies (notes, segments, quality of earnings); customers and suppliers (going concern); media / public (CSR, controversies); government / regulators (compliance). The financial parts (statements, notes, auditor) and the non-financial parts (MD&A, governance, BRSR) must be read together: a claim in MD&A is tested on the P&L, the note, the cash flow and the auditor's KAM. Limitation in one line: the report is historical, aggregated, policy-dependent and can be window-dressed, so it is necessary but not sufficient.

5–8 marks

Write a note on the Directors' Report / Board's Report.

The Directors' Report is the Board's statutory report to members under Section 134 of the Companies Act, 2013, attached to the financial statements. It is a stewardship document, not the same as MD&A.

Principal contents: state of affairs; dividend; transfer to reserves; material post-balance-sheet changes; Directors' Responsibility Statement; frauds reported by the auditor; conservation of energy, technology absorption and foreign exchange; CSR annexure; secretarial audit report; related-party particulars; number of meetings and director changes; risk, internal financial controls, and other prescribed items including the web-link of the annual return.

Directors' Responsibility Statement (134(5)) — directors state that: (a) applicable accounting standards were followed, with explanation of material departures; (b) accounting policies were selected and applied consistently, with reasonable and prudent judgements, so as to give a true and fair view; (c) proper care was taken of accounting records, safeguarding of assets, and prevention and detection of fraud; (d) accounts were prepared on a going concern basis; (e) in a listed company, internal financial controls were laid down, adequate and operating effectively; (f) proper systems for compliance with applicable laws were devised, adequate and operating effectively.

5–8 marks

Write a note on the auditor's report. Why should an MBA read it first?

The Independent Auditor's Report is the statutory auditor's opinion on whether the financial statements give a true and fair view in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework. Management prepares the statements; the auditor examines evidence and reports. For listed companies the report includes Key Audit Matters and, where applicable, internal financial controls and a CARO annexure.

Types of opinion: (1) Unmodified (clean) — true and fair. (2) Qualified — material exception, not pervasive ('except for'). (3) Adverse — material and pervasive misstatement; statements do not give a true and fair view. (4) Disclaimer — insufficient evidence, possible effects material and pervasive; no opinion expressed. Emphasis of Matter and Key Audit Matters highlight issues without, by themselves, being qualifications.

Why read it first. Highlights, MD&A and the Chairman's letter are management's voice. Ratios computed from qualified or adverse statements are unsafe. An MBA therefore reads the opinion, the basis paragraph, EOM and KAMs before believing any dashboard number, then follows each KAM into the matching note.

4–5 marks

What is Management Discussion and Analysis? How is it different from the Directors' Report?

MD&A is a narrative analysis by management, required for listed companies under SEBI (LODR). It typically covers industry structure, opportunities and threats, segment-wise or product-wise performance, outlook, risks, internal control systems, and a discussion of financial performance versus the previous year. It is the 'story of the numbers'.

It differs from the Directors' Report: MD&A is analytical / communication (SEBI), not the Board's Section 134 legal report. MD&A is not a substitute for the financial statements and is not independently audited as a whole. Every quantitative claim in MD&A should be traced to the P&L, the notes and the cash flow. The Directors' Report, by contrast, recommends dividend, includes the Directors' Responsibility Statement, and carries statutory annexures (CSR, secretarial audit, related party).

6.18 Common mistakes (the ones that lose marks, and the ones that lose money)

10. Common mistakes
  • Thinking the annual report is only the financial statements. The statements are the core. The report also has the story layer, the Board's Report, governance, BRSR, the auditor and the AGM notice. A 'contents' answer that stops at Balance Sheet and P&L is incomplete.
  • Ignoring the notes. Face totals are headlines. Contingent liabilities, related parties, ageing, policy choices and subsequent events live in the notes. Skipping notes = not having read the accounts.
  • Ignoring auditor qualifications (and confusing KAM / EOM with a qualification). Always read the opinion first. A KAM is a spotlight on a clean opinion, not a fail mark. A qualification is an 'except for'. Treat them differently.
  • Mixing Directors' Report with MD&A. Directors' Report = Section 134 legal stewardship (dividend, DRS, annexures). MD&A = SEBI analytical narrative. Examiners set this trap on purpose.
  • Mixing annual report with annual return. Annual report → shareholders (this chapter). Annual return (MGT-7) → Registrar of Companies. Different documents.
  • Mixing CSR annexure with BRSR, and secretarial audit with statutory audit. CSR is Companies Act 2% spend. BRSR is SEBI ESG. Secretarial audit (CS, MR-3) checks law and process. Statutory audit (CA) checks whether the numbers are true and fair.
  • Using only standalone or only consolidated without knowing which question you are answering. Dividend and legal entity covenants → standalone. 'How did the group do for owners of Sagar?' → consolidated. Intra-group sales die on consolidation.
  • Believing the Chairman's 20% without checking mix and cash. Sagar's spices were flat; receivables jumped ₹28 crore; CFO lagged PAT. Story layer is a claim generator, not evidence.
  • Starting the 30-minute read with photographs and MD&A. Identity, then auditor, then dashboard, then faces, then notes, then story. Reverse order is how window dressing works on you.
  • Treating an unmodified opinion as an investment recommendation. True and fair ≠ cheap share, ≠ safe loan, ≠ no fraud anywhere, ≠ next year will be good. It means this year's statements, as a whole, under this framework, are fairly presented.
  • Forgetting that the report is historical, delayed, aggregated and policy-dependent. Limitations belong in a mature 8-mark importance answer.
  • Writing one long paragraph for a 5-mark 'contents' question. Numbered headings with one-line explanations. That is the format of marks in this chapter.

6.19 Practice questions (with answers to check yourself)

Practice 1 · Easy

One-mark definitions

Define, in two or three sentences each: (a) annual report (b) MD&A (c) consolidated financial statements.

Answer / solution

(a) Yearly statutory-cum-communication document for shareholders containing audited financial statements, Board's Report, auditor's report and other disclosures.

(b) Management's SEBI-required narrative for listed companies covering industry, performance, risks, outlook and financial review — the story of the numbers, to be tested against the statements.

(c) Statements of the parent and subsidiaries presented as one economic entity after eliminating intra-group transactions and balances, for the owners of the parent.

Practice 2 · Easy

Match the user

Who looks first at (a) contingent liabilities (b) CSR annexure (c) debtor days and CFO (d) Directors' Responsibility Statement (e) BRSR energy numbers?

Answer / solution

(a) Lender / analyst — hidden claims. (b) Regulator / NGO / exam on Section 135 — also a shareholder who cares about stewardship. (c) Banker and quality-of-earnings analyst. (d) Shareholder / court / exam on Section 134 — the Board's signed accountability. (e) ESG analyst / overseas buyer / BRSR reader.

Practice 3 · Moderate

Standalone versus consolidated

Sagar standalone revenue ₹420 crore. Sagar Spices Pvt Ltd (100% subsidiary) revenue ₹40 crore, of which ₹8 crore was sold to Sagar. Sagar Foods USA Inc revenue ₹22 crore, no intra-group sales. Compute consolidated revenue. In one sentence, say what happened to the ₹8 crore in each set of statements.

Answer / solution

Outside-group revenue of subsidiaries = (40 − 8) + 22 = 32 + 22 = ₹54 crore.

Consolidated revenue = 420 + 54 = ₹474 crore. Check: 420 + 40 + 22 − 8 = 482 − 8 = ₹474 crore.

The ₹8 crore is included in standalone revenue of the parent (it sold to another legal entity). It is eliminated on consolidation because the group cannot sell to itself.

Practice 4 · Moderate

Pick the opinion

Sagar's auditor was blocked from testing a branch that holds inventory of ₹18 crore and receivables of ₹9 crore. Everything else was tested and looked fair. Total assets are ₹240 crore. Which opinion, and why not the others?

Answer / solution

Likely qualified — material scope limitation, confined to that branch (inventory + receivables), not said to poison the whole statements, so not pervasive → not adverse, and not a full-book evidence failure → not disclaimer. Not unmodified, because ₹18 + ₹9 = ₹27 crore is material on ₹240 crore assets (27 ÷ 240 = 0.1125 = 11.25% of assets). EOM is wrong because EOM is used when the matter is already fairly stated and the opinion stays clean.

Practice 5 · Exam

Eight-mark mixed question

'An annual report is more than a set of financial statements.' Explain, with reference to need, users, and how the financial and non-financial parts should be read together. Use a company of your choice.

Answer / solution

Shape of the answer (use Sagar or any company):

  1. Definition of annual report as statutory + communication pack (not only FS).
  2. Need: stewardship gap, legal duty, public information spine.
  3. Importance: transparency, compliance, comparison, basis for ratios and cash-flow analysis, capital raising, governance.
  4. Users: at least six, with information needs (table in sentences).
  5. Composition in three layers: story (MD&A, Chairman), stewardship (Board's Report, governance, BRSR), evidence (FS, notes, auditor).
  6. Worked connection: Sagar's 20% claim → P&L → revenue note → cash flow → debtor days → auditor KAM. This paragraph is the 'more than financial statements' proof.
  7. Close with two limitations (historical, window dressing) so you do not sound naive.
Practice 6 · Exam

Directors' Responsibility Statement

List the six clauses of the Directors' Responsibility Statement. Against each, write one sentence of simple meaning and one Sagar-style illustration.

Answer / solution

Use the SPRFGC table in Section 6.10. Sample illustration for (d): Sagar's Board states accounts are prepared as a going concern — they do not expect to liquidate the pickle plants in the next twelve months; if a mega-loan default were likely, this clause would be the first to break and the auditor would add a going-concern paragraph.

Sample for (e): as a listed company Sagar's directors confirm internal financial controls over billing, inventory counts and related-party approvals are adequate and operating — the same system the auditor also reports on.

Connect the chapters

You now have the map of the house. Chapter 4 gave you the furniture of the financial statements. Chapter 5 gave you the plumbing of cash flow. Chapter 7 will give you the measuring tape of ratios. Whenever a later chapter says 'take current assets from the Balance Sheet', remember: that number lives in an annual report, under an auditor's opinion, next to a note, after a story that may be trying to sell you 20%. Read the house, then measure the room.

Chapter 07

Ratio Analysis

Learning outcome. After this chapter you will classify every ratio as Balance Sheet, Revenue or Combined; pick the correct figures from a Profit and Loss Account and a Balance Sheet; compute the ratio with its unit; and interpret whether the result is healthy — including when a ‘high’ number is actually a warning.

What this chapter covers (official syllabus)

  • Need and importance of ratios
  • Ratio formulas
  • Balance Sheet ratios
  • Revenue ratios
  • Combined ratios
  • Numerical problems

A bank manager in Mysore is looking at two trading companies. Both sold goods worth ₹10,00,000 last year. Both show a profit. One of them will get the loan. The other will not. The difference is not the sales figure. The difference is the relationships between the figures — how much of that sale is leftover as profit, how quickly stock turns into cash, whether the firm can pay its bills next month, and whether the owners or the lenders have a bigger claim. Those relationships are ratios.

This chapter uses one company, Kaveri Traders Ltd, for every single ratio. You will first read a short Profit and Loss Account and a short Balance Sheet. Then you will compute every ratio the syllabus names from those two statements. When the exam gives you a different company, the method does not change — only the numbers do.

Connect the chapters

Chapter 4 taught you to prepare a company Balance Sheet and Statement of Profit and Loss (Schedule III). Chapter 6 taught you to read an annual report. This chapter teaches you to analyse those statements with arithmetic. A ratio is not a new statement. It is a smarter way of reading the two you already have.

Key point

A ratio is a fraction. One figure divided by another. The art is (1) choosing the right pair, (2) picking both figures from the correct statement and the correct year, (3) writing the unit (times, %, days, or a : ratio), and (4) saying what the number means. A naked 2.1 with no unit and no sentence scores half marks at best.

1. Need and importance of ratio analysis

1. What is it? — Definition

A ratio is the arithmetical relationship between two figures drawn from the financial statements, expressed as a pure number (times), a percentage, a number of days, or a proportion (a : b). Ratio analysis is the method of computing these relationships, comparing them with a standard, a previous year or another firm, and interpreting what they say about liquidity, solvency, profitability and efficiency.

2. In simple words

A ratio is a comparison written as a short number. ₹3,00,000 of current assets and ₹1,50,000 of current liabilities is a current ratio of 2. The 2 is easier to carry in your head, easier to compare with last year, and easier to compare with a rival, than the two raw rupee totals.

3. Why do we need it?

Financial statements are long. A Balance Sheet of a real company has dozens of lines. The human brain cannot hold “sales ten lakh, stock one lakh twenty thousand, debtors one lakh…” and see the story. Ratios shrink the story to a handful of numbers, each of which answers one managerial question: Can we pay bills? Are we too borrowed? How much of each sale is profit? How fast does stock move?

4. Real-life example

Kaveri’s owner, Meera, wants a bank working-capital limit. The manager will not read every ledger. He will compute (or ask her to compute) current ratio, quick ratio, debt-equity, interest coverage and stock turnover. If those five numbers sit in a healthy range, the file moves. If current ratio is 0.8, the file stops — no matter how colourful the sales graph is.

5. Accounting logic

A single rupee figure has no meaning until it is placed next to another rupee figure. Profit of ₹90,000 sounds pleasant. Profit of ₹90,000 on sales of ₹10,00,000 is a 9% net margin. Profit of ₹90,000 on owners’ funds of ₹6,00,000 is a 15% return on equity. Same profit, two different questions, two different ratios. That is the whole subject.

What ratio analysis is used for — five jobs.

Five jobs of ratio analysis
JobQuestion it answersTypical tool
CompareIs this year better than last year? (trend / intra-firm)Same ratio, two years, side by side
BenchmarkAre we better or worse than other traders? (inter-firm)Our ratio vs industry average
Diagnose liquidityCan we pay what is due in the next 12 months?Current, quick, cash, working-capital turnover
Diagnose solvencyCan we survive in the long run? Is the loan load safe?Debt-equity, proprietary, gearing, interest coverage
Diagnose profitability & efficiencyAre we earning, and are we using assets hard enough?GP, NP, operating, ROCE, ROE, turnovers, EPS

Why ratios, not raw figures?

  • Scale. A firm with sales of ₹1,00,00,000 and a firm with sales of ₹10,00,000 cannot be compared on raw profit. They can be compared on net profit ratio.
  • Trend. Current assets of ₹3,00,000 this year and ₹2,80,000 last year look like an improvement — until you notice current liabilities jumped from ₹1,00,000 to ₹1,50,000. The current ratio fell from 2.8 to 2.0. The ratio caught what the raw total hid.
  • Diagnosis. A falling net profit ratio with a stable gross profit ratio means the leak is below the gross-profit line (operating expenses, interest or tax) — you know where to look.
  • Communication. A board, a bank and an examiner all understand “current ratio 2 : 1”. They do not all want to re-read the whole Balance Sheet.
  • Control. Management sets a target (stock turnover at least 8 times; collection period under 40 days) and watches the ratio the way a driver watches the speedometer.
6. Format — Four-way classification of what a ratio talks about (use this in theory answers)
FamilyAboutExamples in this chapter
LiquidityShort-term ability to payCurrent, quick, absolute liquid
Solvency / leverageLong-term survival and mix of debt vs equityDebt-equity, proprietary, capital gearing, interest coverage
ProfitabilityHow much leftover from sales and from fundsGP, NP, operating profit, ROCE, ROE, ROA, EPS
Efficiency / activity / turnoverHow hard assets and working capital are workedStock, debtors, creditors, FA, capital, WC turnovers

The syllabus classification in the next section is different: it is by where the two figures come from (Balance Sheet, P&L, or one of each). Both classifications are examinable. Do not mix up the names.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Read the question. Is it theory (need, importance, limitations, classification) or a numerical?
  2. If theory: write a definition, then 5–8 numbered points with one line of explanation each. End with a limitation if marks are 8 or more.
  3. If numerical: extract the two statements (or the given ratios), label each figure BS or P&L, then choose the family (liquidity / solvency / profitability / efficiency) and the syllabus bucket (BS / Revenue / Combined).
  4. Write the formula. Substitute. Divide. Write the unit. Write one sentence of meaning if the question says “comment” or “interpret”.
Solved example 7.0 · Easy

Why a ratio beats a raw figure

Firm A earns PAT of ₹90,000 with owners’ funds of ₹6,00,000. Firm B earns PAT of ₹1,20,000 with owners’ funds of ₹12,00,000. Who is using owners’ money better?

Working.

Firm A ROE = ₹90,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000 × 100 = 15%.

Firm B ROE = ₹1,20,000 ÷ ₹12,00,000 × 100 = 10%.

Answer. Firm A. B’s profit is bigger in rupees, but A returns 15 paise per owners’ rupee against B’s 10 paise. Without the ratio, the bigger profit would have fooled you.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “need / importance / advantages / utility of ratio analysis”, write: comparison (intra-firm trend and inter-firm), diagnosis of liquidity, solvency, profitability and efficiency, simplification of statements, help to management / creditors / investors, and use in forecasting. If it says “limitations / disadvantages / drawbacks”, use the next section — do not recycle the importance points with a ‘not’ stuck in front.

10. Common mistakes
  • Treating a ratio as a conclusion. “Current ratio is 2, so the company is good” is incomplete. Good compared with what? Last year? The industry? The 2 : 1 rule of thumb?
  • Using ratios as the only evidence. Window dressing, different accounting policies and non-money facts (a strike, a new patent) do not appear in the ratio.
  • Writing ‘ratios help in decision making’ as a full answer. The examiner wants which decision and which ratio.
11. Memory trick

C-T-D-C — Compare, Trend, Diagnose, Communicate. That is why ratios exist. Four health checks: Liquidity (today’s bills), Solvency (tomorrow’s survival), Profitability (leftover), Efficiency (speed).

12. Exam-ready answer

Ratio analysis is the process of computing, comparing and interpreting arithmetical relationships between figures in the financial statements. It is needed because raw rupee totals of two firms, or of two years, are not comparable when the firms differ in size. Ratios reduce the statements to a small set of indicators of liquidity (current, quick), solvency (debt-equity, proprietary), profitability (gross profit, net profit, ROCE, ROE) and efficiency (stock, debtors, capital turnover). They help management to control operations, help lenders to judge creditworthiness, help investors to judge return, and help the analyst to locate the area in which the business is weak. A ratio has meaning only against a benchmark — a previous period, an industry average, or a conventional ideal — and must be read with the limitations of historical data and window dressing in mind.

Limitations of ratio analysis (always asked)

1. What is it? — Definition

A limitation of ratio analysis is a reason why a computed ratio may mislead, or may not be enough, for a decision. Ratios are a tool. They are not the business itself.

2. In simple words

A ratio is a photograph of the past, taken with the company’s own camera, possibly after the furniture was rearranged for the photo. You still look at the photo — you just do not buy the house from the photo alone.

Nine limitations — write any six in an 8-mark answer, each with one line of explanation
LimitationWhat it meansWhat you do about it
HistoricalFigures are last year’s. The factory may already have burned, or a new contract may already have been signed.Read notes, directors’ report, and subsequent events. Do not treat the ratio as tomorrow’s cash.
Window dressingManagement can postpone a purchase, push a sale, or repay a creditor on 30 March and re-borrow on 2 April, so that 31 March looks liquid.Look at average figures, cash flow, and more than one year. One beautiful year-end is a warning, not a comfort.
Different policiesOne firm uses FIFO, another weighted average; one uses SLM, another WDV. Stock and profit, and therefore every ratio that uses them, are not comparable.Read the accounting-policy note. Adjust, or at least say “not strictly comparable”.
No standalone meaningCurrent ratio 2 : 1 is not ‘good’ by itself. In a supermarket 1.2 may be healthy; in a shipyard 2 may be tight.Always pair with an industry benchmark and with other ratios of the same firm.
Need for a benchmarkWithout last year, a rival, or a rule of thumb, a ratio is a number in a vacuum.Write the comparison in the answer. “1.2, above the 1 : 1 ideal” scores; “1.2” does not.
Ignores qualitative factsSkill of the owner, quality of the product, pending court case, labour unrest — none of these is a ratio.Read the notes and the auditors’ report. Mention qualitative factors in a comment question.
Price-level / inflationFixed assets at 2014 cost sit next to sales at 2026 prices. FA turnover looks better than the real use of capacity.Be careful with any ratio that mixes an old Balance-Sheet cost with a current P&L figure.
Year-end snapshotA seasonal trader may look weak on 31 March and strong on 31 December. One day is not the year.Prefer averages of opening and closing; mention seasonality in the comment.
Arithmetic without causeA ratio tells you that stock is slow. It does not tell you whether the cause is a bad product, a weak salesman, or a flood.Use ratios to locate the room. Then walk into the room (ageing, product mix, visit).
12. Exam-ready answer

Ratio analysis has important limitations. The data are historical and may not continue. Management may window-dress year-end figures. Different accounting policies (stock valuation, depreciation) destroy comparability. A ratio has no meaning in isolation — it needs an industry or trend benchmark. Qualitative factors and subsequent events are ignored. Inflation mixes old costs with current revenues. Year-end figures may be seasonal. And a ratio identifies a symptom, not a cause. Therefore ratios must be read together, over several years, along with notes to accounts and cash-flow information.

Watch out

In a 5-mark “limitations” question, three one-word bullets (“historical, window dressing, not comparable”) are not enough. Give one sentence of meaning under each heading. The marks are in the sentence.

2. Classification of ratios as per this syllabus

1. What is it? — Definition

This syllabus classifies ratios by the source of the two figures. (1) Balance Sheet ratios — numerator and denominator both from the Balance Sheet. (2) Revenue ratios (also called Profit and Loss, income-statement, or P&L ratios) — both from the Statement of Profit and Loss. (3) Combined ratios — one figure from the P&L and one from the Balance Sheet.

2. In simple words

Look at the two numbers you are about to divide. If both live on the Balance Sheet (a photograph of one day), it is a Balance Sheet ratio. If both live on the P&L (a movie of one year), it is a Revenue ratio. If one lives on each statement (a movie divided by a photograph), it is Combined.

3. Why do we need it?

Examiners in this paper ask “classify the following ratios” and they mean this three-bucket split, not the liquidity/solvency/profitability split. If you write ‘current ratio is a liquidity ratio’ when they asked for the syllabus classification, you have answered a different question.

4. Real-life example

Meera’s current assets and current liabilities are both on Kaveri’s Balance Sheet — current ratio is a Balance Sheet ratio. Gross profit and sales are both on the P&L — GP ratio is a Revenue ratio. Cost of goods sold is on the P&L, average stock is on the Balance Sheet — stock turnover is Combined.

5. Accounting logic

A Balance Sheet ratio compares two stocks (positions on one date). A Revenue ratio compares two flows (over a period). A Combined ratio compares a flow with a stock, which is why we so often use an average of opening and closing Balance-Sheet figures — to give the stock a chance to represent the whole year.

6. Format — The three buckets (memorise the test, not a random list)
Syllabus classification — this is the one you must not skip
BucketTest (say this in the exam)What it usually measuresRatios in this chapter
Balance Sheet ratiosBoth numerator and denominator are Balance-Sheet positions.Liquidity and solvency / capital structureCurrent; quick / acid test; absolute liquid; debt-equity; proprietary; capital gearing; fixed assets to long-term funds; current assets to proprietary funds
Revenue ratiosBoth figures are P&L flows for the year.Profitability margins and cost structureGross profit ratio; net profit ratio; operating profit ratio; operating ratio; expense ratios
Combined ratiosOne figure from P&L, one from Balance Sheet (use averages when opening is given).Turnovers / efficiency, and returns on funds, plus EPS and interest coverageInventory turnover and holding period; debtors turnover and collection period; creditors turnover and payment period; WC / FA / capital turnover; ROCE; ROE; ROA; EPS; interest coverage
Spot check — cover the right column and say the bucket
RatioBucket
Current ratioBalance Sheet
Quick ratioBalance Sheet
Debt-equityBalance Sheet
Gross profit ratioRevenue
Operating ratioRevenue
Stock turnoverCombined
ROCECombined
EPSCombined
Why ROCE is Combined, not Revenue

EBIT lives on the P&L. Capital employed lives on the Balance Sheet (equity + long-term debt, or fixed assets + working capital). One from each statement → Combined. Students often dump ROCE into “profitability” and then, when asked for the syllabus bucket, wrongly say Revenue. Profitability is the purpose. Combined is the source.

9. How to identify the question

If the question says “classify as Balance Sheet / Revenue / Combined (or income-statement / mixed)”, apply the source test. Ignore the words liquidity and profitability for that question. If the question says “liquidity / solvency / profitability / activity”, use the four-family table in section 1. Read the question’s own headings before you start listing.

10. Common mistakes
  • Putting stock turnover under Balance Sheet because stock is a Balance-Sheet item. The other half (COGS) is P&L — it is Combined.
  • Putting current ratio under Combined because ‘current assets come from operations’. Both CA and CL are BS positions. It is a Balance Sheet ratio.
  • Calling every profitability ratio a Revenue ratio. ROCE, ROE, ROA and EPS are profitability by purpose but Combined by source.
  • Forgetting that interest coverage (EBIT / Interest) is Combined — EBIT is P&L, but some papers treat both as P&L (interest is a P&L expense too!). In this syllabus we place it under Combined because it is read with solvency; if both figures are from P&L you may also defend it as Revenue. State your reason. In these notes it sits with Combined, next to ROCE, because the exam uses it as a solvency companion of debt-equity.
Key point

Interest coverage: both EBIT and interest appear in the P&L, so a strict source-test would call it a Revenue ratio. Many MBA papers still group it with leverage / Combined because you interpret it together with debt-equity. In the formula table at the end of this chapter it is listed as Combined (solvency companion). If the question is a pure source-test and offers ‘P&L ratio’ as a choice, you may tick that and write ‘both figures from P&L’.

11. Memory trick

BS–BS = Balance Sheet ratio (structure). P&L–P&L = Revenue ratio (margin). P&L–BS = Combined (speed or return). Three buckets. Every ratio in the paper falls into one of them.

12. Exam-ready answer

Ratios are classified, for this syllabus, by the statement from which the two figures are taken. Balance Sheet ratios use two position figures from the Balance Sheet (current ratio, quick ratio, debt-equity, proprietary ratio, capital gearing, fixed assets to long-term funds, current assets to proprietary funds). Revenue ratios use two flow figures from the Statement of Profit and Loss (gross profit ratio, net profit ratio, operating profit ratio, operating ratio, expense ratios). Combined ratios use one flow and one position (inventory, debtors and creditors turnovers and their holding/collection/payment periods, working-capital, fixed-asset and capital turnovers, ROCE, ROE, ROA, EPS, and interest coverage as a solvency companion). This source classification is separate from the purpose classification into liquidity, solvency, profitability and efficiency.

3. The running company — Kaveri Traders Ltd

Every worked ratio in this chapter uses Kaveri Traders Ltd, a wholesale trader, year ended 31 March 2026. The numbers were chosen so that most divisions come out clean. Live with these two statements. By the end of the chapter you should be able to recompute any ratio with the statements closed.

Business. Kaveri buys goods on credit, sells 80% on credit and 20% for cash, owns its godown and office (fixed assets), and has one term loan. There are no preference shares, no prepaid expenses, no marketable securities, and no fictitious assets. That keeps the picking rules visible: when a component is nil, we still name it, then drop it.

Check the Balance Sheet before you touch a ratio: Equity and liabilities ₹9,50,000 = Assets ₹9,50,000. If these two capital-employed workings disagree, you have mis-picked a figure — stop and find it.

Watch out

Credit sales are ₹8,00,000 — not ₹10,00,000. If a question is silent on the cash/credit split, the usual exam assumption is that all sales are credit sales, and you write that assumption on the face of the answer. Kaveri is not silent: 80% credit is given, so debtors turnover must use ₹8,00,000.

Solved example 7.1 · Easy

Prove the two statements lock together

Balance Sheet total.

Equity ₹4,00,000 + Reserves ₹2,00,000 + Long-term debt ₹2,00,000 + Trade payables ₹1,50,000 = ₹6,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 + ₹1,50,000 = ₹8,00,000 + ₹1,50,000 = ₹9,50,000.

Fixed assets ₹6,50,000 + Inventory ₹1,20,000 + Receivables ₹1,00,000 + Cash ₹80,000 = ₹6,50,000 + ₹3,00,000 = ₹9,50,000.

Capital employed, method 1 (liability side).

₹6,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹8,00,000.

Capital employed, method 2 (asset side).

Working capital = ₹3,00,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹1,50,000. FA + WC = ₹6,50,000 + ₹1,50,000 = ₹8,00,000.

Gross profit check.

GP ratio is given as 25% of sales, so GP = 25% × ₹10,00,000 = ₹2,50,000. COGS = sales − GP = ₹10,00,000 − ₹2,50,000 = ₹7,50,000. Purchases = COGS + closing stock − opening stock = ₹7,50,000 + ₹1,20,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹8,70,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹7,90,000.

Answer. The statements lock. You may now compute every ratio from this extract without going back to the ledgers.

4. Exam method that never changes

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Draw a two-column extract: P&L figures on the left, Balance Sheet figures on the right. Include openings if given.
  2. Build the derived figures: GP, COGS, operating cost, EBIT, shareholders’ funds, capital employed, working capital, quick assets, averages.
  3. Read the requirement. Circle the ratio names. Next to each, write BS / Rev / Combined — this chooses the formula family.
  4. Write the formula in words, then in figures, then the arithmetic, then the answer with unit (times, %, days, ₹, or a : b).
  5. If the question says “comment / interpret / evaluate”, add two sentences: (a) against the ideal or last year, (b) one risk if the ratio went further in the same direction.
  6. If an opening figure is missing, use the closing figure and write “opening not given, closing figure used as a proxy for average”.
Exam tip

Units: turnover ratios are in times; margin and return ratios are in %; collection / payment / holding periods are in days (or months/weeks if asked); current and quick are written as x : 1; EPS is in ₹ per share. A correct 7.5 without “times” is a half-done answer.

Key point

365 days in a year is the default in these notes. Some question papers use 360 days to make the division neat, or 12 months, or 52 weeks. If the paper states a convention, obey it. If it is silent, 365 is acceptable; write “taking 365 days in a year”.

5. Balance Sheet ratios

Both figures come from the Balance Sheet. These ratios talk about structure: can Kaveri pay what is due this year (liquidity), and who has financed the firm — owners or lenders (solvency).

There is no P&L number in this section. If you catch yourself reaching for sales or PAT, you have slipped into a Combined or Revenue ratio.

5.1 Current ratio (working capital ratio)

Syllabus bucket. Balance Sheet ratio — both figures from the Balance Sheet. Purpose family: liquidity.

Ideal / usual comment. Textbook ideal ≈ 2 : 1. A conventional rule of thumb, not a law. Trading firms can live a little lower; manufacturers with slow stock need it higher.

1. What is it? — Definition

The current ratio is current assets divided by current liabilities. It asks: for every rupee payable within a year, how many rupees of assets are expected to turn into cash within a year?

2. In simple words

It is the short-term cushion. Current assets are the things that will become cash soon (stock, debtors, cash, prepaid). Current liabilities are the bills due soon (creditors, outstanding expenses, short-term borrowings, overdraft). Divide the first by the second.

3. Why do we need it?

Lenders and the owner want to know whether next year’s bills can be paid from next year’s convertibles, without selling the godown. A bank sanction note almost always quotes this ratio.

Formula

Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities   (written as CA : CL, e.g. 2 : 1)

Working capital = CA − CL is the rupee cousin, not the ratio. Current ratio 2 does not mean working capital is ₹2. Current ratio 2 means CA = 2 × CL.

5.1 Current ratio (working capital ratio) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Current assetsAssets expected to be realised within 12 months: inventory, trade receivables, cash and bank, short-term investments, prepaid expenses, bills receivable.Balance Sheet → Current assets. For Kaveri: inventory ₹1,20,000 + receivables ₹1,00,000 + cash ₹80,000 = ₹3,00,000.
Current liabilitiesObligations due within 12 months: trade payables, outstanding expenses, short-term borrowings, bank overdraft, current maturities of long-term debt, tax payable.Balance Sheet → Current liabilities. For Kaveri: only trade payables ₹1,50,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Add every current asset on the face of the BS (do not skip prepaid or cash). Add every current liability (do not skip outstanding expenses or overdraft if given). Do not include long-term borrowings. Do not include fixed assets.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. From the Balance Sheet, total current assets. From the Balance Sheet, total current liabilities.
  2. Write Current ratio = CA ÷ CL.
  3. Divide. Write the answer as a number of times, or as x : 1.
  4. Compare with 2 : 1 and with last year / industry if given. One sentence of comment if asked.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Comfortable cushion. Suppliers and banks are happier. The firm can take small shocks (a slow customer, a late sale) without defaulting.
Low (or falling)Bills may not be paid on time. A ratio under 1 means current assets do not even cover current liabilities — technically insolvent in the short run.
Too high can also be badIdle cash sitting in the bank earning little, or stock piling up, or debtors not being collected. Owners’ money is sleeping. A current ratio of 5 is not a prize; it is a question: why is capital stuck in working capital instead of earning in the business or being returned to owners?
Solved example K1 · Easy

5.1 Current ratio (working capital ratio) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaCurrent ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities
2. Figures pickedCA = ₹3,00,000 (inventory ₹1,20,000 + receivables ₹1,00,000 + cash ₹80,000). CL = ₹1,50,000 (trade payables).
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹3,00,000 ÷ ₹1,50,000 = 2. Written as 2 : 1.
4. Answer with unit2 : 1 &nbsp;(or 2 times)

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Exactly the textbook ideal of 2 : 1. Short-term bills of ₹1 are covered by ₹2 of current assets. Not tight, not bloated. We still need the quick ratio, because part of that cushion is stock, which is the slowest current asset.

10. Common mistakes
  • Reading “current ratio 2” as CA − CL = 2. No: CA = 2 × CL. If WC is ₹1,50,000 and CR is 2, CL is ₹1,50,000, not ₹2.
  • Leaving prepaid expenses out of CA. Prepaid is a current asset. (It is excluded only when we compute the quick ratio.)
  • Putting long-term debt into CL. A term loan due after 12 months is non-current.
  • Using working capital as the denominator. The denominator is CL, not WC.
11. Memory trick

Current = everything soon-to-be-cash over everything soon-to-be-paid. Ideal 2 : 1 — “two on top, one below”.

Watch out

Bank overdraft: treat it as a current liability (denominator). Do not net it off cash unless the question says “cash net of overdraft”. Proposed dividend, if given as a current liability in the paper’s own BS, stays in CL.

5.2 Quick ratio (acid-test / liquid ratio)

Syllabus bucket. Balance Sheet ratio. Purpose family: liquidity (stricter than current).

Ideal / usual comment. Textbook ideal ≈ 1 : 1. Quick assets should at least equal current liabilities.

1. What is it? — Definition

The quick ratio is quick (liquid) assets divided by current liabilities. Quick assets are current assets minus inventory and minus prepaid expenses. It asks: if we cannot sell a single extra unit of stock, can we still pay the bills from cash, near-cash and debtors?

2. In simple words

The current ratio trusts stock. The acid test does not. Stock may be slow, damaged, or overvalued. Prepaid expenses will not pay a creditor — the landlord already has that rent. So we drop both, and test again.

3. Why do we need it?

To measure immediate liquidity. A firm with a pretty current ratio of 2.5 that is almost all unsold monsoon stock will fail the acid test. Banks look at this after they look at current ratio.

Formula

Quick ratio = (Current assets − Inventory − Prepaid expenses) ÷ Current liabilities

Quick assets = Cash + Bank + Marketable securities + Trade receivables + Bills receivable. Equivalent formula: Quick assets ÷ CL. Ideal ≈ 1 : 1.

5.2 Quick ratio (acid-test / liquid ratio) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Quick assetsCurrent assets that can be converted into cash in a short time without a special sale of stock.Kaveri: CA ₹3,00,000 − inventory ₹1,20,000 − prepaid ₹0 = ₹1,80,000. Check: receivables ₹1,00,000 + cash ₹80,000 = ₹1,80,000.
Inventory (stock)Goods held for sale. Slowest current asset; may not realise book value.BS → Inventories. Kaveri closing stock ₹1,20,000. Deduct it.
Prepaid expensesAlready paid; will not come back as cash. Cannot be used to pay a creditor.Kaveri has none. If a paper gives prepaid ₹20,000, deduct that too.
Current liabilitiesSame CL as in the current ratio.Kaveri: ₹1,50,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Start with total CA. Subtract closing inventory. Subtract prepaid expenses (and any deferred or non-cash current assets the question flags). Do not subtract debtors — debtors are quick. Do not subtract cash. Divide by the same CL you used for the current ratio.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Compute current assets and current liabilities as for the current ratio.
  2. Identify inventory and prepaid (and loose tools / stock of stationery if the paper treats them as non-quick).
  3. Quick assets = CA − inventory − prepaid.
  4. Quick ratio = Quick assets ÷ CL. Write as x : 1.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)The firm can pay short-term dues even if stock freezes. Creditors are well covered by cash and debtors.
Low (or falling)Below 1 : 1, the firm depends on selling stock (or taking a new loan) to pay today’s bills. That is a liquidity risk.
Too high can also be badCash and debtors piled up. Cash earning little; debtors perhaps too generous (check collection period). Capital is idle.
Solved example K2 · Easy

5.2 Quick ratio (acid-test / liquid ratio) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaQuick ratio = (CA − Inventory − Prepaid) ÷ CL
2. Figures pickedCA ₹3,00,000, Inventory ₹1,20,000, Prepaid nil, CL ₹1,50,000. Quick assets = ₹3,00,000 − ₹1,20,000 = ₹1,80,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹1,80,000 ÷ ₹1,50,000 = 1.2. Written as 1.20 : 1.
4. Answer with unit1.20 : 1

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. 1.2 : 1 is above the 1 : 1 ideal. Even with stock ignored, Kaveri covers its bills. The gap between current 2.0 and quick 1.2 is stock of ₹1,20,000 — we will later see whether that stock is moving (spoiler: stock turnover 7.5 times, so it is moving).

10. Common mistakes
  • Forgetting to deduct prepaid expenses. Prepaid is in CA, but it is not a quick asset.
  • Deducting debtors “because they might not pay”. Doubtful debts, if a provision is given, are already netted. Do not drop the whole receivables line.
  • Using opening stock instead of closing stock. The Balance Sheet is a closing photograph. Quick ratio uses closing inventory.
  • Changing the CL between current and quick. Same denominator.
11. Memory trick

Acid test = drop the slow and the already-spent: drop stock, drop prepaid. Ideal 1 : 1 — “one on top, one below”.

Exam tip

If the paper gives “liquid assets” as a ready total, believe it. If it gives a list, you must deduct stock and prepaid yourself. Loose tools and prepaid rent are the two items students most often leave inside quick assets.

5.3 Absolute liquid ratio (cash ratio)

Syllabus bucket. Balance Sheet ratio. Purpose family: liquidity (strictest).

Ideal / usual comment. Conventional ideal ≈ 0.5 : 1 (cash and near-cash equal half of current liabilities). Not always required; many traders run lower because cash earns little.

1. What is it? — Definition

The absolute liquid ratio is cash plus marketable securities (current investments), divided by current liabilities. It asks: without collecting a single debtor and without selling a single unit of stock, can we pay any part of the bills today?

2. In simple words

Only money that is already money (or can be sold on the stock exchange this afternoon). Cash at bank, cash in hand, and Treasury bills / listed securities held as current investments. Nothing else.

3. Why do we need it?

To test emergency liquidity. A firm that looks fine on the current and quick ratios can still bounce a cheque if debtors are slow and the bank will not extend the overdraft. This ratio is that cheque-book test.

Formula

Absolute liquid ratio = (Cash and bank + Marketable securities) ÷ Current liabilities

Also called cash ratio or super-quick ratio. Marketable securities = current investments that can be sold at once. Do not include long-term investments.

5.3 Absolute liquid ratio (cash ratio) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Cash and cash equivalentsCash in hand, cash at bank, short-term deposits that are as good as cash.BS → Cash and cash equivalents. Kaveri: ₹80,000.
Marketable securitiesCurrent investments: listed shares, T-bills, mutual-fund units held to be sold any day.Kaveri: nil. If a paper gives “current investments ₹40,000”, add them to cash.
Current liabilitiesSame CL as current and quick.Kaveri: ₹1,50,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Take the cash-and-cash-equivalents line. Add current investments / marketable securities if given. Do not add debtors. Do not add stock. Divide by CL.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Pick cash and bank. Add marketable securities / current investments.
  2. Pick current liabilities (same as current ratio).
  3. Divide. Write as x : 1.
  4. Comment against 0.5 : 1 if the question asks for a comment.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)The firm can pay a large slice of bills today. Useful in a credit freeze.
Low (or falling)The firm depends on collecting debtors or selling stock or drawing an overdraft. Normal for a well-run trader, dangerous if debtors are already slow.
Too high can also be badCash hoard. Opportunity cost: that cash could repay a loan, earn in the business, or be paid as dividend. A cash ratio of 2 is usually poor treasury management, not strength.
Solved example K3 · Easy

5.3 Absolute liquid ratio (cash ratio) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaAbsolute liquid ratio = (Cash + Marketable securities) ÷ CL
2. Figures pickedCash ₹80,000, marketable securities nil, CL ₹1,50,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹80,000 ÷ ₹1,50,000 = 80,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = 8/15 = 0.5333…
4. Answer with unit0.53 : 1 &nbsp;(exactly 8 : 15)

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Just above the 0.5 : 1 rule of thumb. Kaveri can pay a little more than half its current bills from cash already in the bank, without waiting for a debtor. Comfortable, not idle.

10. Common mistakes
  • Adding debtors. Debtors are quick, not absolute liquid.
  • Adding long-term investments. A 5-year bond is not cash.
  • Netting off overdraft against cash without being asked, then also keeping overdraft in CL — you would double-count the benefit.
11. Memory trick

Absolute = already money. Cash + marketable securities only. Ideal about half a rupee of cash per rupee of CL (0.5 : 1).

5.4 Debt-equity ratio

Syllabus bucket. Balance Sheet ratio. Purpose family: solvency / leverage / capital structure.

Ideal / usual comment. No single ideal. Many Indian textbooks quote 2 : 1 as an outer ceiling for long-term debt : equity (debt not more than twice equity), and 1 : 1 as comfortable. Trading firms often sit well below 1 : 1. Banks have their own covenants.

1. What is it? — Definition

The debt-equity ratio compares long-term outside funds with owners’ funds. It asks: for every rupee the owners have committed, how many rupees have long-term lenders committed?

2. In simple words

It is the see-saw between borrowed money and own money. High debt-equity means the see-saw is heavy on the lenders’ side — cheaper (interest is tax-deductible) but riskier (interest must be paid even in a bad year).

3. Why do we need it?

To judge long-term solvency and financial risk. A lender looks at this before sanctioning a term loan. An owner looks at this before taking more debt to “gear up” return on equity.

Formula

Debt-equity ratio = Long-term debt ÷ Shareholders’ funds   (MBA exam standard)

Two versions exist. (A) Long-term debt ÷ Shareholders’ funds — the common Indian MBA version, used in this chapter. (B) Total debt (long-term + current) ÷ Shareholders’ funds — used when the question says “total debt” or “debt” without “long-term”. Write which version you are using.

5.4 Debt-equity ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Long-term debt (version A)Debentures, term loans, bonds, and sometimes preference share capital (fixed-dividend outsider). Exclude trade payables.Kaveri: long-term borrowings ₹2,00,000. No preference capital.
Total debt (version B)Long-term debt + current liabilities.Kaveri: ₹2,00,000 + ₹1,50,000 = ₹3,50,000.
Shareholders’ funds (equity)Equity share capital + reserves and surplus − fictitious assets (preliminary expenses, P&L debit balance).Kaveri: ₹4,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹6,00,000. No fictitious assets.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Do not use equity share capital alone — reserves belong to owners too. Do not put trade payables into long-term debt for version A. If preference capital is given, check the question: some papers treat it as debt (fixed dividend), some as equity. The common MBA treatment of capital gearing puts preference with debt; for debt-equity, follow the question’s wording. Kaveri has no preference, so the issue does not arise.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Decide version A (long-term) or B (total) from the wording.
  2. Shareholders’ funds = equity share capital + reserves − fictitious assets.
  3. Divide debt by shareholders’ funds. Write as x : 1 (or as a pure number).
  4. Comment: higher = more risk for owners and lenders; lower = more cushion, but maybe unused cheap debt.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Lenders have a large claim. Interest burden is heavy. A bad year can wipe owners out (and then hurt lenders). High financial risk. Some owners like it because a successful year magnifies ROE — that is gearing.
Low (or falling)Owners have financed most of the firm. Safe for lenders. Conservative. ROE will not get a debt-boost.
Too high can also be badA debt-equity of 4 : 1 on long-term funds is usually dangerous outside specialised project finance. One missed season and the firm cannot service interest. Banks will not lend more. Too low (say 0 : 1 with no debt at all) can also be ‘bad’ in a value sense: the firm may be refusing cheap, tax-deductible funds.
Solved example K4 · Easy

5.4 Debt-equity ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaDebt-equity (long-term) = Long-term debt ÷ Shareholders’ funds
2. Figures pickedLong-term debt ₹2,00,000; Shareholders’ funds ₹4,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹6,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹2,00,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000 = 2,00,000 ÷ 6,00,000 = 1/3 = 0.333…
4. Answer with unit0.33 : 1 &nbsp;(or 1 : 3)

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Conservative. For every ₹3 of owners’ money there is ₹1 of long-term debt. Lenders are well covered. Version B (total debt) = ₹3,50,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000 = 0.58 : 1 — still modest, because current liabilities are only trade credit, not a bank overdraft.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using only share capital ₹4,00,000 as equity and ignoring reserves ₹2,00,000. That would wrongly give 2,00,000/4,00,000 = 0.5 instead of 0.33.
  • Putting current liabilities into long-term debt when the question said “long-term debt-equity”.
  • Inverting the ratio (equity/debt) without saying so. Some papers want Equity-debt; read the name.
  • Treating a bank overdraft as long-term debt. It is current.
11. Memory trick

Debt over Equity = outsiders over owners. “DE” — Debt first, Equity under it. Low is safe; high is geared.

Solved example K4b · Easy

Both versions, side by side, from Kaveri

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaVersion A: LTD ÷ SF    Version B: (LTD + CL) ÷ SF
2. Figures pickedLTD ₹2,00,000, CL ₹1,50,000, SF ₹6,00,000
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)A: ₹2,00,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000 = 0.33 : 1.   B: ₹3,50,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000 = 3,50,000 ÷ 6,00,000 = 35/60 = 7/12 = 0.58 : 1.
4. Answer with unitA = 0.33 : 1 (use unless the question says total debt); B = 0.58 : 1

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

In the rest of this chapter, “debt-equity” means version A (long-term), which is the common MBA exam version.

5.5 Proprietary ratio

Syllabus bucket. Balance Sheet ratio. Purpose family: solvency / capital structure.

Ideal / usual comment. Higher is safer. A common comfort zone is 0.60 to 0.75 (60%–75% of assets financed by owners). There is no single statutory ideal.

1. What is it? — Definition

The proprietary ratio is shareholders’ funds divided by total assets (or total of the Balance Sheet). It is the owners’ slice of the whole pie. It asks: what fraction of every rupee of assets is financed by the owners, not by outsiders?

2. In simple words

If the proprietary ratio is 0.63, then 63 paise of every asset-rupee is owners’ money, and 37 paise is owed to lenders and creditors. It is the complement of the outsider’s-funds ratio.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge the cushion available to creditors. A high proprietary ratio means outsiders have a thick layer of owners’ money standing in front of them if the firm is wound up.

Formula

Proprietary ratio = Shareholders’ funds ÷ Total assets   (or × 100 for a percentage)

Total assets = total of the Balance Sheet = Equity + all liabilities. Outsiders’ funds ratio = 1 − proprietary ratio (when both are in the same units).

5.5 Proprietary ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Shareholders’ fundsEquity share capital + reserves − fictitious assets. Same equity you used in debt-equity.Kaveri: ₹6,00,000.
Total assetsNon-current assets + current assets. Equals the Balance Sheet total.Kaveri: ₹6,50,000 + ₹3,00,000 = ₹9,50,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Numerator is not share capital alone. Denominator is the BS total, not just fixed assets. If fictitious assets exist, deduct them from shareholders’ funds and also from total assets (they are not real assets).

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Compute shareholders’ funds.
  2. Take the Balance Sheet total as total assets.
  3. Divide. Express as a ratio (0.63 : 1) or as 63%.
  4. Optionally compute outsiders’ funds ratio = 1 − this, as a check.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Strong owner-cushion. Easy to borrow more if needed. Conservative structure.
Low (or falling)Assets are mostly outsider-financed. Creditors are less protected. A sequence of losses will wipe equity fast.
Too high can also be badAlmost no debt. Safe, but the firm may be under-levered: it is not using tax-deductible interest, and ROE may be lower than it could be. “Too high” here is a strategy comment, not a distress comment.
Solved example K5 · Easy

5.5 Proprietary ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaProprietary ratio = Shareholders’ funds ÷ Total assets
2. Figures pickedSF ₹6,00,000; Total assets ₹9,50,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹6,00,000 ÷ ₹9,50,000 = 6,00,000 ÷ 9,50,000 = 60/95 = 12/19 = 0.631578…
4. Answer with unit0.63 : 1 &nbsp;or 63.16%

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Owners finance about 63% of assets. Outsiders finance about 37% (₹3,50,000 ÷ ₹9,50,000 = 36.84%). A healthy owner-majority. Matches the low debt-equity of 0.33 : 1.

10. Common mistakes
  • Denominator = fixed assets only. Wrong. It is total assets.
  • Numerator = equity share capital only, skipping reserves.
  • Adding long-term debt to the numerator. That would be capital employed / total assets, a different ratio.
11. Memory trick

Proprietary = proprietors’ piece of the pie = owners’ funds / total assets. Bigger slice, safer creditors.

5.6 Capital gearing ratio

Syllabus bucket. Balance Sheet ratio. Purpose family: solvency / leverage.

Ideal / usual comment. A firm is low-geared when equity funds exceed fixed-charge funds (ratio < 1 in the version used here). High-geared when fixed-charge funds exceed equity (ratio > 1). Neither is “ideal”; high gearing magnifies both profit and loss.

1. What is it? — Definition

Capital gearing measures the mix of fixed-interest (and fixed-dividend) funds versus equity owners’ funds. It is debt-equity with preference capital parked on the debt side, because preference pays a fixed dividend just as debt pays a fixed interest.

2. In simple words

Gearing is a bicycle gear. In a high gear, a small push on the pedals (a rise in EBIT) moves the bicycle a long way (a big rise in profit for equity). Going uphill (a fall in EBIT) then becomes very hard. Low gear is safer and slower.

3. Why do we need it?

To see how sensitive equity earnings are to a change in EBIT, and to classify the firm as high-geared or low-geared. This is a favourite theory-plus-small-numerical question.

Formula

Capital gearing = (Preference share capital + Long-term debt) ÷ Equity shareholders’ funds

This is the common MBA exam version (fixed-charge funds / equity funds). Some papers invert it: Equity funds ÷ (Preference + long-term debt). Some use equity share capital only in the denominator (excluding reserves). State the version. In these notes: numerator = pref + LTD; denominator = equity share capital + reserves (no pref in Kaveri).

5.6 Capital gearing ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Fixed-charge fundsPreference share capital (fixed dividend) + debentures + long-term loans (fixed interest).Kaveri: preference nil + LTD ₹2,00,000 = ₹2,00,000.
Equity shareholders’ fundsEquity share capital + reserves − fictitious assets. Do not put preference here.Kaveri: ₹6,00,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

If there is no preference capital (Kaveri, and many numericals), capital gearing collapses to the same arithmetic as long-term debt-equity. Still write the full formula with “preference = 0”, so the examiner sees you know where preference would go.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. List preference capital and all long-term borrowings. Add them. This is the numerator.
  2. Equity share capital + reserves − fictitious assets. This is the denominator.
