  3. Divide. If the ratio is less than 1, say “low geared”. If more than 1, say “high geared”.
  4. One sentence: high gearing helps equity in good years and hurts it in bad years.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)High geared: a large share of capital carries a fixed charge. Equity earnings swing more than EBIT. Risk for equity holders and for lenders.
Low (or falling)Low geared: most capital is equity. Earnings are more stable. Safer, less magnified.
Too high can also be badA very high gearing next to a thin interest-coverage is a distress signal. Too low means unused leverage — a comment, not a crisis.
Solved example K6 · Easy

5.6 Capital gearing ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaCapital gearing = (Preference capital + Long-term debt) ÷ Equity shareholders’ funds
2. Figures pickedPreference nil; LTD ₹2,00,000; Equity funds ₹6,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)(0 + ₹2,00,000) ÷ ₹6,00,000 = 2,00,000 ÷ 6,00,000 = 1/3 = 0.33.
4. Answer with unit0.33 &nbsp;(low geared, because 0.33 < 1)

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Low geared. Equity funds are three times fixed-charge funds. A fall in EBIT will not quickly wipe the equity residual. Combined with interest coverage of 5 times (computed later), gearing is comfortable.

10. Common mistakes
  • Putting preference capital in the denominator. Preference is a fixed-charge fund — numerator in this version.
  • Using only equity share capital in the denominator and leaving out reserves, unless the paper’s formula is printed that way.
  • Saying “high geared” because a 0.33 exists. High/low is judged against 1 in this version, or by the paper’s own wording.
  • Confusing capital gearing with operating gearing (fixed operating costs). Capital gearing is about finance, not about rent and depreciation.
11. Memory trick

Gearing = fixed-charge money over equity money. Preference sits with debt, not with equity. Below 1 = low gear = safer.

Key point

If a paper prints Capital gearing = Equity / (Preference + Debentures), then a ratio greater than 1 is low geared (more equity). Always read the printed formula. The words “high geared” and “low geared” follow whichever version the paper chose, not a universal fraction.

5.7 Fixed assets to long-term funds ratio

Syllabus bucket. Balance Sheet ratio. Purpose family: solvency / asset-financing structure.

Ideal / usual comment. Should be less than 1 (or < 100%). Fixed assets should be financed by long-term funds, with some long-term funds left over for working capital. A ratio above 1 means part of the factory was paid for with money that has to be repaid this year — dangerous.

1. What is it? — Definition

This ratio is net fixed assets divided by long-term funds (shareholders’ funds + long-term debt = capital employed). It asks: what fraction of long-term money is locked in long-term assets?

2. In simple words

A godown should be paid for with a term loan or with owners’ money, not with next month’s creditor money. This ratio checks that matching: long-term assets against long-term funds.

3. Why do we need it?

To test whether the firm has used short-term funds to buy fixed assets (a classic way firms get into a liquidity trap). Also to see how much long-term finance remains for working capital.

Formula

Fixed assets to long-term funds = Net fixed assets ÷ Long-term funds

Long-term funds = Shareholders’ funds + Long-term debt = Capital employed. Net fixed assets = gross FA − accumulated depreciation. Express as a ratio or as a percentage.

5.7 Fixed assets to long-term funds ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Net fixed assetsProperty, plant and equipment after depreciation. Exclude current assets. Include capital work-in-progress if the question treats it as FA.Kaveri: ₹6,50,000.
Long-term fundsEquity + reserves + long-term borrowings. Same as capital employed.Kaveri: ₹6,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹8,00,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Use net FA, not gross, unless the question gives only gross and no depreciation. Denominator is not total liabilities — current liabilities stay out.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Pick net fixed assets from the asset side.
  2. Long-term funds = shareholders’ funds + long-term debt.
  3. Divide. If the answer is more than 1, write a warning sentence: part of FA is financed by current liabilities.
  4. The leftover fraction (1 − this ratio) is the share of long-term funds supporting working capital.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)A larger share of long-term funds is locked in FA. If the ratio is still below 1, this is a structure comment, not yet distress.
Low (or falling)Plenty of long-term funds sit in working capital. Very liquid structure. Check that WC itself is not idle (current ratio, stock turnover).
Too high can also be badAbove 1: the firm bought a machine with creditor money or with an overdraft. When the creditor asks to be paid, the machine cannot be sold overnight. This is a classic cause of failure. Too low (say 0.3 in a factory) may mean under-investment in capacity.
Solved example K7 · Easy

5.7 Fixed assets to long-term funds ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaFA to long-term funds = Net fixed assets ÷ (SF + LTD)
2. Figures pickedNet FA ₹6,50,000; long-term funds ₹8,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹6,50,000 ÷ ₹8,00,000 = 6,50,000 ÷ 8,00,000 = 65/80 = 13/16 = 0.8125.
4. Answer with unit0.81 : 1 &nbsp;or 81.25%

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. 81.25% of long-term funds are in the godown and office; 18.75% (₹1,50,000 out of ₹8,00,000) supports working capital. The ratio is below 1, so no short-term money is trapped in FA. Healthy matching of funds.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using gross fixed assets when accumulated depreciation is given. Use net.
  • Denominator = shareholders’ funds only, omitting long-term debt. That is a different (stricter) ratio.
  • Comparing with 2 : 1 (the current-ratio ideal). Wrong family. Here the ceiling of comfort is 1 : 1.
11. Memory trick

Match the life: long asset, long money. FA / long-term funds should stay under 1. Above 1 = a machine bought on a credit card.

5.8 Current assets to proprietary funds ratio

Syllabus bucket. Balance Sheet ratio. Purpose family: structure / liquidity of owners’ money.

Ideal / usual comment. No universal ideal. A high ratio means a large share of owners’ money is in working capital (typical of a trader). A low ratio means owners’ money is mostly in fixed assets (typical of a heavy manufacturer).

1. What is it? — Definition

Current assets divided by shareholders’ funds. It asks: how many rupees of current assets does the firm hold for every rupee of owners’ funds?

2. In simple words

It is a snapshot of where the owners’ money is sitting on the asset side — in stock, debtors and cash, versus in the building. A trader like Kaveri should show a noticeable slice of owners’ funds in current assets; a cement plant should not.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge whether owners’ funds are tied up in working capital (which should revolve) or in long-term assets. Useful when comparing a trader with a manufacturer, or this year with last year.

Formula

Current assets to proprietary funds = Current assets ÷ Shareholders’ funds

Proprietary funds = shareholders’ funds. Same numerator as the current ratio; different denominator.

5.8 Current assets to proprietary funds ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Current assetsInventory + receivables + cash + prepaid + other CA.Kaveri: ₹3,00,000.
Shareholders’ / proprietary fundsEquity share capital + reserves − fictitious assets.Kaveri: ₹6,00,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Same CA as current ratio. Same SF as debt-equity and proprietary ratio. Do not use capital employed in the denominator — that would include long-term debt.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Total current assets.
  2. Compute shareholders’ funds.
  3. Divide. Write as a ratio or as a percentage.
  4. Read it with the nature of the business (trader vs manufacturer).
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)A large part of owners’ money is in stock, debtors and cash. Fine for a wholesaler. For a factory it may mean idle WC or thin FA.
Low (or falling)Owners’ money is mostly in fixed assets. Fine for a factory. For a trader it may mean the firm is under-stocked or under-banked.
Too high can also be badOwners have funded a mountain of stock and debtors. Check stock turnover and collection period — the mountain may not be moving. Too low in a trading firm: possible stock-outs and lost sales.
Solved example K8 · Easy

5.8 Current assets to proprietary funds ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaCA to proprietary funds = Current assets ÷ Shareholders’ funds
2. Figures pickedCA ₹3,00,000; SF ₹6,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹3,00,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000 = 3,00,000 ÷ 6,00,000 = 1/2 = 0.50.
4. Answer with unit0.50 : 1 &nbsp;or 50%

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Half of owners’ funds sit in current assets — sensible for a trader. The other half, plus the entire long-term loan, sits in the godown (see FA to long-term funds 81%). Structure fits the business.

10. Common mistakes
  • Denominator = capital employed. That mixes lenders’ money into “proprietary” funds — the name of the ratio forbids it.
  • Using working capital as the numerator. The name says current assets, not net current assets.
11. Memory trick

CA over owners’ money. A trader’s number is higher than a factory’s. Do not hunt for a 2 : 1 ideal — that ideal belongs to the current ratio.

6. Revenue (P&L) ratios

Both figures come from the Statement of Profit and Loss. These are margin ratios: how many paise of each sales-rupee survive at each layer of cost. No Balance-Sheet number is allowed in this section.

Picture the P&L as a staircase down from sales: COGS is cut first (gross profit remains), then operating expenses (operating profit remains), then interest (PBT remains), then tax (PAT remains). Each ratio is one step’s leftover, as a percentage of sales.

Formula

Operating ratio + Operating profit ratio ≈ 100%  (when other income is nil, as in Kaveri)

If your two answers do not add to 100, you have either included interest in operating cost, or included other income in sales, or used PAT instead of operating profit. Check before you move on.

6.1 Gross profit ratio (GP ratio)

Syllabus bucket. Revenue ratio — both figures from the P&L. Purpose family: profitability (trading margin).

Ideal / usual comment. Depends on the trade. A grocer may live on 12%; a boutique on 50%. Kaveri’s 25% is a healthy wholesale-trading margin. Compare with last year and with rivals, not with a universal number.

1. What is it? — Definition

Gross profit ratio is gross profit divided by revenue from operations (net sales), times 100. It is the margin left after paying for the goods themselves, and before paying people, rent, interest and tax.

2. In simple words

Out of every ₹100 of sales, how many rupees are left after the cost of those goods? If GP ratio is 25%, ₹25 is left and ₹75 went to COGS.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge trading efficiency: buying well, selling well, not leaking goods. A fall in GP ratio, with selling prices unchanged, usually means cost of goods rose or stock was lost. It is the first profitability ratio any analyst computes.

Formula

Gross profit ratio = (Gross profit ÷ Revenue from operations) × 100

Gross profit = Sales − COGS. COGS = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock (+ direct expenses if given). Use net sales (after returns). Do not use total assets or capital.

6.1 Gross profit ratio (GP ratio) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Gross profitSales minus cost of goods sold. The trading leftover.Kaveri: ₹10,00,000 − ₹7,50,000 = ₹2,50,000. Also 25% × sales, by construction.
Revenue from operations / Net salesSales of goods and services, after returns, usually excluding other income (interest, rent received, profit on sale of asset).Kaveri: ₹10,00,000. Other income is nil.
COGS (to build GP if GP is not given)Opening stock + purchases − closing stock (+ carriage inward, wages if the paper treats them as direct).Kaveri: ₹80,000 + ₹7,90,000 − ₹1,20,000 = ₹7,50,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Use net sales, not cash sales only, and not sales + other income. If the question gives GP ratio and sales, GP = rate × sales. If it gives opening, purchases, closing, build COGS first, then GP = sales − COGS.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Compute COGS if needed: opening stock + purchases − closing stock.
  2. GP = Sales − COGS. (Or GP = GP% × Sales if the rate is given.)
  3. GP ratio = GP ÷ Sales × 100. Unit is %.
  4. Comment: a fall is a trading problem (price, cost, or theft); a rise is a trading improvement — or a change in mix.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Strong trading margin. Either selling prices are firm, or the firm buys cheap, or the mix has shifted to richer goods.
Low (or falling)Thin trading margin. A small rise in cost or a discount war will wipe GP. Danger if operating expenses are already high.
Too high can also be badPrices may be too high and volume may be suffering (check sales trend and stock turnover). Or closing stock may have been overvalued — window dressing that inflates GP. Always read GP with stock turnover.
Solved example K9 · Easy

6.1 Gross profit ratio (GP ratio) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaGP ratio = (GP ÷ Sales) × 100
2. Figures pickedGP ₹2,50,000; Sales ₹10,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)(₹2,50,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000) × 100 = (2,50,000 ÷ 10,00,000) × 100 = 0.25 × 100 = 25%.
4. Answer with unit25%

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. A quarter of every sales-rupee is gross profit. For a wholesaler this is a solid trading margin. Whether it is “good” depends on rivals; as a standalone number it is healthy, and it leaves room for ₹1,00,000 of operating expenses, ₹30,000 of interest and ₹30,000 of tax, with ₹90,000 still standing at the end.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using PAT or operating profit in the numerator. Those are different ratios.
  • Using credit sales only. GP is on total sales (cash + credit).
  • Adding other income to sales. Other income is not operations (unless the question says so).
  • Computing GP as Sales − Purchases, ignoring stock. You must adjust for opening and closing inventory.
11. Memory trick

GP sits on the top step: only COGS has been cut. GP / Sales × 100. If stock changes, Purchases ≠ COGS.

6.2 Net profit ratio (NP ratio)

Syllabus bucket. Revenue ratio. Purpose family: profitability (bottom-line margin).

Ideal / usual comment. Depends on the industry. A 9% net margin on a trading business is respectable. Always pair with GP ratio: the gap between GP% and NP% is everything that is not COGS.

1. What is it? — Definition

Net profit ratio is profit after tax (the year’s leftover for owners) divided by sales, times 100. Some papers use profit before tax. Read the question. These notes use PAT as the default “net profit”.

2. In simple words

Out of every ₹100 of sales, how many rupees finally belong to the owners after every cost, including interest and tax? For Kaveri, 9 rupees.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge overall profitability of sales. Investors, owners and the tax officer all look here. A stable GP ratio with a falling NP ratio means the leak is below GP — operating expenses, interest or tax.

Formula

Net profit ratio = (Profit after tax ÷ Revenue from operations) × 100

MBA default in these notes: PAT / Sales × 100. PBT version = PBT / Sales × 100 — mention it if the question says “net profit before tax”. Do not deduct preference dividend unless the question asks for profit available to equity / net profit ratio for equity holders.

6.2 Net profit ratio (NP ratio) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Profit after tax (PAT)Profit for the year after interest and tax. The bottom line.Kaveri: ₹90,000.
Profit before tax (PBT version)EBIT − interest. Used when the paper says “net profit before tax”.Kaveri: ₹1,20,000, which would give 12%.
SalesRevenue from operations, same as GP ratio.Kaveri: ₹10,00,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Default numerator is PAT (after tax, after interest). If the trial balance gives only “net profit” with no tax line, use that figure and say so. Denominator is sales, not capital, not total assets (those become ROE and ROA).

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Identify whether the paper wants PAT or PBT.
  2. Pick sales (revenue from operations).
  3. Divide × 100. Unit is %.
  4. Read next to GP ratio: the gap is operating expenses + interest + tax (and other income, if any).
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)A large slice of sales reaches owners. Pricing, cost control and a light interest burden are all working.
Low (or falling)Sales are busy but owners see little. Find the layer: GP low? Then trading. GP healthy but NP low? Then opex, interest or tax.
Too high can also be badUnusually high NP% can mean under-investment (too little depreciation, too little marketing) or a one-time other income. Check quality of earnings. Too high is rare; more often “high” is simply good.
Solved example K10 · Easy

6.2 Net profit ratio (NP ratio) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaNP ratio = (PAT ÷ Sales) × 100
2. Figures pickedPAT ₹90,000; Sales ₹10,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)(₹90,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000) × 100 = (90,000 ÷ 10,00,000) × 100 = 9%.
4. Answer with unit9% &nbsp;(PBT version = 12%)

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. 9 paise of every sales-rupee is leftover for owners. GP was 25 paise, so 16 paise were spent on employees, other opex, interest and tax (6 + 4 + 3 + 3). The margin is thin enough that an interest-rate rise or a wage rise would be felt, but it is a real profit, not a rounding error.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using EBIT in the numerator and still calling it net profit ratio. That is the operating profit ratio.
  • Using shareholders’ funds in the denominator. That is ROE.
  • Taking PAT after an extra deduction of drawings or dividend. Dividend is an appropriation, not an expense; NP ratio uses PAT.
11. Memory trick

Net = the last leftover. PAT / Sales × 100. Default is after tax. If the paper says before tax, obey the paper.

6.3 Operating profit ratio

Syllabus bucket. Revenue ratio. Purpose family: profitability of operations (before financing and tax).

Ideal / usual comment. Higher is better, given the industry. It should sit between GP% and NP%. For Kaveri: GP 25%, operating 15%, net 9% — a clean staircase.

1. What is it? — Definition

Operating profit ratio is operating profit (EBIT / PBIT) divided by sales, times 100. Operating profit is profit from the core business, before interest (a financing choice) and before tax (a government claim).

2. In simple words

Ignore how the firm is financed. Ignore tax. Just ask: of each sales-rupee, how much does the business itself produce as profit from operations? That is this ratio.

3. Why do we need it?

To compare two firms with different debt and different tax situations on the quality of the business, not the quality of the financing. Also the numerator of ROCE, so this ratio and capital turnover together drive ROCE (see DuPont later).

Formula

Operating profit ratio = (Operating profit ÷ Sales) × 100

Operating profit = EBIT = GP − operating expenses (employee + other opex including depreciation), or = PBT + interest, or = PAT + tax + interest. Other income that is not operating is kept out.

6.3 Operating profit ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Operating profit / EBIT / PBITProfit before interest and tax, from operations.Kaveri three checks: GP ₹2,50,000 − opex ₹1,00,000 = ₹1,50,000; PBT ₹1,20,000 + interest ₹30,000 = ₹1,50,000; PAT ₹90,000 + tax ₹30,000 + interest ₹30,000 = ₹1,50,000.
SalesRevenue from operations.Kaveri: ₹10,00,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Build EBIT from whatever the paper gives. The safest rebuild is PBT + interest, because those two lines are almost always present. Do not use PAT. Do not deduct interest.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Build operating profit: GP − operating expenses, or PBT + interest.
  2. Confirm interest is not already deducted (if you started from GP, do not deduct it; if you started from PBT, add it back).
  3. Divide by sales × 100.
  4. Check: operating profit% + operating ratio should be 100% if other income is nil.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)The core business is earning well, regardless of how it is financed.
Low (or falling)Operations are weak. Even a zero-debt firm would struggle. Look at GP (trading) and at opex (overheads).
Too high can also be badMay mean the firm is starving marketing, maintenance or depreciation. Check whether the profit is repeatable. Also check other income: a one-time sale of a building is not operating profit.
Solved example K11 · Easy

6.3 Operating profit ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaOperating profit ratio = (EBIT ÷ Sales) × 100
2. Figures pickedEBIT ₹1,50,000; Sales ₹10,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)(₹1,50,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000) × 100 = (1,50,000 ÷ 10,00,000) × 100 = 15%.
4. Answer with unit15%

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. 15 paise of every sales-rupee is operating profit. That is the pool from which interest ₹30,000 (3 paise) and tax ₹30,000 (3 paise) are paid, leaving 9 paise of PAT. Operations, not financing, are doing the work.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using PAT or PBT and still labelling it operating profit ratio.
  • Deducting interest when you started from GP. Interest is not an operating expense.
  • Including other income (rent received, profit on sale of FA) inside operating profit when the paper separates it. If the paper is silent and the amount is small, state your assumption.
11. Memory trick

Operating profit = the business before the banker and the tax officer. EBIT / Sales × 100. Add interest back if you start from PBT.

6.4 Operating ratio

Syllabus bucket. Revenue ratio. Purpose family: cost / efficiency of operations. It is the cost-cousin of the operating profit ratio.

Ideal / usual comment. Lower is better. There is no universal number. For Kaveri it should be 85% because operating profit is 15% and other income is nil.

1. What is it? — Definition

Operating ratio is operating cost divided by sales, times 100. Operating cost is COGS plus operating expenses (employee benefits, other expenses including depreciation, selling and admin). Interest and tax are not operating costs.

2. In simple words

Out of every ₹100 of sales, how many rupees were spent on running the business (goods + people + rent + depreciation + selling)? The rest is operating profit. High operating ratio = a heavy cost stomach.

3. Why do we need it?

To measure the cost-heaviness of operations. A rising operating ratio is a warning even if sales are rising: costs are eating a bigger bite. Management uses the pieces (material, labour, overhead) as expense ratios to find the bite.

Formula

Operating ratio = (Operating cost ÷ Sales) × 100    where Operating cost = COGS + Operating expenses

Interest is a finance cost, not an operating cost. Tax is not an operating cost. Operating ratio + operating profit ratio = 100% when other income is ignored.

6.4 Operating ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
COGSCost of the goods that were sold.Kaveri: ₹7,50,000.
Operating expensesEmployee benefits, other expenses, depreciation, selling and distribution, admin. Not interest. Not tax. Not loss on sale of FA (non-operating) unless the paper dumps it in “other expenses” without a split.Kaveri: employee ₹60,000 + other opex ₹40,000 = ₹1,00,000.
Operating costCOGS + operating expenses.Kaveri: ₹7,50,000 + ₹1,00,000 = ₹8,50,000.
SalesRevenue from operations.Kaveri: ₹10,00,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Add COGS and every operating expense. Stop before finance costs and tax. If the paper gives a single “expenses” total that includes interest, subtract interest before you call it operating cost.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Build COGS.
  2. Add operating expenses. Do not add interest or tax.
  3. Operating ratio = operating cost ÷ sales × 100.
  4. Cross-check: 100% − operating profit% should equal this, if other income is nil.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Operations swallow most of the sales-rupee. Little left as EBIT. A high-cost business, or an inefficient one.
Low (or falling)Lean operations. More of each sale survives as operating profit.
Too high can also be badAbove 100% means operations lose money before interest — the core business is sick. “Too low” is unusual; if operating ratio is 40% in a grocery, check whether COGS was forgotten.
Solved example K12 · Easy

6.4 Operating ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaOperating ratio = (COGS + Operating expenses) ÷ Sales × 100
2. Figures pickedCOGS ₹7,50,000 + opex ₹1,00,000 = operating cost ₹8,50,000; Sales ₹10,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)(₹8,50,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000) × 100 = (8,50,000 ÷ 10,00,000) × 100 = 85%.
4. Answer with unit85%

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. 85 paise of every sales-rupee go in operating cost, 15 paise remain as EBIT. Check: 85% + 15% = 100%. The arithmetic of the two cousins agrees, so neither figure is mis-picked.

10. Common mistakes
  • Including interest in operating cost. Interest is finance, not operations. That mistake would give (₹8,80,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000) × 100 = 88%, and then 88% + 15% ≠ 100%.
  • Using only COGS (that is a COGS-to-sales expense ratio, 75% for Kaveri, not the operating ratio).
  • Using PAT in a “100 − NP%” shortcut. 100 − 9 = 91, which is not the operating ratio. The shortcut is 100 − operating profit%.
11. Memory trick

Operating ratio is the COST twin. Operating profit ratio is the PROFIT twin. They add to 100. Interest stays out of both twins’ cost.

Key point

Kaveri cross-check, write this once in the answer booklet: operating ratio 85% + operating profit ratio 15% = 100%. If a numerical you are solving does not add to 100, you have mixed interest or other income into the wrong line.

6.5 Expense ratios

Syllabus bucket. Revenue ratios. Purpose family: cost structure.

Ideal / comment. Lower is better for each cost, but a zero employee-cost ratio means there are no people. Read the mix, not a single line.

1. What is it? — Definition

An expense ratio is any single expense (or a group of expenses) divided by sales, times 100. The syllabus wants you to be able to write the formula for each material, labour, overhead, interest or tax line.

2. In simple words

GP ratio told you that 75 paise of each Kaveri sales-rupee went to COGS. Expense ratios name the other paise: employees 6, other opex 4, interest 3, tax 3. Together they are a pie chart of the P&L.

3. Why do we need it?

A rising operating ratio is a fog. Expense ratios turn on the light: was it wages, was it rent, was it interest? Management can only attack a named cost.

Formula

Expense ratio = (Particular expense ÷ Sales) × 100

Use the same sales figure as GP ratio. Name the expense in the answer: “Employee-cost ratio 6%”, not “expense ratio 6%”.

Kaveri expense ratios — every paise of the sales-rupee
ExpenseAmountRatio = amount ÷ sales × 100What a rise would mean
COGS / material₹7,50,00075%Buying cost up, or selling price down, or wastage / theft of goods
Employee benefits₹60,0006%Wage rise, extra hiring, or sales falling faster than the payroll
Other operating expenses₹40,0004%Rent, power, selling, depreciation heavier relative to sales
Finance costs (interest)₹30,0003%More debt, or a higher interest rate — a financing problem, not an operating one
Tax₹30,0003%Higher taxable profit or a higher rate; usually not “inefficiency”

COGS 75 + employee 6 + other opex 4 = 85 (operating ratio). Then interest 3 + tax 3 = 6, and 85 + 6 + NP 9 = 100.

Solved example K13 · Easy

Employee-cost ratio and the 100% check, Kaveri

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaEmployee-cost ratio = Employee benefits ÷ Sales × 100
2. Figures pickedEmployee ₹60,000; Sales ₹10,00,000
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)(₹60,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000) × 100 = (60,000 ÷ 10,00,000) × 100 = 6%.
4. Answer with unit6%

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Full sales-rupee. COGS 75 + employee 6 + other opex 4 + interest 3 + tax 3 + PAT 9 = 100. If your expense ratios plus NP ratio do not make 100, a line has been missed or double-counted.

10. Common mistakes
  • Dividing the expense by GP or by PAT instead of by sales.
  • Calling the interest-to-sales ratio an operating-expense ratio. Interest is a finance cost.
  • Forgetting that a fall in the ratio can come from sales rising, not from the expense falling. Always look at the rupee amount too.
11. Memory trick

Every expense ratio is “this cost / sales × 100”. Name the cost. They are slices of the same sales-rupee; they must add up.

7. Combined ratios

One figure from the P&L (a flow over the year) and one figure from the Balance Sheet (a position on a day). Because a day is not a year, we average the opening and closing Balance-Sheet figures whenever the question gives both.

Two sub-families live here: (A) turnover / activity / efficiency — how many times an asset flipped during the year, and how many days a flip takes; (B) return and coverage — ROCE, ROE, ROA, EPS, interest coverage. Both are Combined by source.

Key point

When the question does not give an opening figure, use the closing Balance-Sheet figure and write the assumption. When it does give opening (Kaveri does), you must use the average. Using only closing when opening was given is a named common mistake.

Formula

Average of a BS item = (Opening + Closing) ÷ 2

Kaveri averages: inventory ₹1,00,000; trade receivables ₹80,000; trade payables ₹1,30,000.

7.1 Inventory / stock turnover ratio

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio — COGS from P&L, average inventory from Balance Sheet. Purpose family: efficiency.

Ideal / usual comment. Higher generally means stock is moving. A wholesaler at 7–10 times is healthy; a jeweller at 2 times may also be healthy. Compare with the industry and with the holding period.

1. What is it? — Definition

Stock turnover is the number of times, during the year, that the firm sold and replaced its average stock. The preferred formula uses cost of goods sold, because stock is valued at cost.

2. In simple words

Imagine the godown holds ₹1,00,000 of goods, on average. In the year Kaveri sold goods that cost ₹7,50,000. So the godown was emptied and refilled 7.5 times. That is stock turnover.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge merchandising efficiency and to spot slow-moving or dead stock. A falling turnover with a rising current ratio often means the “liquidity” is unsold goods.

Formula

Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ Average inventory

Preferred MBA version: COGS / average stock. Alternative (used in some papers): Sales / average stock — this mixes selling price with cost and overstates turnover. If the paper prints Sales in the formula, obey the paper and say so. Average inventory = (opening + closing) ÷ 2.

7.1 Inventory / stock turnover ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
COGSCost of goods sold, at cost. Matches the valuation of stock.Kaveri: ₹7,50,000.
Average inventoryTypical stock carried during the year.(₹80,000 + ₹1,20,000) ÷ 2 = ₹2,00,000 ÷ 2 = ₹1,00,000.
Sales (alternative formula)Revenue from operations. Use only if the question says so.Kaveri alternative: ₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = 10 times — higher, because sales are at selling price.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

COGS is not purchases. Purchases for Kaveri are ₹7,90,000; COGS is ₹7,50,000. If GP and sales are given, COGS = sales × (1 − GP%). Opening stock is on last year’s BS or in this year’s P&L working; closing stock is on this year’s BS.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Build COGS (opening + purchases − closing, or sales − GP).
  2. Average inventory = (opening + closing) ÷ 2. If opening is missing, use closing and write the assumption.
  3. Divide COGS by average inventory. Unit: times.
  4. Optionally convert to days: 365 ÷ turnover (next ratio).
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Stock is moving. Less money is locked in the godown. Lower risk of obsolescence.
Low (or falling)Stock is sleeping. Cash is trapped. Possible dead stock, over-buying, or a weak sales season.
Too high can also be badThe godown is almost empty. Risk of stock-outs and lost sales. The firm may be buying in tiny lots and losing bulk discounts. “Higher” is not always “better” past a point.
Solved example K14 · Easy

7.1 Inventory / stock turnover ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaInventory turnover = COGS ÷ Average inventory
2. Figures pickedCOGS ₹7,50,000; average inventory (₹80,000 + ₹1,20,000) ÷ 2 = ₹1,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹7,50,000 ÷ ₹1,00,000 = 7,50,000 ÷ 1,00,000 = 7.5.
4. Answer with unit7.5 times

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. The godown flipped 7.5 times in the year — a little over once every two months. For a wholesaler this is a healthy pace. We will convert it to 48.67 days of holding next. The alternative (sales / average stock) would have given 10 times; we do not use it unless asked, because it mixes selling price with cost.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using sales instead of COGS when the paper did not ask for that version. This is the most common stock-turnover mistake in the paper.
  • Using closing stock only when opening was given. Kaveri’s closing is ₹1,20,000; using it alone would give 7,50,000/1,20,000 = 6.25 times — wrong.
  • Using purchases instead of COGS. Purchases feed the godown; COGS empties it. Turnover is about emptying.
  • Comparing a COGS-based 7.5 with a rival’s sales-based 10 and concluding the rival is faster. They used different formulas.
11. Memory trick

Stock lives at cost, so flip it at cost: COGS / average stock. Sales / stock is the second-best formula, used only when COGS cannot be built or the paper prints it.

7.2 Inventory holding period (stock velocity in days)

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio (derived from stock turnover). Purpose family: efficiency / working-capital days.

Ideal / usual comment. Shorter is generally better, provided there are no stock-outs. Compare with the credit period you get from suppliers (payment period) and with the industry.

1. What is it? — Definition

Holding period is the number of days, on average, for which goods sit in the godown before they are sold. It is 365 divided by the stock turnover (or 360, 12 months, 52 weeks — whatever the paper uses).

2. In simple words

If stock turns 7.5 times in 365 days, one turn takes 365 ÷ 7.5 ≈ 49 days. Goods bought today are, on average, sold about seven weeks later.

3. Why do we need it?

Managers think in days more easily than in “times”. A holding period of 49 days next to a creditors’ payment period of 60 days means suppliers are financing the stock with 11 days to spare — a sweet working-capital position.

Formula

Inventory holding period (days) = 365 ÷ Inventory turnover   or   (Average inventory ÷ COGS) × 365

Both formulas are the same algebra. If the paper says 360 days, use 360. If it asks for months, use 12 ÷ turnover. If weeks, 52 ÷ turnover.

7.2 Inventory holding period (stock velocity in days) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Inventory turnoverCOGS ÷ average inventory, already computed.Kaveri: 7.5 times.
Days in a year365 unless the paper says 360.We take 365. Write that sentence in the answer.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Use the same turnover you just computed. Do not mix a sales-based turnover with a COGS-based days formula. If the paper asks “stock velocity in months”, do not give days.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Compute inventory turnover in times.
  2. Read the required unit (days / weeks / months) and the day’s convention (365 or 360).
  3. Days = 365 ÷ turnover. Show the division.
  4. One sentence: goods sit for X days.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Goods sit for a long time. Cash trapped, obsolescence risk, godown cost.
Low (or falling)Goods sit briefly. Fresh stock, less cash trapped.
Too high can also be badDead stock. Too low: empty shelves, lost sales, emergency purchases at poor prices.
Solved example K15 · Easy

7.2 Inventory holding period (stock velocity in days) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaHolding period (days) = 365 ÷ Inventory turnover
2. Figures pickedTurnover 7.5 times; 365 days in a year.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)365 ÷ 7.5. 7.5 = 15/2, so 365 × 2 ÷ 15 = 730 ÷ 15 = 48.666… . In months: 12 ÷ 7.5 = 1.6 months. In weeks: 52 ÷ 7.5 = 6.933… weeks.
4. Answer with unit48.67 days &nbsp;(or 1.6 months, or 6.93 weeks)

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Stock sits for about 49 days. Combined with a 60-day payment period (computed later), Kaveri sells the goods before it has to pay the supplier. That is a working-capital plus.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using 365 ÷ average inventory (forgetting to use turnover, or forgetting × COGS).
  • Mixing 365 with a 360-based industry benchmark.
  • Writing “48.67 times” — the unit is days, not times.
  • Using 365 ÷ Sales-based turnover and comparing with a COGS-based holding period from last year.
11. Memory trick

Times go into the year: 365 / turnover = days in one turn. Months: 12 / turnover. Weeks: 52 / turnover. Same idea.

7.3 Debtors / receivables turnover ratio

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio — credit sales from P&L, average debtors from Balance Sheet. Purpose family: efficiency / credit control.

Ideal / usual comment. Higher means faster collection. A turnover of 10 times ≈ a 36.5-day collection period, which is tight and healthy for a wholesaler who might offer 30–45 days of credit.

1. What is it? — Definition

Debtors turnover is the number of times, during the year, that average trade receivables were converted into cash. It is credit sales divided by average trade receivables.

2. In simple words

Kaveri sold ₹8,00,000 on credit and was owed, on average, ₹80,000. So the debtors’ book was collected and refilled 10 times in the year.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge collection efficiency and the quality of debtors. A falling turnover means customers are taking longer to pay — a liquidity leak and a bad-debt risk.

Formula

Debtors turnover = Credit sales ÷ Average trade receivables

Credit sales = total sales − cash sales. If the cash/credit split is not given, assume all sales are on credit and write the assumption. Average receivables = (opening + closing) ÷ 2. Use net receivables (after provision for doubtful debts) if a provision is given.

7.3 Debtors / receivables turnover ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Credit salesSales made on credit, after returns. Cash sales do not create debtors, so they do not belong here.Kaveri: 80% of ₹10,00,000 = ₹8,00,000. Cash sales ₹2,00,000 stay out.
Average trade receivablesTypical amount customers owed during the year. Include bills receivable if the paper lists them with debtors.(₹60,000 + ₹1,00,000) ÷ 2 = ₹1,60,000 ÷ 2 = ₹80,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

If the question says “sales” and is silent on cash sales, write “assumed all credit”. Kaveri is not silent: 20% cash is given, so you must use 80%. Opening debtors, if given, must be averaged with closing. Closing debtors live on the BS as trade receivables.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Compute credit sales. Subtract cash sales if given.
  2. Average debtors = (opening + closing) ÷ 2.
  3. Divide. Unit: times.
  4. Convert to days if asked (next ratio).
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Customers pay fast. Cash comes in. Less bad-debt risk. Credit control is tight.
Low (or falling)Customers delay. Cash is stuck in receivables. Possible weak credit checks, disputes, or a recession in the customer’s industry.
Too high can also be badCredit policy may be so strict that sales are being refused. A turnover of 50 times (collection in a week) in a trade where 45 days is custom will lose customers to a rival who offers credit. High can be a marketing problem.
Solved example K16 · Easy

7.3 Debtors / receivables turnover ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaDebtors turnover = Credit sales ÷ Average trade receivables
2. Figures pickedCredit sales ₹8,00,000; average receivables ₹80,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹8,00,000 ÷ ₹80,000 = 8,00,000 ÷ 80,000 = 10.
4. Answer with unit10 times

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. The debtors’ book flipped 10 times. Collection is brisk. If a student wrongly uses total sales ₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹80,000 = 12.5 times, they have pretended that cash customers were also debtors. That is the classic mistake on this ratio.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using total sales when cash sales are given. Kaveri would then show 12.5 instead of 10.
  • Using closing debtors only when opening was given: 8,00,000/1,00,000 = 8 times — wrong.
  • Including cash-sales customers in “debtors”. They never were debtors.
  • Forgetting to net off provision for doubtful debts when a provision is given.
11. Memory trick

Only credit sales create debtors. Credit sales / average debtors. If the split is silent, assume all sales are credit and write that down.

7.4 Average collection period (debtors’ velocity in days)

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio (derived from debtors turnover). Purpose family: efficiency / liquidity of receivables.

Ideal / usual comment. Should sit at or inside the credit period the firm offers. If Kaveri offers 45 days and collects in 36.5, credit control is working. If it offers 30 days and collects in 70, it is not.

1. What is it? — Definition

Average collection period is the number of days, on average, that a credit customer takes to pay. It is 365 divided by debtors turnover (or 360, as the paper says).

2. In simple words

Turnover 10 times in 365 days means one collection-cycle is 36.5 days. A bill raised today is, on average, cash in a little over a month.

3. Why do we need it?

To compare with the stated credit period, with last year, and with the creditors’ payment period. Collection slower than payment is a cash-cycle hole.

Formula

Average collection period (days) = 365 ÷ Debtors turnover   or   (Average debtors ÷ Credit sales) × 365

Same algebra. Months = 12 ÷ turnover. Weeks = 52 ÷ turnover.

7.4 Average collection period (debtors’ velocity in days) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Debtors turnoverCredit sales ÷ average debtors.Kaveri: 10 times.
Credit sales / average debtorsSame figures as the turnover ratio.₹8,00,000 and ₹80,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Use credit sales, not total sales, unless you assumed all sales are credit. Use the same 365/360 convention as for stock days, unless the paper mixes them (rare).

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Compute debtors turnover.
  2. Days = 365 ÷ turnover. Show 365 ÷ 10 = 36.5.
  3. Compare with the credit period allowed, if given.
  4. Write the unit: days.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Customers take long to pay. Cash delayed. Bad-debt risk up. Possible need to tighten credit or offer a cash discount.
Low (or falling)Customers pay promptly. Cash is in. Credit policy is strict or the trade is cash-heavy.
Too high can also be badA 90-day collection in a 30-day trade is a red flag — possible window-dressed sales (bills raised to friends who will never pay). Too low: refusing credit and losing volume.
Solved example K17 · Easy

7.4 Average collection period (debtors’ velocity in days) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaCollection period = 365 ÷ Debtors turnover
2. Figures pickedTurnover 10 times; 365 days.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)365 ÷ 10 = 36.5. Alternative: (₹80,000 ÷ ₹8,00,000) × 365 = (80,000 ÷ 8,00,000) × 365 = 0.10 × 365 = 36.5.
4. Answer with unit36.5 days

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. A credit customer pays in about 37 days. That is prompt. Set next to a 60-day payment period, Kaveri collects 23 days before it pays — a cash-cycle advantage.

10. Common mistakes
  • 365 ÷ closing debtors, skipping the turnover step, and skipping credit sales.
  • Using 365 ÷ total sales / debtors when cash sales exist.
  • Writing 36.5 times. Unit is days.
11. Memory trick

Days to collect = 365 / how many times debtors flipped. Same pattern as stock days.

7.5 Creditors / payables turnover ratio

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio — credit purchases from P&L working, average creditors from Balance Sheet. Purpose family: efficiency / trade-credit use.

Ideal / usual comment. There is no “higher is better”. A higher turnover means you pay faster (you use less free credit). A lower turnover means you pay slower (you use more free credit, but you may anger suppliers). Match it to the credit period allowed by suppliers.

1. What is it? — Definition

Creditors turnover is the number of times, during the year, that average trade payables were paid off. It is credit purchases divided by average trade payables.

2. In simple words

Kaveri bought ₹7,90,000 of goods, all on credit, and owed suppliers, on average, ₹1,30,000. So the creditors’ book was paid and refilled about 6.08 times.

3. Why do we need it?

To see how the firm uses supplier credit — a free source of working capital — and whether it is stretching payables dangerously.

Formula

Creditors turnover = Credit purchases ÷ Average trade payables

Credit purchases = total purchases − cash purchases. If the split is silent, assume all purchases are on credit. Purchases = COGS + closing stock − opening stock. Average payables = (opening + closing) ÷ 2.

7.5 Creditors / payables turnover ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Credit purchasesGoods bought on credit. Not COGS. Not sales.Kaveri: all purchases are credit = ₹7,90,000. Working: COGS ₹7,50,000 + closing ₹1,20,000 − opening ₹80,000 = ₹7,90,000.
Average trade payablesTypical amount owed to suppliers of goods. Include bills payable if grouped with creditors.(₹1,10,000 + ₹1,50,000) ÷ 2 = ₹2,60,000 ÷ 2 = ₹1,30,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Rebuild purchases from COGS and stock if purchases are not printed. Do not use COGS as the numerator (COGS is for stock turnover). Do not use sales. If opening creditors are given, average them.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Build credit purchases. Purchases = COGS + closing stock − opening stock.
  2. Average creditors = (opening + closing) ÷ 2.
  3. Divide. Unit: times.
  4. Convert to days if asked.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)You pay suppliers often / quickly. You may be missing free credit. Liquidity is used up faster.
Low (or falling)You pay slowly. Free credit is being used. Cash is conserved — until a supplier stops supplying.
Too high can also be badPaying cash-on-delivery when 45 days are on offer is a gift to the supplier, not a virtue, if your own cash is tight. Too low: suppliers may refuse credit, charge a premium, or take legal action. “Lower” is not a prize past the allowed credit period.
Solved example K18 · Easy

7.5 Creditors / payables turnover ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaCreditors turnover = Credit purchases ÷ Average trade payables
2. Figures pickedCredit purchases ₹7,90,000; average payables ₹1,30,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹7,90,000 ÷ ₹1,30,000 = 7,90,000 ÷ 1,30,000 = 79/13 = 6.0769…
4. Answer with unit6.08 times &nbsp;(2 d.p.; exact 79/13)

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Suppliers are paid a little over 6 times a year. That will become about 60 days in the next ratio — two months of free credit, which is common in wholesale trade and longer than the 36.5 days Kaveri takes to collect. The cash cycle is in Kaveri’s favour.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using COGS instead of purchases. For Kaveri that would be 7,50,000/1,30,000 = 5.77 times — wrong. Purchases and COGS differ by the stock increase of ₹40,000.
  • Using sales in the numerator.
  • Using closing creditors only when opening was given: 7,90,000/1,50,000 = 5.27 times — wrong.
  • Treating a loan creditor or outstanding wages as trade payables. This ratio is about suppliers of goods.
11. Memory trick

Creditors come from purchases, not from sales, not from COGS. Credit purchases / average creditors. Rebuild purchases from COGS ± stock if needed.

7.6 Average payment period (creditors’ velocity in days)

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio (derived from creditors turnover). Purpose family: efficiency / working-capital days.

Ideal / usual comment. Sit at the credit period the supplier allows. Paying 5 days early loses free cash; paying 40 days late costs reputation and future credit.

1. What is it? — Definition

Average payment period is the number of days, on average, that the firm takes to pay its suppliers. It is 365 divided by creditors turnover.

2. In simple words

If creditors turn 6.08 times in 365 days, one payment-cycle is about 60 days. A purchase billed today is paid in about two months.

3. Why do we need it?

To complete the operating-cycle story: holding days + collection days − payment days = net cash cycle. Also to check that the firm is not funding itself by starving suppliers.

Formula

Average payment period (days) = 365 ÷ Creditors turnover   or   (Average creditors ÷ Credit purchases) × 365

Months = 12 ÷ turnover. Use 360 if the paper says so.

7.6 Average payment period (creditors’ velocity in days) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
Creditors turnoverCredit purchases ÷ average creditors.Kaveri: 6.0769… times.
Credit purchases / average creditorsSame figures as the turnover.₹7,90,000 and ₹1,30,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Use credit purchases, not COGS, not sales. Same 365/360 convention as the other day-ratios unless told otherwise.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Compute creditors turnover.
  2. Days = 365 ÷ turnover. Show the long division.
  3. Compare with the credit period allowed by suppliers, if given.
  4. Place it next to collection period: collecting faster than paying is a cash plus.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)The firm takes long to pay. Free credit, but strained suppliers.
Low (or falling)The firm pays promptly. Good relations, less free credit.
Too high can also be badA 120-day payment in a 45-day trade is a distress signal (or a bullying of small suppliers). Too low: paying at the counter when 60 days are free, while the firm itself borrows at 12% — a treasury mistake.
Solved example K19 · Easy

7.6 Average payment period (creditors’ velocity in days) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaPayment period = 365 ÷ Creditors turnover
2. Figures pickedTurnover = 7,90,000 ÷ 1,30,000 = 79/13. 365 days.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)365 ÷ (79/13) = 365 × 13 ÷ 79 = 4,745 ÷ 79. 79 × 60 = 4,740, remainder 5, so 60 + 5/79 = 60.06 days.
4. Answer with unit60.06 days &nbsp;(≈ 60 days)

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Suppliers are paid in about 60 days. Customers pay in 36.5 days. Stock sits 48.67 days. A rough cash-cycle check: 48.67 + 36.5 − 60.06 ≈ 25 days of net operating cycle — Kaveri needs about 25 days of its own working capital to run the trade, the rest is funded by suppliers. Comfortable.

10. Common mistakes
  • 365 ÷ COGS / creditors, mixing stock formula with creditors.
  • Using 365 ÷ purchases without averaging creditors when opening was given.
  • Calling a longer payment period “more efficient”. It is cheaper cash, not more efficient operations, and it has a relationship cost.
11. Memory trick

Days to pay = 365 / creditors turnover. Put it next to days to collect. Collect before you pay, and you sleep.

Formula

Net operating / cash cycle (days) ≈ Holding period + Collection period − Payment period

Kaveri: 48.67 + 36.50 − 60.06 = 25.11 days. A short cycle is a liquidity blessing. A negative cycle (paying after collecting-plus-holding) means suppliers finance the whole trade.

7.7 Working capital turnover ratio

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio — sales from P&L, working capital from Balance Sheet. Purpose family: efficiency.

Ideal / usual comment. Higher generally means each rupee of working capital is supporting more sales. Too high can mean WC is inadequate for the volume (overtrading).

1. What is it? — Definition

Working capital turnover is sales divided by working capital (current assets minus current liabilities). It asks: how many rupees of sales does each rupee of net current assets support?

2. In simple words

Kaveri has ₹1,50,000 of working capital and sells ₹10,00,000. Each rupee of WC supports ₹6.67 of sales.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge whether the firm is using its net current assets hard enough, and to spot overtrading (sales far too large for the WC, so a small delay in collection can freeze the firm).

Formula

Working capital turnover = Sales ÷ Working capital   where Working capital = CA − CL

Some papers use average working capital if a previous BS is fully given. Kaveri has only this year’s CA and CL (openings of stock, debtors, creditors are given, but not a full opening BS), so we use closing WC and state that.

7.7 Working capital turnover ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
SalesRevenue from operations.Kaveri: ₹10,00,000.
Working capitalCurrent assets − current liabilities. The net current cushion.₹3,00,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹1,50,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

WC is not current assets. It is CA minus CL. If CA = CL, WC is zero and this ratio is undefined — write that, do not divide by zero. If CL > CA, WC is negative and the ratio is not meaningful as a turnover; say “negative working capital”.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. CA − CL = working capital.
  2. Confirm it is positive.
  3. Sales ÷ WC. Unit: times.
  4. Comment on overtrading if the number is very high next to a thin current ratio.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Each WC-rupee is working hard. Good use of funds — unless it is overtrading.
Low (or falling)A lot of WC is supporting little sales. Idle stock or idle cash, or a collapsed top line.
Too high can also be badOvertrading: sales have outgrown the cushion. A slow month of collections and the firm cannot pay wages. Too low: capital stuck in WC, ROCE suffers.
Solved example K20 · Easy

7.7 Working capital turnover ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaWC turnover = Sales ÷ (CA − CL)
2. Figures pickedSales ₹10,00,000; WC ₹3,00,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹1,50,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹1,50,000 = 10,00,000 ÷ 1,50,000 = 100/15 = 20/3 = 6.666…
4. Answer with unit6.67 times

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Each rupee of working capital supports ₹6.67 of sales. Paired with a current ratio of 2 : 1, this is use, not overtrading. Overtrading would look like WC turnover of 20 times next to a current ratio of 1.1.

10. Common mistakes
  • Dividing by current assets instead of working capital.
  • Using COGS in the numerator. This ratio uses sales.
  • Taking WC as CA + CL. It is CA − CL.
11. Memory trick

Sales over the cushion. WC = CA − CL. High = hard-working cushion; extremely high = overtrading.

7.8 Fixed asset turnover ratio

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio — sales from P&L, net fixed assets from Balance Sheet. Purpose family: efficiency of long-term assets.

Ideal / usual comment. Higher means the factory/godown is generating more sales per rupee of FA. A trader (low FA) will show a higher number than a manufacturer (heavy FA). Compare within the industry.

1. What is it? — Definition

Fixed asset turnover is sales divided by net fixed assets. It asks: how many rupees of sales does each rupee invested in the godown, plant and office generate?

2. In simple words

Kaveri’s godown and office (net) cost ₹6,50,000 and produced ₹10,00,000 of sales. About ₹1.54 of sales per rupee of net FA.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge capacity utilisation and the productivity of long-term assets. A falling FA turnover can mean idle capacity, or a newly bought asset that has not yet started selling (which is not a crime — mention it).

Formula

Fixed asset turnover = Sales ÷ Net fixed assets

Use net FA (after depreciation). Some papers use gross FA; some use average net FA. Default: closing net FA. State it.

7.8 Fixed asset turnover ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
SalesRevenue from operations.Kaveri: ₹10,00,000.
Net fixed assetsPPE after accumulated depreciation. Exclude current assets and investments unless the paper says “capital assets” more broadly.Kaveri: ₹6,50,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Net, not gross, unless only gross is given. Do not add current assets (that would be total-asset turnover, which is ROA’s cousin).

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Pick net FA from the BS.
  2. Pick sales from the P&L.
  3. Divide. Unit: times.
  4. Read with the nature of the business (trader vs factory).
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Assets are working hard. Good utilisation.
Low (or falling)Idle capacity, over-investment, or a newly commissioned plant.
Too high can also be badThe firm may be sweating old, fully-depreciated assets (net FA is small because of accumulated depreciation, so the ratio looks brilliant). Check gross FA and the age of assets. Too low: money locked in a building that does not sell.
Solved example K21 · Easy

7.8 Fixed asset turnover ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaFA turnover = Sales ÷ Net FA
2. Figures pickedSales ₹10,00,000; Net FA ₹6,50,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹6,50,000 = 10,00,000 ÷ 6,50,000 = 100/65 = 20/13 = 1.53846…
4. Answer with unit1.54 times

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Each rupee of net FA produces ₹1.54 of sales. For a trader who owns a godown, this is modest (the godown is a large slice of the BS). It is not comparable with a stall-trader who rents and shows FA turnover of 20 times — different asset strategy.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using gross FA when net is given. Net is smaller, so using gross understates turnover.
  • Adding working capital to FA (that is capital turnover).
  • Using PAT in the numerator (that is a return, not a turnover).
11. Memory trick

Sales over the godown. Net FA, not gross. High looks good; with fully-depreciated assets it can be an illusion.

7.9 Capital turnover ratio

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio — sales from P&L, capital employed from Balance Sheet. Purpose family: efficiency of long-term funds.

Ideal / usual comment. Higher means each rupee of long-term funds supports more sales. Pair it with operating profit ratio: ROCE ≈ operating profit% × capital turnover.

1. What is it? — Definition

Capital turnover is sales divided by capital employed. It asks: how many rupees of sales does each rupee of long-term funds generate?

2. In simple words

Kaveri has ₹8,00,000 of capital employed (owners + long-term lenders) and sells ₹10,00,000. Each long-term rupee supports ₹1.25 of sales.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge the activity of the total long-term pool. It is one of the two engines of ROCE (the other is operating profit margin). A firm can have a modest margin and a high capital turnover (a grocer) or a fat margin and a low capital turnover (a jeweller) and the same ROCE.

Formula

Capital turnover = Sales ÷ Capital employed

Capital employed = Shareholders’ funds + Long-term debt = Net FA + Working capital. Use the same CE you will use for ROCE.

7.9 Capital turnover ratio — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
SalesRevenue from operations.Kaveri: ₹10,00,000.
Capital employedLong-term funds in the business.Method 1: ₹6,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹8,00,000. Method 2: ₹6,50,000 + ₹1,50,000 = ₹8,00,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Do not use only share capital. Do not use total assets (that includes assets financed by current liabilities). CE is the long-term pool.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Compute capital employed two ways and confirm they match.
  2. Sales ÷ CE. Unit: times.
  3. Keep the CE figure — you need it for ROCE in a moment.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Long-term funds are supporting a large top line. An activity-driven business.
Low (or falling)Heavy capital for the sales achieved. Possible idle FA or idle WC.
Too high can also be badOvertrading at the capital level: sales too big for the long-term funds, so the firm is leaning on current liabilities. Too low: over-capitalised, ROCE will sag.
Solved example K22 · Easy

7.9 Capital turnover ratio from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaCapital turnover = Sales ÷ Capital employed
2. Figures pickedSales ₹10,00,000; CE ₹8,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹8,00,000 = 10,00,000 ÷ 8,00,000 = 10/8 = 1.25.
4. Answer with unit1.25 times

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Each rupee of long-term funds supports ₹1.25 of sales. Combined with a 15% operating margin, ROCE should be 15% × 1.25 = 18.75%. We will confirm that identity in the ROCE section — it is a free arithmetic check.

10. Common mistakes
  • Denominator = equity share capital only.
  • Denominator = total assets. That is total-asset turnover = 1.05 times for Kaveri, a different ratio.
  • Mixing one CE definition for this ratio and another for ROCE in the same answer.
11. Memory trick

Sales over the long-term pool. Capital turnover × operating profit% = ROCE. Use it as a check.

7.10 Return on capital employed (ROCE)

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio — EBIT from P&L, capital employed from Balance Sheet. Purpose family: profitability of long-term funds.

Ideal / usual comment. Should beat the cost of capital. As a rule of thumb, comfortably above the interest rate on the firm’s debt (Kaveri’s interest is ₹30,000 on ₹2,00,000 = 15% pre-tax coupon; ROCE of 18.75% clears it). Compare with industry and with last year.

1. What is it? — Definition

ROCE is operating profit (EBIT) divided by capital employed, times 100. It is the return earned on every rupee of long-term funds, before the split between lenders (interest) and owners (the residual), and before tax.

2. In simple words

The business, as a machine, was given ₹8,00,000 of long-term money and produced ₹1,50,000 of operating profit. That is an 18.75% return on the machine, before the banker and the tax officer take their cuts.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge the overall earning power of the firm’s long-term resources. It is the fairest profitability ratio for comparing two firms with different debt levels, because EBIT is before interest. Banks and boards quote it constantly.

Formula

ROCE = (EBIT ÷ Capital employed) × 100

EBIT = PBIT = operating profit. Capital employed = SF + LTD = FA + WC. Some papers use PBT (after interest) — that is not ROCE, that is closer to a return on total long-term funds after debt cost; do not mix. Some use average CE; default here is closing CE.

7.10 Return on capital employed (ROCE) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
EBIT / operating profitProfit before interest and tax. The pool that belongs to both lenders and owners.Kaveri: ₹1,50,000. Rebuild: PBT ₹1,20,000 + interest ₹30,000.
Capital employedShareholders’ funds + long-term debt. Equals net FA + working capital.Kaveri: ₹8,00,000 (both methods).
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Numerator is EBIT, not PAT, not PBT. PAT is for ROE. PBT has already paid the lenders, so it understates the return on the whole pool. Denominator includes debt — so the numerator must include the profit that debt helped to earn, i.e. before interest.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Build EBIT (PBT + interest, or GP − opex).
  2. Build capital employed two ways; they must match.
  3. ROCE = EBIT ÷ CE × 100. Unit: %.
  4. Check: operating profit% × capital turnover should equal ROCE.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)The long-term funds are earning well. Value is being created if ROCE exceeds the cost of those funds.
Low (or falling)Funds are earning poorly. Either margins are thin, or capital is idle (low turnover), or both. DuPont (next sections) tells you which.
Too high can also be badA spectacular ROCE can be a fully-depreciated plant (tiny CE) or a one-time operating windfall. Or it can be genuine. Check both years and the notes. Too low: the firm is destroying value if it is below what those funds could earn elsewhere.
Solved example K23 · Easy

7.10 Return on capital employed (ROCE) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaROCE = (EBIT ÷ Capital employed) × 100
2. Figures pickedEBIT ₹1,50,000; CE ₹8,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)(₹1,50,000 ÷ ₹8,00,000) × 100 = (1,50,000 ÷ 8,00,000) × 100 = 0.1875 × 100 = 18.75%.
4. Answer with unit18.75%

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Long-term funds earned 18.75% before interest and tax. Check: operating profit ratio 15% × capital turnover 1.25 = 18.75%. The two engines agree. The 18.75% is above the 15% coupon on the term loan (30,000/2,00,000), so the debt is earning its keep and leaving a surplus for owners.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using PAT in the numerator. That understates ROCE and confuses it with ROE. For Kaveri, PAT/CE = 90,000/8,00,000 = 11.25% — a different, unnamed number.
  • Using only share capital as CE.
  • Using total assets as CE (that is closer to ROA’s denominator).
  • Using PBT (after interest) with a CE that still includes debt — the numerator and denominator then do not match.
11. Memory trick

ROCE = return on the whole long-term pool = EBIT / CE × 100. EBIT, not PAT. CE includes debt, so the profit must be before interest. Check: OP% × capital turnover.

Key point

Matching rule, write it once and it will save you in every paper: if the denominator includes a fund-provider, the numerator must be the profit before that provider has been paid. CE includes lenders → use EBIT. Equity includes only owners → use PAT (ROE). Break the matching rule and the ratio is meaningless.

7.11 Return on equity (ROE / return on shareholders’ funds)

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio — PAT from P&L, equity shareholders’ funds from Balance Sheet. Purpose family: profitability for owners.

Ideal / usual comment. Higher is better for owners, provided it is not bought with reckless gearing. Compare with ROCE, with the interest rate, and with what owners could earn elsewhere. Kaveri’s 15% is a solid owners’ return for a trading company.

1. What is it? — Definition

ROE is profit after tax (and after preference dividend, if any) divided by equity shareholders’ funds, times 100. It is the return on the owners’ own rupee.

2. In simple words

Owners have left ₹6,00,000 in Kaveri. This year they earned ₹90,000 after tax. That is 15 paise in the rupee, or 15%.

3. Why do we need it?

This is the owners’ scoreboard. It is what a shareholder compares with a bank-deposit rate, a mutual fund, or another company’s ROE. It is also the top of the DuPont identity.

Formula

ROE = (PAT ÷ Equity shareholders’ funds) × 100

If preference dividend exists: numerator = PAT − preference dividend, denominator = equity funds (exclude preference capital). Kaveri has no preference. Do not use EBIT here — EBIT belongs to lenders as well.

7.11 Return on equity (ROE / return on shareholders’ funds) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
PAT (less preference dividend if any)Profit for equity owners after interest, tax and preference dividend.Kaveri: ₹90,000, no preference dividend.
Equity shareholders’ fundsEquity share capital + reserves − fictitious assets. Exclude preference capital.Kaveri: ₹4,00,000 + ₹2,00,000 = ₹6,00,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Denominator is not “equity share capital” alone. Reserves belong to owners. Numerator is PAT, not EBIT, not PBT (unless the paper says pre-tax ROE). If a P&L debit balance (loss) sits on the asset side, net it off equity.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. PAT, minus preference dividend if given.
  2. Equity funds = equity share capital + reserves − fictitious assets.
  3. Divide × 100. Unit: %.
  4. Compare with ROCE: if ROE > ROCE after tax, gearing is helping owners; if ROE < after-tax ROCE, gearing is hurting.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Owners are earning well on their money. The share is more attractive, other things equal.
Low (or falling)Owners are earning poorly. Either the business is weak (low ROCE) or debt is eating the residual (high interest) or equity is bloated.
Too high can also be badA 60% ROE with a debt-equity of 5 : 1 is a tightrope, not a triumph. A 60% ROE with tiny equity because of accumulated losses that just reversed can also mislead. Too low: owners would have been better off in a fixed deposit — a harsh but fair comment if it persists.
Solved example K24 · Easy

7.11 Return on equity (ROE / return on shareholders’ funds) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
