2. Figures pickedPAT ₹90,000; Equity funds ₹6,00,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)(₹90,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000) × 100 = (90,000 ÷ 6,00,000) × 100 = 0.15 × 100 = 15%.
4. Answer with unit15%

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Owners earned 15% after tax. ROCE was 18.75% before interest and tax. After paying 15% coupon on a small loan and 25% tax on PBT, 15% remains for owners — a fair translation, not a magic trick. Gearing is mild, so ROE is not being inflated by a mountain of debt.

10. Common mistakes
  • Denominator = equity share capital ₹4,00,000 only, giving 90,000/4,00,000 = 22.5%. That ignores ₹2,00,000 of reserves which are also owners’ money. This is the most common ROE mistake in the paper.
  • Numerator = EBIT. That is ROCE’s numerator. Matching rule broken.
  • Including preference capital in the denominator while also not deducting preference dividend.
11. Memory trick

ROE = owners’ leftover over owners’ money = PAT / (share capital + reserves) × 100. Never skip reserves. Never use EBIT.

7.12 Return on assets (ROA / return on total assets)

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio — profit from P&L, total assets from Balance Sheet. Purpose family: profitability of the whole asset base.

Ideal / usual comment. Higher is better. It will usually sit below ROCE because total assets (9.5 lakh) are bigger than capital employed (8 lakh) — current liabilities finance part of the assets.

1. What is it? — Definition

Return on assets is profit divided by total assets, times 100. Two versions: (A) PAT / total assets — common “bottom-line” version; (B) EBIT / total assets — “operating” version, comparable across different debt levels. These notes compute both and lead with PAT.

2. In simple words

Every rupee of asset — godown, stock, debtors, cash — earned how many paise of profit? For Kaveri, PAT version: 9.47 paise. EBIT version: 15.79 paise.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge how productively the whole asset base is used, including the slice financed by creditors. Useful for comparing firms with very different current-liability levels.

Formula

ROA = (PAT ÷ Total assets) × 100   (lead version); also (EBIT ÷ Total assets) × 100

Total assets = Balance Sheet total. If fictitious assets exist, use tangible total assets. Average total assets if both years’ BS are given; Kaveri uses closing, stated.

7.12 Return on assets (ROA / return on total assets) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
PAT (version A)Bottom-line profit.Kaveri: ₹90,000.
EBIT (version B)Operating profit, for a debt-neutral view.Kaveri: ₹1,50,000.
Total assetsFA + CA = BS total.Kaveri: ₹9,50,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Denominator is the BS total, not CE, not FA. Write which numerator you used. In a “compute ROA” question with no formula printed, PAT / TA is the safe MBA default; mention the EBIT version if marks are generous.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Pick PAT (and EBIT if you want both).
  2. Pick total assets = BS total.
  3. Divide × 100.
  4. Place it next to ROCE and ROE: ROA < ROCE typically, because CL assets sit in the ROA denominator.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Assets are earning well, including those financed by creditors.
Low (or falling)A large asset base is producing little profit. Idle FA, slow stock, or thin margins.
Too high can also be badCan be a fully-depreciated asset base (same illusion as FA turnover). Too low: the firm is too fat in assets for its profit.
Solved example K25 · Easy

7.12 Return on assets (ROA / return on total assets) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaROA = (PAT ÷ Total assets) × 100
2. Figures pickedPAT ₹90,000; Total assets ₹9,50,000. Also EBIT ₹1,50,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)PAT version: (90,000 ÷ 9,50,000) × 100 = 9.4736…%. EBIT version: (1,50,000 ÷ 9,50,000) × 100 = 15.789…%.
4. Answer with unit9.47% (PAT) &nbsp;; 15.79% (EBIT version)

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. The whole asset base earned 9.47% after tax. ROCE was 18.75% on a smaller, long-term, denominator. The gap is mostly the extra ₹1,50,000 of assets that creditors financed, plus the fact that PAT is after interest and tax while EBIT is not. Both numbers can live in the same answer as long as you label them.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using capital employed as the denominator and calling it ROA.
  • Using net FA only.
  • Mixing PAT in the numerator with a comment that “this is before interest”.
11. Memory trick

ROA = profit / whole pie of assets. PAT/TA is the default. EBIT/TA is the operating cousin. TA is the BS total.

7.13 Earnings per share (EPS)

Syllabus bucket. Combined ratio — PAT from P&L, number of equity shares from the Balance Sheet / notes. Purpose family: profitability per owner-unit.

Ideal / usual comment. Higher is better, but EPS cannot be compared across companies with different face values or different retained-earnings histories without care. Compare with the same company’s previous EPS, and with the market price (P/E, which is not in this syllabus).

1. What is it? — Definition

EPS is the profit after tax (minus preference dividend) that belongs to one equity share. It is PAT available to equity holders divided by the number of equity shares outstanding.

2. In simple words

Kaveri has 40,000 equity shares and earned ₹90,000. Each share earned ₹2.25 this year. That ₹2.25 is not a dividend — it is earnings. Some of it may be kept as reserves.

3. Why do we need it?

To report the year’s earning power in the unit that a shareholder actually holds: one share. It is a compulsory line in a listed company’s P&L (Ind AS 33 / AS 20), and a standard MBA numerical.

Formula

EPS = (PAT − Preference dividend) ÷ Number of equity shares outstanding

Number of shares = Equity share capital ÷ Face value. Kaveri: ₹4,00,000 ÷ ₹10 = 40,000 shares. If new shares were issued mid-year, a weighted average is used (advanced; only if the paper gives dates). Face value is not market price.

7.13 Earnings per share (EPS) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
PAT − preference dividendEarnings for equity shareholders.Kaveri: ₹90,000 − 0 = ₹90,000.
Number of equity sharesIssued and outstanding equity shares, usually assumed equal to shares at year-end unless dates of issue are given.₹4,00,000 ÷ ₹10 = 4,00,000 ÷ 10 = 40,000 shares.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Do not divide PAT by share capital in rupees and call it EPS — that would be a return on face-capital, missing reserves and missing the “per share” unit. Do not use market price in the denominator (that is the P/E reciprocal when used with EPS). If preference dividend is given, subtract it.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. PAT minus preference dividend.
  2. Number of equity shares = equity share capital ÷ face value. (Or take the number if it is printed.)
  3. Divide. Unit: ₹ per share.
  4. One sentence: each equity share earned ₹X this year. Do not call it dividend.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Each share earned more. Owners are better off, other things equal.
Low (or falling)Each share earned little. Either profit is weak or there are many shares (a recent issue, a bonus).
Too high can also be badA bonus issue last year would have cut EPS in half without the business worsening — always check the number of shares. A one-time gain can spike EPS. Too low after a fresh issue may simply mean the new capital has not yet started earning.
Solved example K26 · Easy

7.13 Earnings per share (EPS) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaEPS = (PAT − Preference dividend) ÷ Number of equity shares
2. Figures pickedPAT ₹90,000; preference dividend nil; shares = ₹4,00,000 ÷ ₹10 = 40,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹90,000 ÷ 40,000 = 90,000 ÷ 40,000 = 9/4 = 2.25.
4. Answer with unit₹2.25 per share

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Each of the 40,000 shares earned ₹2.25. Face value is ₹10, so earnings are 22.5% of face — but that is not ROE, because ROE uses share capital plus reserves. EPS is a per-share number for owners and for market ratios, not a substitute for ROE.

10. Common mistakes
  • Dividing PAT by share capital: 90,000/4,00,000 = 0.225, then writing “EPS = 0.225 times”. Wrong unit, wrong denominator.
  • Forgetting to subtract preference dividend when preference shares exist.
  • Using the market price of the share as the denominator.
  • Calling EPS the dividend per share. DPS is a different number; Kaveri’s dividend is not even given.
11. Memory trick

EPS = leftover for equity ÷ how many equity shares. Shares = capital / face value. Answer is ₹ per share, not %.

7.14 Interest coverage ratio (times interest earned)

Syllabus bucket. Combined as a solvency companion (both figures can also be read from the P&L — see the classification note). Purpose family: solvency / debt-servicing.

Ideal / usual comment. Higher is safer. Below 2–3 times is usually uncomfortable. 5 times is a healthy cover for a trading firm. A term-loan covenant often demands a minimum (say 2.5 times).

1. What is it? — Definition

Interest coverage is EBIT divided by interest (finance cost). It asks: how many times can the operating profit pay the interest bill?

2. In simple words

Kaveri earned ₹1,50,000 of operating profit and owes ₹30,000 of interest. It can pay the interest bill 5 times over. The banker sleeps.

3. Why do we need it?

To judge whether the debt load is serviceable from operations. Debt-equity tells you the stock of debt; interest coverage tells you whether this year’s profit can carry this year’s interest. You need both.

Formula

Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest

EBIT, not PAT, not PBT. PAT has already paid the interest (and tax), so PAT / interest understates cover and is the wrong matching. If interest is zero, the ratio is not defined — write “no interest, coverage not applicable”.

7.14 Interest coverage ratio (times interest earned) — every piece of the formula
ComponentWhat it meansHow to pick it from the statements
EBITProfit before interest and tax. The pool available to pay lenders.Kaveri: ₹1,50,000.
Interest / finance costInterest on long-term and short-term borrowings for the year. Not the principal repayment. Not preference dividend.Kaveri: ₹30,000.
6. Format — How to pick the figure (any paper, and Kaveri)

Add back interest if you are looking at PBT: EBIT = PBT + interest. Do not use “debt service” (principal + interest) unless the question asks for DSCR, which is a different ratio and not in this list.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Build EBIT.
  2. Pick the interest line (finance costs).
  3. Divide. Unit: times.
  4. Comment with debt-equity: low D/E + high coverage = safe; high D/E + low coverage = danger.
A ratio is a sentence, not a trophy
SignalInterpretation
High (or rising)Interest is easily earned. Lenders are safe. The firm can take a profit dip without defaulting.
Low (or falling)A small fall in EBIT and interest cannot be paid. Distress. Fresh lending will be refused or expensive.
Too high can also be badA coverage of 50 times usually means almost no debt — safe, but perhaps under-levered. Too low (under 1): EBIT does not even cover interest; the firm is paying interest by selling assets, raising new loans, or delaying other bills.
Solved example K27 · Easy

7.14 Interest coverage ratio (times interest earned) from Kaveri Traders Ltd (31 March 2026)

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaInterest coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest
2. Figures pickedEBIT ₹1,50,000; Interest ₹30,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)₹1,50,000 ÷ ₹30,000 = 1,50,000 ÷ 30,000 = 15/3 = 5.
4. Answer with unit5 times

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Reading for Kaveri. Operating profit can pay the interest bill five times. Combined with debt-equity of 0.33 : 1, Kaveri is a low-risk borrower. A drop of 80% in EBIT would still just cover interest (coverage of 1) — there is a wide buffer.

10. Common mistakes
  • Using PAT / interest = 90,000/30,000 = 3 times. That is after tax, after the interest has already been paid — it is not coverage.
  • Using PBT / interest = 1,20,000/30,000 = 4 times. PBT is after interest, so this is “leftover / interest”, not coverage.
  • Putting principal repayment in the denominator (that is DSCR territory).
  • Using total debt in the denominator. Coverage is a flow/flow ratio, not a flow/stock ratio.
11. Memory trick

Coverage = how many times EBIT can pay the interest. EBIT over Interest. PAT is too late; the interest has already left.

8. DuPont identity (short, useful in MBA papers)

1. What is it? — Definition

The DuPont identity splits ROE into three Combined / Revenue pieces: a margin (net profit ratio), an activity ratio (asset turnover), and a leverage ratio (equity multiplier = total assets ÷ equity). ROE = Net profit margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier.

2. In simple words

Owners’ 15% return did not fall from the sky. It is 9% leftover on sales, times how hard the assets were worked, times how much the asset base is bigger than owners’ money. DuPont names the three knobs. If ROE falls, you know which knob moved.

Formula

ROE = (PAT ÷ Sales) × (Sales ÷ Total assets) × (Total assets ÷ Equity)

Sales and total assets cancel: the identity equals PAT ÷ Equity, which is ROE. The point is the split, not a new number.

Solved example K28 · Moderate

DuPont split of Kaveri’s 15% ROE

Net profit margin = ₹90,000 ÷ ₹10,00,000 = 0.09 = 9%.

Asset turnover = ₹10,00,000 ÷ ₹9,50,000 = 10,00,000 ÷ 9,50,000 = 20/19 = 1.0526 times.

Equity multiplier = ₹9,50,000 ÷ ₹6,00,000 = 9,50,000 ÷ 6,00,000 = 19/12 = 1.5833.

Product = 0.09 × 1.052632 × 1.583333 = 0.094737 × 1.583333 = 0.150000 = 15%.

Reading. Kaveri’s ROE is driven more by margin (9%) and a modest multiplier (1.58 — low gearing) than by furious asset turnover (only 1.05). To raise ROE without taking more debt, Meera must either lift the 9% margin or sweat the 9.5 lakh of assets harder. Taking more debt would lift the multiplier and ROE — and lift risk. DuPont makes that trade-off visible.

Exam tip

DuPont is optional in many B-school papers but scores easily as a 4-mark “explain ROE” add-on. Write the three-factor formula, plug in, and name which factor is the lever.

11. Memory trick

M-A-L: Margin × Activity × Leverage = ROE. If ROE moved, circle which of the three moved.

12. Exam-ready answer

Kaveri Traders is liquid: the current ratio sits at the textbook 2 : 1, the acid test at 1.2 : 1 and the cash ratio at 0.53 : 1, so short-term bills are covered even if stock is ignored. The firm is conservatively financed — debt-equity 0.33 : 1, proprietary ratio 63%, low capital gearing, interest covered 5 times — and fixed assets are fully funded by long-term money (FA to long-term funds 81%). Profitability is decent for a wholesaler: gross 25%, operating 15%, net 9%, ROCE 18.75% and ROE 15%, with EPS ₹2.25; ROCE clears the 15% coupon on the term loan, so gearing is helping, not hurting. Efficiency is the quiet strength: stock turns 7.5 times (held ~49 days), debtors pay in 36.5 days and suppliers are paid in ~60 days, which produces a short net cash cycle of about 25 days. Watch-outs are modest rather than alarming — FA turnover is only 1.54 because the firm owns its godown, the 9% net margin will feel any wage or interest shock, and the current ratio of 2.0 is not a licence to let stock go stale (though 7.5 turns says it has not). Overall, Kaveri is a solvent, moderately profitable trader with a healthy operating cycle and unused debt capacity.

Key point

A health comment always has four beats: liquidity, solvency, profitability, efficiency. Then one watch-out. Then one overall sentence. That structure scores even when your adjectives are cautious.

10. Reconstruction numericals — the exam favourite

A large slice of MBA ratio marks does not give you a P&L and a BS. It gives you some ratios and one rupee figure, and asks you to rebuild CA, CL, stock, COGS or sales. The method is algebra with the formula, not memory of Kaveri.

Golden reconstruction rules. (1) Write the ratio formula. (2) Replace the words with letters (CA, CL, WC). (3) Write any extra identity (WC = CA − CL). (4) Solve the two equations. (5) Never treat “current ratio 2.5” as WC = 2.5.

Type A — Current ratio and working capital → CA and CL

Solved example R1 · Moderate

Current ratio 2.5, working capital ₹1,50,000. Find CA and CL. Then quick ratio 1.5; find inventory.

Given. Current ratio = 2.5, Working capital = ₹1,50,000, Quick ratio = 1.5. Prepaid expenses are nil. Find current assets, current liabilities and inventory.

Step 1 — names.

Let CL = x. Then CA = 2.5x, because current ratio = CA/CL = 2.5.

Step 2 — working-capital identity.

WC = CA − CL = 2.5x − x = 1.5x.

1.5x = ₹1,50,000.

Step 3 — solve for x.

x = ₹1,50,000 ÷ 1.5 = ₹1,50,000 ÷ (3/2) = ₹1,50,000 × 2/3 = ₹3,00,000 ÷ 3 = ₹1,00,000.

So CL = ₹1,00,000.

CA = 2.5 × ₹1,00,000 = (5/2) × ₹1,00,000 = ₹2,50,000.

Check. CA − CL = ₹2,50,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹1,50,000 = WC. And CA/CL = 2.5. Both given facts return.

Step 4 — quick ratio.

Quick ratio = Quick assets / CL = 1.5, so Quick assets = 1.5 × ₹1,00,000 = ₹1,50,000.

Inventory = CA − Quick assets − Prepaid = ₹2,50,000 − ₹1,50,000 − 0 = ₹1,00,000.

Answer. Current assets ₹2,50,000, current liabilities ₹1,00,000, inventory ₹1,00,000.

Watch out

If prepaid had been given, inventory would be CA − QA − prepaid, not CA − QA. If the paper gives “liquid assets include debtors and cash only”, you are already looking at QA.

Type B — GP ratio, stock turnover, opening = closing → COGS, sales, GP, purchases

Solved example R2 · Exam

GP ratio 20%, stock turnover 5 times, opening stock ₹40,000 = closing stock. Find COGS, sales, GP and purchases.

Given. Gross profit ratio = 20% of sales. Inventory turnover = 5 times (COGS version). Opening stock = closing stock = ₹40,000.

Step 1 — average stock.

Opening = closing, so average stock = ₹40,000. (If they had been different you would add and divide by 2.)

Step 2 — COGS from turnover.

Stock turnover = COGS / average stock = 5, so COGS = 5 × ₹40,000 = ₹2,00,000.

Step 3 — sales from GP ratio.

GP = 20% of sales, so COGS = 80% of sales (because GP + COGS = Sales).

0.80 × Sales = ₹2,00,000.

Sales = ₹2,00,000 ÷ 0.80 = ₹2,00,000 ÷ (4/5) = ₹2,00,000 × 5/4 = ₹10,00,000 ÷ 4 = ₹2,50,000.

Step 4 — GP.

GP = Sales − COGS = ₹2,50,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹50,000. Check: 20% of ₹2,50,000 = ₹50,000.

Step 5 — purchases.

COGS = Opening + Purchases − Closing. Opening = closing, so Purchases = COGS = ₹2,00,000.

Answer. COGS ₹2,00,000, Sales ₹2,50,000, GP ₹50,000, Purchases ₹2,00,000.

Type C — Opening ≠ closing, GP ratio and stock turnover → closing stock and sales

Solved example R3 · Exam

Sales are not given. GP ratio 20%, stock turnover 8, opening stock ₹40,000, closing stock ₹60,000. Find COGS, sales and GP.

Given. GP ratio 20%. Stock turnover 8 (COGS / average stock). Opening ₹40,000, closing ₹60,000.

Average stock.

(₹40,000 + ₹60,000) ÷ 2 = ₹1,00,000 ÷ 2 = ₹50,000.

COGS.

8 × ₹50,000 = ₹4,00,000.

Sales.

COGS = 80% of sales, so Sales = ₹4,00,000 ÷ 0.80 = ₹5,00,000.

GP.

20% of ₹5,00,000 = ₹1,00,000. Check: ₹5,00,000 − ₹4,00,000 = ₹1,00,000.

Purchases, if asked.

Purchases = COGS + closing − opening = ₹4,00,000 + ₹60,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹4,20,000.

Answer. COGS ₹4,00,000, Sales ₹5,00,000, GP ₹1,00,000, Purchases ₹4,20,000.

Type D — Current ratio 3, WC ₹80,000 (a different number, so you cannot copy R1)

Solved example R4 · Moderate

Current ratio 3 : 1, working capital ₹80,000. Find CA and CL.

Let CL = x, CA = 3x.

3x − x = ₹80,000 so 2x = ₹80,000, x = ₹40,000.

CL = ₹40,000, CA = 3 × ₹40,000 = ₹1,20,000.

Check. ₹1,20,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹80,000; ₹1,20,000 ÷ ₹40,000 = 3.

Answer. CA ₹1,20,000, CL ₹40,000.

9. How to identify the question

If the question gives a ratio and working capital (or one of CA / CL) and asks for the missing BS items, it is Type A algebra. If it gives GP% and stock turnover and stock, it is Type B/C — build COGS first, then sales from the complement of GP%. If it gives proprietary ratio and total assets, SF = rate × TA. Always write the identity WC = CA − CL; it is the second equation you need.

10. Common mistakes
  • Current ratio 2.5 and WC ₹1,50,000 → “CA = 2.5 × 1,50,000”. That treats WC as CL. The 2.5 applies to CL, not to WC.
  • GP 20% and COGS ₹2,00,000 → “Sales = 20% × 2,00,000”. No: 20% is of sales, not of COGS. COGS is 80% of sales.
  • Stock turnover 5, opening 40,000, closing 60,000 → “COGS = 5 × 40,000”. Use the average, not opening alone.
  • Quick ratio 1.5, CA 2,50,000 → “Inventory = 1.5 × 2,50,000”. Quick ratio is QA/CL, not inventory/CA.
11. Memory trick

Two equations, two unknowns. Ratio gives you CA = k × CL. WC gives you CA − CL = a rupee amount. Solve. For GP% + turnover: turnover → COGS, complement of GP% → Sales.

“Times interest earned / ability to pay interest / coverage”EBIT / Interest — not PAT / InterestComb
Current ratio + working capital, find CA and CLAlgebra Type A (section 10)Rebuild
Quick ratio after that, find inventoryQA = QR × CL; Inventory = CA − QA − prepaidRebuild
GP% + stock turnover + stock, find sales / COGSAlgebra Type B/C: turnover → COGS, complement of GP% → salesRebuild
“Comment on liquidity” with a full set of statementsCurrent + quick + cash, then one sentence eachComment
“Comment on solvency / capital structure”Debt-equity + proprietary + gearing + interest coverageComment
“Comment on profitability”GP, OP, NP, ROCE, ROE (and EPS if shares are given)Comment
“Comment on efficiency / activity”Stock, debtors, creditors, FA, capital, WC turnovers + daysComment
Exam tip

When a question gives a full P&L and BS and says “compute ratios” without naming them, do not compute all 27. Compute a balanced set: 2 liquidity, 2 solvency, 3 profitability, 3 efficiency — ten ratios, each with formula, figure, unit, one-line comment. That is a 16–20 mark answer. Dumping 27 numbers with no comment scores worse.

12. Common mistakes (chapter-wide)

10. Common mistakes
  • Using sales instead of COGS for stock turnover. Stock is at cost. Kaveri would wrongly show 10 times instead of 7.5.
  • Including prepaid expenses in quick assets. Prepaid will not pay a creditor.
  • Using PAT instead of EBIT for ROCE. Matching rule: CE includes lenders, so profit must be before interest.
  • Using only share capital instead of shareholders’ funds (capital + reserves) for ROE, debt-equity, proprietary ratio. Reserves are owners’ money.
  • Mixing 365-day and 360-day conventions, or writing days as “times”.
  • Not using averages when opening stock / debtors / creditors are given. Closing-only is allowed only when opening is not given, and you must say so.
  • Reading current ratio 2 as CA − CL = 2. It means CA = 2 × CL.
  • Using total sales for debtors turnover when cash sales are given.
  • Using COGS (or sales) instead of credit purchases for creditors turnover.
  • Including interest in operating cost, so that operating ratio + operating profit ratio no longer add to 100%.
  • Calling every profitability ratio a Revenue ratio. ROCE, ROE, ROA, EPS are Combined by source.
  • Comparing two firms’ GP% without checking that one includes depreciation in COGS and the other does not — policies differ.
  • A beautiful ratio on 31 March after window dressing (repaying a creditor on 30 March, re-borrowing on 2 April).
  • Writing a number with no unit and no sentence, and calling it “analysis”.
  • Inverting a ratio (equity/debt when the paper asked debt/equity) and then applying the “high is risky” comment to the inverted number.
  • Treating a high current ratio as automatically good, and a high stock turnover as automatically good. Both have a “too high” side.
Watch out

If you remember only six mistakes for the night before the paper, remember these six: sales-for-COGS, prepaid-in-quick, PAT-for-ROCE, capital-without-reserves, no-average-when-opening-given, current-ratio-2-means-CA-minus-CL-equals-2.

13. Memory tricks for the whole chapter

11. Memory trick

Three buckets: BS–BS structure, P&L–P&L margin, P&L–BS speed-or-return. Liquidity staircase: current (trust stock) → quick (drop stock and prepaid) → cash (already money). Ideals 2 : 1, 1 : 1, 0.5 : 1. Solvency: outsiders over owners (D/E); owners over the pie (proprietary); fixed-charge over equity (gearing); FA over long money (should be under 1). Margins staircase down the P&L: GP, then operating, then net. Operating ratio is the cost twin of operating profit%; they add to 100. Turnover = a flow over an average stock. Days = 365 / times. Stock at cost (COGS), debtors from credit sales, creditors from credit purchases. Matching rule: whoever is in the denominator must not already have been paid in the numerator. CE includes lenders → EBIT. Equity is owners → PAT. EPS is ₹ per share, not %. Shares = capital / face. Reconstruction: ratio is a k, WC is a rupee difference; two equations. GP% complement gives COGS/Sales.

15. Practice set with solutions

Do each question on paper before you open the solution. Copy the four-line working (formula, figures, arithmetic, answer with unit). Questions 1–2 are Easy, 3–5 Moderate, 6–8 Exam-level. Question 8 is a full Kaveri-style comment from a different company, so you cannot copy section 9.

Practice 7.1 · Easy

Current, quick and cash ratios from a list of assets

From the following, compute current ratio, quick ratio and absolute liquid ratio. Current assets: inventory ₹1,20,000, trade receivables ₹1,80,000, cash ₹80,000, prepaid insurance ₹20,000. Current liabilities: trade payables ₹2,00,000. There are no marketable securities.

Hint. Add CA first. Deduct stock and prepaid for quick. Cash only for absolute liquid.

Answer / solution

Four-line working — the examiner awards marks on each line
Line of workingWhat you write in the answer booklet
1. FormulaCR = CA/CL; QR = (CA − inv − prepaid)/CL; Cash = (cash + mkt sec)/CL
2. Figures pickedCA = ₹1,20,000 + ₹1,80,000 + ₹80,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹4,00,000. CL = ₹2,00,000. Quick assets = ₹4,00,000 − ₹1,20,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹2,60,000.
3. Arithmetic (nothing skipped)CR = ₹4,00,000 ÷ ₹2,00,000 = 2. QR = ₹2,60,000 ÷ ₹2,00,000 = 2,60,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 1.3. Cash ratio = ₹80,000 ÷ ₹2,00,000 = 0.40.
4. Answer with unitCurrent 2 : 1; Quick 1.3 : 1; Cash 0.40 : 1

If you jump from the formula to a final number, you lose method marks when the arithmetic slips.

Comment. Current is at ideal. Quick is above 1 : 1 (prepaid was correctly dropped — leaving it in would have given 1.4). Cash is a little under 0.5 : 1, so the firm leans on debtors for immediate bills.

Practice 7.2 · Easy

GP, NP and operating ratios

Sales ₹5,00,000, COGS ₹3,50,000, operating expenses ₹50,000, interest ₹20,000, tax ₹20,000. Compute GP ratio, operating profit ratio, operating ratio and NP ratio. Show that operating ratio + operating profit ratio = 100%.

Answer / solution

GP = ₹5,00,000 − ₹3,50,000 = ₹1,50,000.

GP ratio = (1,50,000 ÷ 5,00,000) × 100 = 30%.

EBIT = GP − opex = ₹1,50,000 − ₹50,000 = ₹1,00,000.

Operating profit ratio = (1,00,000 ÷ 5,00,000) × 100 = 20%.

Operating cost = ₹3,50,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹4,00,000.

Operating ratio = (4,00,000 ÷ 5,00,000) × 100 = 80%.

Check: 80% + 20% = 100%.

PAT = EBIT − interest − tax = ₹1,00,000 − ₹20,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹60,000.

NP ratio = (60,000 ÷ 5,00,000) × 100 = 12%.

Answer. GP 30%, OP 20%, operating ratio 80%, NP 12%.

Practice 7.3 · Moderate

Rebuild CA, CL, inventory from ratios

Current ratio 2.5, working capital ₹1,50,000, quick ratio 1.5. Prepaid nil. Find current assets, current liabilities and inventory.

Answer / solution

This is reconstruction Type A (example R1).

CL = x, CA = 2.5x, 2.5x − x = 1.5x = ₹1,50,000, x = ₹1,00,000.

CA = ₹2,50,000, CL = ₹1,00,000.

QA = 1.5 × ₹1,00,000 = ₹1,50,000.

Inventory = ₹2,50,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹1,00,000.

Answer. CA ₹2,50,000, CL ₹1,00,000, inventory ₹1,00,000.

Practice 7.4 · Moderate

GP 20%, stock turnover 5, opening = closing = ₹40,000

Find average stock, COGS, sales, GP and purchases.

Answer / solution

Average stock = ₹40,000 (opening = closing).

COGS = 5 × ₹40,000 = ₹2,00,000.

COGS = 80% of sales, so Sales = ₹2,00,000 ÷ 0.80 = ₹2,50,000.

GP = ₹2,50,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹50,000 = 20% of sales.

Purchases = COGS (stock unchanged) = ₹2,00,000.

Answer. Avg stock ₹40,000, COGS ₹2,00,000, Sales ₹2,50,000, GP ₹50,000, Purchases ₹2,00,000.

Practice 7.5 · Moderate

Stock turnover with unequal opening and closing

GP ratio 20%. Stock turnover 8 times. Opening stock ₹40,000, closing stock ₹60,000. Find COGS, sales, GP and purchases.

Answer / solution

Average stock = (₹40,000 + ₹60,000) ÷ 2 = ₹50,000.

COGS = 8 × ₹50,000 = ₹4,00,000.

Sales = ₹4,00,000 ÷ 0.80 = ₹5,00,000.

GP = ₹1,00,000.

Purchases = ₹4,00,000 + ₹60,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹4,20,000.

Answer. COGS ₹4,00,000, Sales ₹5,00,000, GP ₹1,00,000, Purchases ₹4,20,000.

Practice 7.6 · Exam

ROCE, ROE, EPS and interest coverage from a short extract

Equity share capital (₹10 shares) ₹2,00,000, reserves ₹1,00,000, long-term loan ₹1,00,000. EBIT ₹80,000, interest ₹10,000, tax ₹14,000. Compute capital employed, ROCE, PAT, ROE, number of shares, EPS, interest coverage. Does gearing help the owners? One sentence.

Answer / solution

SF = ₹2,00,000 + ₹1,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.

CE = ₹3,00,000 + ₹1,00,000 = ₹4,00,000.

ROCE = (80,000 ÷ 4,00,000) × 100 = 20%.

PBT = 80,000 − 10,000 = 70,000. PAT = 70,000 − 14,000 = 56,000.

ROE = (56,000 ÷ 3,00,000) × 100 = 18.67% (18.666…%).

Shares = 2,00,000 ÷ 10 = 20,000. EPS = 56,000 ÷ 20,000 = ₹2.80 per share.

Interest coverage = 80,000 ÷ 10,000 = 8 times.

Gearing sentence. ROCE is 20% pre-tax; the loan costs 10,000/1,00,000 = 10% pre-tax, so the extra return on borrowed money accrues to owners — gearing helps. After tax, ROE 18.67% is still a healthy owners’ return, and coverage of 8 times says the help is not reckless.

Answer. CE ₹4,00,000, ROCE 20%, PAT ₹56,000, ROE 18.67%, 20,000 shares, EPS ₹2.80, coverage 8 times. Gearing helps owners.

Practice 7.7 · Exam

Debtors and creditors days, with a cash-cycle comment

Credit sales ₹6,00,000, opening debtors ₹40,000, closing debtors ₹60,000. Credit purchases ₹3,60,000, opening creditors ₹30,000, closing creditors ₹50,000. Compute debtors turnover, collection period, creditors turnover, payment period (365 days). Holding period of stock is given as 40 days. Comment on the cash cycle in two sentences.

Answer / solution

Avg debtors = (40,000 + 60,000) ÷ 2 = ₹50,000.

Debtors turnover = 6,00,000 ÷ 50,000 = 12 times.

Collection period = 365 ÷ 12 = 30.416… = 30.42 days.

Avg creditors = (30,000 + 50,000) ÷ 2 = ₹40,000.

Creditors turnover = 3,60,000 ÷ 40,000 = 9 times.

Payment period = 365 ÷ 9 = 40.555… = 40.56 days.

Cash cycle ≈ 40 + 30.42 − 40.56 = 29.86 days.

Comment. The firm collects in about 30 days and pays in about 41 days, so customers fund themselves 11 days before suppliers are paid. Adding 40 days of stock, the net cycle is about 30 days of the firm’s own working capital — a manageable cycle, not a trap.

Answer. DTO 12 times, ACP 30.42 days, CTO 9 times, APP 40.56 days, cash cycle ≈ 30 days.

Practice 7.8 · Exam

A different company — pick, compute, comment (do not copy Kaveri)

Hemavati Stores Ltd, year ended 31 March 2026. Sales ₹8,00,000 (all credit). GP ratio 25%. Opening stock ₹50,000, closing stock ₹70,000. Operating expenses ₹80,000. Interest ₹20,000. Tax ₹25,000. Equity share capital ₹2,00,000 (₹10 shares), reserves ₹1,00,000, long-term loan ₹2,00,000, trade payables ₹1,00,000. Closing debtors ₹80,000 (opening not given — use closing and state the assumption). Cash ₹50,000. Prepaid nil.

Compute: COGS, GP, EBIT, PAT, CA, total assets, CE, WC; then current ratio, quick ratio, debt-equity, GP ratio (check), NP ratio, stock turnover, debtors turnover, ROCE, ROE, EPS, interest coverage. End with a 4-sentence health comment.

Answer / solution

Build the figures.

GP = 25% × ₹8,00,000 = ₹2,00,000. COGS = ₹8,00,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹6,00,000.

EBIT = ₹2,00,000 − ₹80,000 = ₹1,20,000.

PBT = 1,20,000 − 20,000 = 1,00,000. PAT = 1,00,000 − 25,000 = ₹75,000.

CA = stock 70,000 + debtors 80,000 + cash 50,000 = ₹2,00,000.

SF = 2,00,000 + 1,00,000 = ₹3,00,000. CE = 3,00,000 + 2,00,000 = ₹5,00,000.

WC = 2,00,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹1,00,000.

FA = CE − WC = 5,00,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹4,00,000. TA = FA + CA = 4,00,000 + 2,00,000 = ₹6,00,000.

Check BS: SF 3,00,000 + LTD 2,00,000 + CL 1,00,000 = 6,00,000 = TA.

Ratios.

Current = 2,00,000/1,00,000 = 2 : 1. Quick = (2,00,000 − 70,000)/1,00,000 = 1.3 : 1.

Debt-equity = 2,00,000/3,00,000 = 0.67 : 1.

GP ratio given 25% (check: 2,00,000/8,00,000 × 100 = 25%). NP = 75,000/8,00,000 × 100 = 9.375%.

Avg stock = (50,000 + 70,000) ÷ 2 = 60,000. Stock turnover = 6,00,000/60,000 = 10 times. Holding = 365/10 = 36.5 days.

Debtors turnover (closing used as proxy): 8,00,000/80,000 = 10 times. Collection = 36.5 days. Assumption written.

ROCE = 1,20,000/5,00,000 × 100 = 24%. ROE = 75,000/3,00,000 × 100 = 25%.

Shares = 2,00,000/10 = 20,000. EPS = 75,000/20,000 = ₹3.75.

Interest coverage = 1,20,000/20,000 = 6 times.

Health comment. Hemavati is liquid (current 2 : 1, quick 1.3 : 1). Solvency is moderate rather than conservative — debt-equity 0.67 is still under 1 and interest is covered 6 times, so the extra debt is serviceable. Profitability is strong: GP 25%, net 9.4%, ROCE 24% (well above the 10% coupon on the loan) and ROE 25%, which is slightly above ROCE-after-tax and shows gearing helping owners. Efficiency is brisk — stock and debtors both turn 10 times (36.5 days) — and EPS is ₹3.75. Watch-out: opening debtors were not given, so collection days rest on a closing-only assumption; and a 0.67 debt-equity leaves less unused debt capacity than Kaveri had. Overall, a profitable, liquid trader using moderate gearing well.

Practice 7.9 · Easy

Identify the ratio

Name the ratio (and the bucket) for each trigger:

  1. The paper gives CA, CL and asks “short-term solvency”.
  2. The paper uses the words “acid test”.
  3. “Overall profitability of long-term funds”.
  4. “How quickly stock sells”.
  5. GP 25% of sales, find leftover after COGS as a %.
  6. PAT, 50,000 shares, preference dividend nil.
  7. EBIT ₹1,50,000, interest ₹30,000, “ability to pay interest”.
  8. Current ratio 2.5 and WC ₹1,50,000, find CA.

Answer / solution

  1. Current ratio — BS / liquidity.
  2. Quick ratio — BS / liquidity.
  3. ROCE = EBIT/CE — Combined / profitability.
  4. Inventory turnover (COGS/avg stock) — Combined / efficiency.
  5. GP ratio — Revenue / profitability.
  6. EPS — Combined / profitability per share.
  7. Interest coverage — Combined (solvency companion) / 5 times if the figures are Kaveri’s.
  8. Reconstruction Type A: CL = 1,00,000, CA = 2,50,000.

16. Theory questions (write these from memory)

8

What is ratio analysis? Explain its need and importance. (8 marks)

12. Exam-ready answer

Ratio analysis is the computation, comparison and interpretation of arithmetical relationships between figures in the financial statements. It is needed because raw rupee totals of two years or two firms cannot be compared when size differs. Importance: (1) intra-firm trend comparison, (2) inter-firm benchmarking, (3) diagnosis of liquidity, solvency, profitability and efficiency, (4) simplification of bulky statements into a few indicators, (5) help to management for control, (6) help to lenders and investors for credit and investment decisions, (7) a base for forecasting. Ratios must be read against a benchmark and with their limitations.

8

State the limitations of ratio analysis. (8 marks)

12. Exam-ready answer

Ratios use historical data and may not continue. Management may window-dress year-end figures. Different accounting policies (stock, depreciation) destroy comparability. A ratio has no meaning in isolation and needs a benchmark. Qualitative factors are ignored. Inflation mixes old costs with current revenues. Year-end figures may be seasonal. A ratio identifies a symptom, not a cause. Therefore ratios must be read together, over several years, with notes and cash-flow information.

5

Classify ratios as Balance Sheet, Revenue and Combined, with two examples of each. (5 marks)

12. Exam-ready answer

Classification is by the source of the two figures. Balance Sheet ratios use two BS positions — e.g. current ratio, debt-equity. Revenue ratios use two P&L flows — e.g. gross profit ratio, operating ratio. Combined ratios use one flow and one position — e.g. inventory turnover, ROCE. This is different from the purpose classification into liquidity, solvency, profitability and efficiency.

5

Distinguish between current ratio and quick ratio. (5 marks)

12. Exam-ready answer

Both are Balance Sheet liquidity ratios with current liabilities in the denominator. Current ratio uses all current assets, including inventory and prepaid, and has a conventional ideal of 2 : 1. Quick (acid-test) ratio uses only quick assets = CA − inventory − prepaid, and has a conventional ideal of 1 : 1. Current ratio trusts stock; the acid test does not, because stock may be slow or overvalued and prepaid will not pay a creditor. A firm can look liquid on the current ratio and illiquid on the quick ratio when most CA is stock.

5

Distinguish between ROCE and ROE. (5 marks)

12. Exam-ready answer

ROCE = EBIT / Capital employed × 100. It is the return on the whole long-term pool (equity + long-term debt), before interest and tax, and is used to compare firms with different gearing. ROE = PAT / Equity shareholders’ funds × 100. It is the return on owners’ money only, after interest and tax. Matching rule: whoever is in the denominator must not already have been paid in the numerator. ROCE answers “how well did the business use long-term funds?”. ROE answers “how well did owners do?”. If ROE exceeds after-tax ROCE, gearing is helping owners; the reverse means gearing is hurting.

5

Operating ratio and operating profit ratio. (5 marks)

12. Exam-ready answer

Both are Revenue ratios with sales in the denominator. Operating ratio = operating cost / sales × 100, where operating cost = COGS + operating expenses (interest and tax excluded). Operating profit ratio = EBIT / sales × 100. They are cost and profit twins: when other income is nil, they add to 100%. A rising operating ratio is a cost warning; a rising operating profit ratio is an operations improvement. A common error is to include interest in operating cost, which breaks the 100% identity.

5

What is capital gearing? When is a firm said to be high geared? (5 marks)

12. Exam-ready answer

Capital gearing is the mix of fixed-charge funds (preference share capital + long-term debt) and equity shareholders’ funds. In the common MBA version, capital gearing = (preference + LTD) / equity funds. A firm is high geared when this ratio exceeds 1 (fixed-charge funds exceed equity) and low geared when it is less than 1. High gearing magnifies equity earnings in good years and magnifies losses in bad years. If the paper prints the inverted formula, high/low follows that formula — always read the printed version.

3

Why is COGS preferred to sales in stock turnover? (3 marks)

12. Exam-ready answer

Inventory is valued at cost. COGS is also at cost. Dividing a cost flow by a cost stock is consistent. Sales are at selling price; Sales / average stock mixes two valuations and overstates turnover by the GP margin. Use the sales version only when the paper prints it or when COGS cannot be built.

Connect the chapters

You now have the full analytical toolkit of this paper: the statements (Ch 4, Ch 6), the cash-flow story (Ch 5), and the ratio language (this chapter). In the exam, a 20-mark analysis question is almost always: compute a short set, then write the four-beat comment (liquidity, solvency, profitability, efficiency) plus one watch-out. That is the whole chapter, used as a professional uses it.

Chapter A

Master Formula Sheet

Learning outcome. Every formula you need in the examination, in one place. Know what each symbol means before you memorise.

What this chapter covers (official syllabus)

  • Accounting equation
  • Inventory (FIFO, WAM, COGS)
  • Depreciation SLM & WDV
  • Company accounts workings
  • Cash flow derivations
  • All ratios

Copy this sheet once into your rough notes. In the hall, write the formula first, then substitute, then compute. Marks are often given for the formula even if arithmetic slips.

1. Accounting equation

Formula

Assets = Liabilities + Capital

Formula

Assets = Liabilities + Opening capital + Profit − Loss − Drawings + Additional capital

Profit = Revenue − Expenses. Drawings reduce capital, they are not a business expense.

Formula

Closing capital = Opening capital + Additional capital + Profit − Drawings

2. Inventory and trading

Formula

Cost of goods sold (COGS) = Opening stock + Purchases + Direct expenses − Closing stock

Formula

Gross profit = Sales − COGS   (or Sales + Closing stock − Opening stock − Purchases − Direct expenses)

Formula

Net profit = Gross profit + Other income − Indirect expenses

FIFO

Rule. Issues are taken from the oldest layer still in stock. Closing stock is the latest layers that remain.

Formula

Closing stock (FIFO) = remaining quantity in each leftover layer × that layer’s purchase cost

Formula

COGS (FIFO) = cost of layers issued  |  Check: Opening cost + Purchases cost = COGS + Closing stock

Weighted average (WAM)

Formula

Weighted average cost = Total cost of units on hand ÷ Total units on hand

Perpetual / moving average (usual exam method): recompute the average after every purchase. Issues go out at the average then ruling. Do not recompute on an issue.

Periodic average: one average for the whole period using opening + all purchases, then closing quantity × that average.

Formula

Unit check: Opening qty + Purchases qty − Issues qty = Closing qty

3. Depreciation

Formula

Depreciable amount = Cost − Residual (scrap) value

Cost includes purchase price, non-refundable taxes, freight inward, and installation needed to bring the asset to use.

Straight Line Method (SLM) / Original cost / Fixed instalment

Formula

Annual depreciation = (Cost − Residual) ÷ Useful life in years

Formula

SLM rate on original cost = (Annual depreciation ÷ Cost) × 100

Formula

Part-year depreciation = Annual depreciation × (Months of use ÷ 12)

Written Down Value (WDV) / Diminishing / Reducing balance

Formula

Depreciation for the year = Book value at the start of the period × Rate

Formula

Part-year WDV = Cost (or WDV) × Rate × (Months of use ÷ 12)

Formula

Optional WDV rate if life and scrap are given: R = 1 − (Scrap ÷ Cost)1/n

MBA papers almost always give the rate. Do not invent a rate.

Sale of asset

Formula

Net book value (NBV) on sale date = Cost − Accumulated depreciation till date of sale

Formula

Profit on sale = Sale proceeds − NBV   |   Loss on sale = NBV − Sale proceeds

4. Company accounts workings

Formula

Revenue from operations + Other income = Total income

Formula

Profit before tax = Total income − Total expenses ± Exceptional items

Formula

Profit after tax = Profit before tax − Tax expense

Formula

Changes in inventories = Opening inventory − Closing inventory (a positive figure is an expense)

Formula

Manager’s commission on profit after commission = Profit before commission × Rate ÷ (100 + Rate)

If the question says ‘on profit before commission’, just multiply profit × rate.

Formula

Trade receivables (net) = Gross receivables − Provision for doubtful debts

Formula

PPE (net) = Gross cost − Accumulated depreciation

Formula

Shareholders’ funds = Share capital + Reserves and surplus − Fictitious assets if any

Formula

New provision for doubtful debts = Required % × Debtors (after writing off further bad debts)

Formula

If an old provision already exists: P&L charge (or credit) = New provision − Old provision + Fresh bad debts

5. Cash flow (indirect method) — derivations

Formula

Net increase in cash = Operating (A) + Investing (B) + Financing (C)

Formula

Closing cash & cash equivalents = Opening + Net increase (must equal the Balance Sheet)

Formula

Tax paid = Opening tax provision + Current tax charged − Closing tax provision (adjust for prepaid tax if given)

Formula

Dividend paid = Opening proposed/unpaid dividend + Dividend declared − Closing unpaid dividend

Formula

Purchase of PPE (if missing) : Opening cost + Purchases − Cost of asset sold = Closing cost

Formula

Depreciation for the year (if missing): Opening accum. dep. + Dep. charged − Accum. dep. on asset sold = Closing accum. dep.

Formula

Sale proceeds of PPE = NBV of asset sold ± Profit/Loss on sale

6. Ratio analysis

Balance Sheet ratios (both figures from the Balance Sheet)

Formula

Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities

Formula

Quick (acid-test) ratio = (Current assets − Inventory − Prepaid expenses) ÷ Current liabilities

Formula

Absolute liquid / cash ratio = (Cash + Cash equivalents + Marketable securities) ÷ Current liabilities

Formula

Debt–equity ratio = Long-term debt ÷ Shareholders’ funds

Formula

Proprietary ratio = Shareholders’ funds ÷ Total assets

Formula

Capital gearing ratio = (Preference capital + Long-term debt) ÷ Equity shareholders’ funds

Formula

Fixed assets to long-term funds = Net fixed assets ÷ (Shareholders’ funds + Long-term debt)

Formula

Current assets to proprietary funds = Current assets ÷ Shareholders’ funds

Revenue ratios (both figures from the P&L)

Formula

Gross profit ratio = (Gross profit ÷ Revenue from operations) × 100

Formula

Net profit ratio = (Profit after tax ÷ Revenue from operations) × 100

Formula

Operating profit ratio = (Operating profit (EBIT) ÷ Revenue from operations) × 100

Formula

Operating ratio = (COGS + Operating expenses) ÷ Revenue from operations × 100

Formula

Expense ratio = (Particular expense ÷ Revenue from operations) × 100

Combined ratios (P&L figure with a Balance Sheet figure)

Formula

Inventory turnover = COGS ÷ Average inventory

Formula

Average inventory = (Opening inventory + Closing inventory) ÷ 2

Formula

Inventory holding period (days) = 365 ÷ Inventory turnover

Formula

Debtors turnover = Credit sales ÷ Average trade receivables

Formula

Average collection period = 365 ÷ Debtors turnover

Formula

Creditors turnover = Credit purchases ÷ Average trade payables

Formula

Average payment period = 365 ÷ Creditors turnover

Formula

Working capital turnover = Revenue from operations ÷ Working capital

Formula

Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities

Formula

Fixed asset turnover = Revenue from operations ÷ Net fixed assets

Formula

Capital turnover = Revenue from operations ÷ Capital employed

Formula

Capital employed = Shareholders’ funds + Long-term debt (or Net fixed assets + Working capital)

Formula

ROCE = (EBIT ÷ Capital employed) × 100

Formula

ROE = (Profit after tax ÷ Equity shareholders’ funds) × 100

Formula

Return on assets = (PAT ÷ Total assets) × 100

Formula

EPS = Profit after tax (less preference dividend) ÷ Number of equity shares

Formula

Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest

Exam tip

If opening figures are not given, use closing balances for turnover ratios and write the assumption. Never mix a % ratio with a ‘times’ ratio without stating the unit.

7. Step-by-step method (exam procedure)
  1. Read the sentence. Underline the two (or more) things that changed.
  2. Name the accounts in textbook language (not ‘the guy we buy from’ — Creditor / Kabir A/c).
  3. Classify each: asset, liability, capital, income, expense.
  4. Ask: did it increase or decrease?
  5. Apply the modern table. One account is debited, one is credited (compound if more).
  6. Amounts on both sides must be equal.
  7. Write a narration in brackets: (Being …).

10. Common mistakes
  • Debiting cash when cash comes in is correct; students often reverse cash because they think ‘credit means money in’ from banking language. Bank language ≠ accounting language.
  • Buying furniture is not Purchases. Purchases = goods in which the firm trades.
  • Drawings are not an expense. They never appear in the P&L as a cost.
  • A company has no drawings account in the owner sense.
  • Outstanding expense is a liability, not an asset. Prepaid is an asset, not an expense of this year.
